title: AI, Tariffs & a New FedEx CFO: November Supply Chain Moves

AI, Tariffs & a New FedEx CFO: November Supply Chain Moves
Prioritise Us
on Google
Jamere Jackson will be joining FedEx on November 30.
FedEx hires AutoZone’s CFO, Maersk bets on customs expertise as tariffs bite and Danone names a new US president to oversee operations
Jamere Jackson, FedEx
Jamere Jackson will be starting his new role at FedEx, joining the company as EVP and CFO, effective November 30. Throughout his career, he has used strong financial management and precise capital allocation in order to develop business growth. Upon joining the global logistics company, Jamere will be working to support FedEx's profitable growth strategy and deliver long-term value.
I am pleased to welcome Jamere to FedEx and the executive leadership team. Jamere brings a deep understanding of how disciplined financial strategy translates into strong operational performance.
Raj Subramaniam, President and Chief Executive Officer of FedEx Corporation
Kevin Shoemaker
Kevin Shoemaker has joined A.P. Moller - Maersk as Regional Head of Global Trade and Customs Consulting (GTCC) NAM
Kevin is joining Maersk, bringing more than 20 years of experience to the job. In this role, he will be making use of his knowledge in customs and trade tech products, alongside tariff management, optimisation and upstream trade compliance. Kevin has a strong understanding of supply chain risk, global trade management and AI.
Today, I'm excited to share the next step in my journey: I'm joining A.P. Moller - Maersk as Regional Head of Global Trade & Customs Consulting (GTCC) for North America. The timing couldn't be better. Tariffs and shifting trade regulations have turned customs from a back-office function into a board-level issue. Importers are facing higher and less predictable duties, more complex rules of origin and growing enforcement risk.
Kevin Shoemaker, Regional Head of Global Trade and Customs Consulting (GTCC) NAM at A.P. Moller - Maersk
Francois Lacombe, Danone
Francois Lacombe has taken on the role of President of Danone USA
Francois has spent his almost 30-year career at Danone working in various countries around the world, including Argentina, Mexico, Colombia and Amsterdam. Now, he is returning to the US as President of Danone USA. He will be bringing his rich career experience of operating with trusted brands and innovative strategies in order to lead the US branch of the company.
I’m ready to hit the ground running alongside our US teams, to listen and learn from our consumers and customers, and to keep growing a business that can make a real difference to people’s health.
Francois Lacombe, President of Danone USA
Ralf Finzel, ADM
Ralf Finzel is joining ADM in a new career move
Ralf Finzel has joined ADM, a global agricultural supply chain manager and processor, empowering across beverages, biofuels, home care and pet treats. Ralf is joining from his four-year career at IFF, and brings more than 23 years of experience working within the supply chain at Honeywell. In his new role, he is leading the nutrition team and working to strengthen ADM's end-to-end supply chain capabilities.
I am honored to be part of the Nutrition leadership team and look forward to working with colleagues across the global business to strengthen our end-to-end supply chain capabilities, support growth, and create value for our customers and stakeholders.
Ralf Finzel, President, Nutrition E2E Supply Chain at ADM
Julie Tracy Lockwood, Genpact
Julie Tracy Lockwood has joined the team at Genpact
Julie is bringing her 15+ years of experience to Genpact, following an extensive career history of driving global go-to-market strategies, operational transformation and leadership. Much of her focus is on bringing data maturity, AI and generative AI to business processes, working as a Professor in Emerging Technologies at the University of Colorado. In her new role at Genpact, Julie will be leveraging AI and ensuring seamless collaboration between humans and technology.
I’m happy to share that I’m starting a new position as VP and Partner Supply Chain, Order Management LifeSciences at Genpact!
Julie Tracy Lockwood, VP and Partner Supply Chain, Order Management LifeSciences at Genpact
Zara Ward, Baringa
Zara Ward, Manager at Baringa
Following a six-year career at Deecon, Zara is bringing her experience to the supply chain and procurement team at Baringa. Her experience focuses on programme delivery, procurement and commercial strategy, overseeing the end-to-end delivery of complex projects. With an emphasis on relationship building and trust across cross-functional teams, Zara has led many effective transformation initiatives.
I'm looking forward to combining my existing procurement and commercial experience with new perspectives, new challenges and opportunities to create meaningful impact for clients.
Zara Ward, Manager at Baringa
Ian A. Arroyo, Accenture
Ian A. Arroyo, Managing Director at Accenture
For more than 20 years, Ian has worked within global logistics, technology and corporate growth leading strategy. In his roles, he has helped enterprise leaders as they scale and unlock measurable operating outcomes through complex strategies. In his new role at Accenture, Ian is leading Logistics, Transportation & Fulfillment (LTF) transformation, partnering with C-suite and senior supply chain leaders to scale next-generation supply chain networks.
I’m happy to share that I’m starting a new position as Managing Director, Logistics, Transportation, and Fulfillment at Accenture!

title: CATL explores lithium-air batteries as a long-term research focus - electrive.com
content:
CATL is considering lithium-air batteries as a long-term research option. The technology theoretically promises a significantly higher energy density than today's lithium-ion batteries. However, it is still far from market-ready vehicle batteries or a range of 2,000 km.
SNE Research estimates CATL's market share outside China at 33.7 percent.
Image: CATL
CATL Chief Scientist Wu Kai has positioned lithium-air batteries as a long-term research focus for the company at the
Equipment Powerhouse Forum 2026
. Sodium-ion and solid-state technologies remain closer to commercialisation at CATL. Current attention is primarily drawn to the potential for ranges of up to 2,000 km. The basis for such projections is the very high theoretical specific energy of lithium-air chemistry, at around 3,505 Wh/kg. However, this value describes the electrochemical potential of the reaction, not the energy density of a complete vehicle battery.
The difference from conventional lithium-ion cells lies in the structure. Lithium-air systems use metallic lithium as the negative electrode and oxygen from the surrounding environment as the reaction partner. During discharge, lithium peroxide forms in a porous cathode; during charging, the reaction is reversed, and oxygen is released again.
Because the oxygen does not need to be carried as a traditional cathode material within the battery, this theoretically results in a very high specific energy. However, for a real battery system, electrolyte, electrodes, housing, protective systems, and – above all – components for air processing must be added. Even higher theoretical values of around 12,000 Wh/kg are based on calculations that exclude the mass of the required oxygen.
The gap between theoretical energy density and a production-ready vehicle battery is significant, as demonstrated by current laboratory results. In 2024, researchers from Jilin University and the Chinese Academy of Sciences achieved 757.5 Wh/kg and 241 charge cycles with a lithium-air pouch cell under defined laboratory conditions.
CATL’s lithium-air Batteries still face challenges
Another approach comes from Argonne National Laboratory and the Illinois Institute of Technology. A
solid-state lithium-air cell
introduced in 2023 completed at least 1,000 charge and discharge cycles at room temperature. The architecture used was said to have a theoretical potential of around 1,200 Wh/kg. Both results show progress but are not equivalent to a validated battery for production vehicles.
A central challenge remains the air supply. The battery requires oxygen, while moisture and carbon dioxide must be reliably kept out. Both substances can cause unwanted chemical reactions, damaging electrodes and electrolytes. A vehicle would therefore need a controlled air supply system with filtration and humidity management. This peripheral equipment, in turn, increases weight, space requirements, and energy consumption. Additional unresolved or only partially solved issues include cycle stability, charging efficiency, and the stability of the lithium-metal anode.
The reaction products in the cathode are also problematic. Lithium peroxide can deposit in the pores, hindering oxygen transport. During charging, it must be completely removed without side reactions damaging the electrolyte or electrodes.
A high specific energy alone is not sufficient for use in electric vehicles. Volumetric energy density, power output, fast-charging capability, safety, lifespan, and the weight of the overall system are also decisive. The frequently cited 2,000 km cannot, therefore, currently be applied to a concrete vehicle.
CATL is simultaneously pursuing significantly more market-ready technologies. Sodium-ion batteries and solid-state cells are much further along in the company’s development roadmap. At the same time, CATL is already the clear market leader with established lithium-ion systems. According to SNE Research, the company installed 143.7 GWh of battery capacity outside China in the first nine months of 2026, achieving a market share of 33.7 per cent.
The current trend towards LFP also shows how strongly the battery market is evolving with already available cell chemistries. According to
SNE Research
, the LFP share of the market outside China increased from 15.8 to 27.7 per cent within a year. Chinese manufacturers, in particular, are benefiting from this development.
The technology remains a long-term research option for CATL. Whether it will eventually lead to electric vehicles with four-digit ranges depends less on the theoretical energy density and more on whether the numerous chemical and technical challenges can be resolved in a long-lasting, safe, and affordable battery system.

title: BYD considers building a battery factory in Portugal - electrive.com
content:
BYD is reportedly considering building a battery factory in Portugal - potentially at the former Galp refinery in Matosinhos near Porto. It remains unclear whether battery cells or complete battery systems would be manufactured there. Such a battery factory would align well with a potential BYD car factory in Spain.
BYD battery production in Chongqing, China (archive image)
Image: BYD
Chinese electric vehicle and battery manufacturer BYD is reportedly considering building a battery factory in Portugal. According to the Portuguese business newspaper
Expresso
, the company is already in discussions with the Portuguese government and the national trade and investment agency AICEP (Agência para o Investimento e Comércio Externo de Portugal) regarding a potential investment. The former oil refinery site of Portuguese energy company Galp in Matosinhos, near Porto, is being considered as a possible location. A source familiar with the matter states that the project is already relatively advanced.
However, there has been no official confirmation from BYD to date. Portugal’s Minister of Economy, Manuel Castro Almeida, merely confirmed a “fruitful dialogue” with a Chinese automaker regarding the establishment of a plant in Portugal, without providing further details. The city administration of Matosinhos also states that it has not yet been formally informed about the project. Nevertheless, Mayor Luísa Salgueiro described such an investment as a “very welcome project”.
Former refinery site as potential location
The former Galp refinery in Matosinhos was closed in 2021. The approximately 240-hectare site near the Atlantic is currently being dismantled. Of this, 100 hectares have already been transferred to the city administration. A 40-hectare site is planned for the University of Porto, while another 20 hectares are set to become a park. The remaining areas do not yet have a designated use. According to Galp, the ongoing demolition work is expected to be completed by the end of 2026, followed by further soil remediation measures.
The location’s advantages include its proximity to the Port of Leixões and excellent transport links. Additionally, the planned lithium extraction at the Barroso mine in northern Portugal is set to begin production in 2028. A battery factory in Matosinhos could therefore benefit from shorter transport routes for some of the required raw materials in the future.
No details yet on the type of battery production
It remains unclear exactly what BYD intends to produce in Portugal. Current reports only refer to a battery factory in general terms. Whether the focus will be on the production of battery cells, the manufacturing of modules, and/or the assembly of complete battery packs is not yet known. BYD has the expertise for all these production steps: the company develops and manufactures its own lithium iron phosphate (LFP) cells as well as the associated battery systems.
The second generation Blade battery
A key in-house development is the so-called Blade Battery. Introduced in 2020 and now in
its second generation
, this battery technology is based on particularly long, flat LFP cells that resemble sword blades due to their shape. BYD uses a cell-to-pack concept, where the cells are integrated directly into the battery pack without traditional intermediate modules. This saves space and increases pack efficiency. The Blade Battery is used in numerous electric vehicles and plug-in hybrids from the manufacturer. BYD is thus not only an automaker but also an established cell producer with its own battery technology and manufacturing expertise.
Potential battery hub for the Iberian Peninsula
According to information from
Expresso
, the potential factory could serve as a production hub for the entire Iberian Peninsula. This would also include a
potential future car factory for BYD in Spain
. The Chinese manufacturer is already evaluating additional sites in Europe for expanded production capacity. Besides Spain, France is also being considered as a potential location for further investments. In Hungary, BYD is already constructing its first European passenger car plant in Szeged.
Meanwhile, Portugal is actively seeking investments in the battery industry. Chinese cell manufacturer
CALB is already planning a battery factory in Sines
. This project involves an investment of around two billion euros and a planned production capacity of 15 GWh per year. With a potential second major battery investment, Portugal could further strengthen its position within the European value chain for electric vehicles.
However, it remains uncertain whether BYD will indeed invest in Matosinhos. No details have yet been provided regarding the potential investment amount, production capacity, or number of jobs.

title: 96% of battery value sits after the mine, this week the race moved downstream - Batteries News
content:
96% of battery value sits after the mine, this week the race moved downstream – Lithium supply grows, but the real money is in making the battery
Welcome to BatteriesNews: the battery market in five minutes. Cells, materials, storage, gigafactories and M&A, with the insight behind every headline.
📣 SPONSOR ALERT – this spot is available to showcase your brand and solutions across our network of battery industry decision makers. Book it today,
send us an email
⚡ The 60-Second Brief
Lithium supply keeps growing.
Rio Tinto opened $1.4 billion of lithium projects in Argentina, adding 25,000 tonnes of annual capacity, and LibertyStream signed to supply up to 17,500 tonnes of US-made lithium carbonate to a cathode maker.
But the value is downstream.
Australia’s CSIRO says 96% of battery revenue sits after mining, and points to two practical first steps: aluminium cell cans and copper foil.
Manufacturing know-how is now for sale.
LG’s production engineering arm, which has built 260+ battery lines including 76 in the US, is offering turnkey lines to North American manufacturers.
The lead: everyone has lithium, few can make batteries
This week’s stories add up to one message: the battery race is shifting from digging to making.
More lithium is coming:
Rio Tinto
opened its Fénix 1B expansion and new Sal de Vida operation in Catamarca, Argentina, with President Milei in attendance. Combined investment: about $1.4 billion. Capacity: 25,000 tonnes LCE a year once ramped. Both reached first production ahead of plan. Rio targets 200,000 tonnes LCE by 2028.
LibertyStream
will supply 500 tonnes of US-origin lithium carbonate in 2027 to an unnamed cathode maker serving the US, with binding terms for 17,000 more tonnes through 2031. It extracts lithium from Texas oilfield brine. But it still needs to build and finance the capacity to deliver.
But that’s not where the money is:
says 96% of the battery revenue opportunity sits downstream of mining, yet Australia exports most of its minerals. Its two practical first steps: prismatic cell cans made from Australian aluminium, and electrodeposited copper foil (about 6 microns thick) using local copper refining skills.
LG Electronics’ Production Engineering Research Institute
has supported 260+ battery lines globally, 76 in the US, and appointed Ratel Consulting to sell turnkey lines in North America, starting with module and pack.
Ratel’s founder put it plainly: the hard part is not building a plant, it’s ramping it to hit yield, quality and throughput.
→ Why it matters:
Lithium is getting easier to secure. Ramping a factory isn’t. The winners in the next phase will be the countries and companies that can turn raw materials into reliable components and running lines. That’s why LG is now selling its experience, and why Australia is starting with cans and foil, not full cells.
🔢 Number of the Week: 96%
🚗 EV & MOBILITY
Mercedes-Benz
shows a battery Power Converter.
Programmable micro-converters control energy flow from individual cells, delivering a steady output of up to 800V regardless of each cell’s charge or age. The current version handles up to 3 kW and supports AC/DC and bidirectional charging.
High voltage no longer depends on how many cells are wired in series; software sets it instead.
→ Why it matters:
If voltage is set by software, pack design gets more flexible and a few weak cells no longer limit the whole pack. Still research, not production.
targets two-wheelers at EICMA.
Its battery-swapping network in Africa has completed 17 million swaps over 2.5 years, with each pack averaging over 1,000 cycles.
New off-road cells use high-nickel cathodes and silicon-carbon anodes; its tabless design cuts internal resistance by 80%.
🔋 STORAGE & SECOND LIFE
EDENenergy
turns used e-scooter batteries into industrial storage.
The Fraunhofer ISE spin-off delivered its first 70 kWh system in October, built from 112 second-life e-scooter batteries.
Germany discards about one million e-bike and e-scooter batteries a year. Of the first 350 tested, many still had well over 90% capacity, beating the 80% expected.
Modules can be swapped while running, so the system holds 70 kWh even after 10 years. Next step: 300 kWh systems.
→ Why it matters:
Micromobility batteries are an untapped second-life source, but each brand uses different connectors and software. Standard protocols and second-life rules will decide whether this scales.
🧪 MATERIALS & SOLID STATE
ISU Specialty Chemical
and Ares Materials team up on solid-state polymers.
ISU, which completed a commercial lithium sulfide plant this year, will produce; Ares will use AI trained on real cell test data to tune formulations.
The goal: when cell specs change, a new formulation becomes an adjustment rather than a restart.
Stryten Energy
brings Trojan batteries to AAPEX.
After acquiring C&D Technologies and Trojan Battery Company, Stryten now offers advanced lead, marine/RV and lithium golf cart batteries under one US-based roof.
🔍 Contrarian Corner
More lithium is coming online just as everyone chases downstream value. That’s good for cell makers, but it raises a question for miners.
Rio Tinto is targeting 200,000 tonnes by 2028, and new players like LibertyStream are signing long-term offtakes. If supply keeps outpacing demand, lithium prices stay low and the margin moves even further down the chain. The CSIRO report is right: the money is in making things. The mines may end up subsidising the factories.
👀 What to Watch
LibertyStream’s long-term agreement:
whether 2028–2031 volumes get finalised and financed.
CSIRO online panel:
November 24, on Australian battery manufacturing.
Rio Tinto ramp-up:
progress at Fénix and Sal de Vida toward 25,000 tonnes.
Second-life rules:
EU and German moves on standards for reusing mobile batteries.

Solidion Technology Reaffirms Commitment to Address Growing Energy Storage Needs of AI Data Centers
Solidion’s patented anode technology and PEAK UPS design target the space, lifespan and cost demands of AI-scale infrastructure.
DALLAS, Oct. 14, 2026 /PRNewswire/ —
Solidion Technology, Inc.
(NASDAQ:
) (“Solidion Technology” or “the Company”), an advanced battery technology solutions provider, today reaffirmed its commitment to address energy storage for artificial intelligence and data center infrastructure, centered on its PEAK Series uninterruptible power supply (UPS) system.
As AI workloads increase the power density of data centers, operators face growing pressure on the systems that keep facilities running during grid disruptions. Uninterruptible power supply (UPS) batteries take up floor space that could otherwise hold AI servers and additional computing equipment, and they require periodic replacement.
Solidion’s approach is built around its PEAK Series, a UPS battery system built for AI data centers using its proprietary 5500 silicon-carbon anode cell, designed for AI data center environments and well positioned to address these evolving requirements.
The Company’s strategy focuses on three priorities:
Energy density and space efficiency:
Based on Company testing, PEAK is designed to reduce UPS footprint by up to 30%, freeing floor space for servers.
Reliability and longevity:
The 5500 cell is designed to last up to three times longer than conventional backup systems, reducing replacement cycles and maintenance. Solidion is focused on advancing technologies intended to support demanding data center operating environments.
Materials-level innovation:
Solidion’s portfolio of +385 patents covering silicon anodes, graphene and next generation battery chemistries, together with its pilot production facility in Dayton, Ohio, gives the Company a U.S. based foundation for developing data center energy storage.
Jaymes Winters,
Chairman and CEO of Solidion, said,
AI infrastructure represents a compelling market for advanced energy storage,
“Our focus is on translating our technology into practical commercial solutions that address real customer demand. We are not betting on which chips win; we are focused on supplying something every data center needs.”
Solidion intends to continue pursuing opportunities to apply its battery technologies directly to end users

title: Data Center Battery Rules Differ by Country - Americase International and OCP Experts Will Tackle the "Compliance Gap" - Batteries News
content:
Data Center Battery Rules Differ by Country – Americase International and OCP Experts Will Tackle the “Compliance Gap”
Oct. 15 OCP Global Summit panel will draw on a January 2026 Open Compute Project white paper to help operators navigate conflicting energy storage codes.
WAXAHACHIE, Texas, Oct. 13, 2026 /PRNewswire/ — Rules for shipping, installing, storing and disposing of data center lithium batteries differ across countries and jurisdictions, and operators are left to reconcile them as AI drives demand growth for battery energy storage systems (ESS). Americase International will address that “compliance gap” in a panel at the 2026 Open Compute Project (OCP) Global Summit, Oct. 12–15 at the San Jose Convention Center, with two Americase International team members participating.
Battery failures in critical infrastructure can have far-reaching consequences. On Sept. 26, 2025, a lithium-ion battery fire at South Korea’s National Information Resources Service data center in Daejeon affected
647 government information systems
, disrupting public services nationwide. Officials said the fire started in an uninterruptible power supply (UPS) battery being relocated during maintenance. The incident shows why consistent rules for handling, relocating and replacing batteries matter as data centers expand their energy storage capabilities.
The Oct. 15 session, “The Compliance Gap: ESS Safety in the Age of AI Infrastructure,” will explore findings from the Open Compute Project’s white paper,
Requirements for Energy Storage Systems Used in Data Centers
Mike Pagel,
Senior Consultant at HazMat Safety Consulting and a contributing author of the white paper, said:
Investment in energy storage for AI data centers is moving faster than the regulations that govern it, and operators often don’t know what they really have until the batteries are tested and classified.
”Too often, they find out when a shipment is held, a permit is delayed or an insurer pushes back. This panel is about replacing guesswork with clear, practical steps teams can act on right away.”
The 25-minute session, part of the OCP Ready™ Facilities / Power & Energy track, will examine how U.S. and international codes governing battery transportation, installation and operation overlap and conflict, whether emerging chemistries such as nickel-zinc should be treated differently from lithium-ion under current codes, and what operators, equipment manufacturers (OEMs) and supply chain partners can do now to identify compliance gaps and reduce risk exposure.
Moderator and Panelists
Joel Chakkalakal (Moderator), Director of Data Centers and Sustainability, Americase, an Americase International company — An active member of the OCP community, Chakkalakal brings expertise in supply chain challenges, regulatory compliance and data center safety.
Mike Pagel, Senior Consultant, HazMat Safety Consulting, an Americase International company — A contributing author of the white paper, Pagel specializes in lithium battery transportation regulations and helped inform the paper’s guidance on dangerous goods transportation, regulatory compliance and lifecycle safety.
Shrikanth “Sri” Venkateshappa, Director of Accounts DACH, Anord Mardix, a Flex company — Venkateshappa was a work stream lead and author of the white paper.
Mauro Leuce, Senior Director, Global Design & Engineering Standards, Digital Realty — A co-author of the white paper, Leuce brings an operator’s perspective on the challenges of deploying and managing energy storage systems across different regulatory environments.
Session Details
Session:
The Compliance Gap: ESS Safety in the Age of AI Infrastructure
OCP Ready™ Facilities / Power & Energy
Thursday, Oct. 15, 2026
8:40–9:05 a.m. PDT
Location:
2026 OCP Global Summit, San Jose Convention Center, Room 210CG, San Jose, Calif.
For additional information about the session, visit Americase International’s
event page.
Frequently Asked Questions
Q: Who should attend this session?
Hyperscale and colocation operators, facilities and fire protection engineers, hardware OEMs, procurement and supply chain leaders, and anyone responsible for permitting, insuring or deploying energy storage at scale.
Q: Does the session cover only U.S. codes?
No. Panelists will address how NFPA 855, the National Fire Protection Association’s standard for installing stationary energy storage systems, is widely adopted by U.S. jurisdictions but is not legally binding in markets such as Germany, Japan or Singapore, and how operators manage differing local requirements across the more than 15 countries profiled in the white paper’s appendix.
Q: Do attendees need to read the OCP white paper beforehand?
No. The panel is designed to make the white paper’s findings accessible without prior familiarity, and the session includes time for audience questions.

title: W L Gore & Associates Launches GORE® Battery Vents – MultiVent Series at the Battery Show - Batteries News
content:
W L Gore & Associates Launches GORE® Battery Vents – MultiVent Series at the Battery Show
The integrated battery vent combines pressure equalization, moisture protection, and resealable thermal-runaway evacuation in a single part, with one opening in the pack wall.
DETROIT, Mich.–(
BUSINESS WIRE
)–Today, W. L. Gore & Associates (Gore) introduced GORE® Battery Vents – MultiVent Series at The Battery Show North America 2026, a new integrated venting architecture that combines all three functions into a single device. Designed for lithium-ion battery packs in electric vehicles and energy storage systems, GORE® MultiVent is an integrated battery vent: one device that equalizes pressure, protects against moisture and evacuates gas during thermal runaway, then reseals. It gives pack designers an alternative to combining dual-stage vents, separate evacuation valves and desiccants.
GORE MultiVent builds on technology Gore acquired from Vernay Laboratories in 2026 and combines Gore membrane expertise with Vernay’s advanced valve technology.
Battery pack designers have traditionally relied on multiple components to manage pressure equalization, moisture ingress, and thermal-runaway evacuation. Every additional component adds validation requirements, sealing complexity, and potential paths for moisture intrusion, which can lead to corrosion, sensor faults, and warranty costs. As packs get larger, these decisions are harder to make in isolation.
GORE MultiVent handles all three functions in a single part mounted through one opening, using two valves and a Gore microporous membrane:
Pressure equalization.
In normal operation, the valve opens at defined pressures which, combined with the membrane, allows the pack to breathe while blocking water, dust and debris. Airflow of 1,200 L/h at 100 mbar pressure – up to six times that of alternative venting options – allows for higher airflow per vent, reducing the number of vents a pack needs.
Moisture protection.
In Gore laboratory testing at 22 °C and 50 percent relative humidity, moisture ingress measured less than 20 mg per day, under one-tenth that of many commercially available dual vents – addressing an inherent venting tradeoff.
Thermal-runaway evacuation.
The larger valve opens at 50 mbar, providing an evacuation flow of 50 L/s at 180 mbar, and then reseals the housing. Gore testing shows MultiVent consistently performs after standard automotive aging tests and can resist typical thermal runaway temperature exposure.
David Slupe,
Strategic Marketing Leader for Batteries at W. L. Gore & Associates, said:
For years, battery pack designers have been forced to balance airflow, moisture control and safety using separate components,
“We think those challenges are connected. GORE MultiVent gives engineers a way to address them together with a simpler architecture. By combining Gore’s decades of experience in venting, moisture management and materials science with Vernay’s valve innovation and expertise, we’re helping customers design safer, more reliable battery systems.”
Gore application engineers work with pack design teams early in a program. Gore’s simulation models have closely matched measured moisture performance in validation testing, which helps customers assess an application before committing to extensive prototype testing.
At The Battery Show North America 2026, Gore will:
Show GORE MultiVent at Booth 6205
(Huntington Place), Oct. 13–15, alongside GORE® Battery Insulation, an ultra-thin insulation that maintains thermal resistance under sustained compression to help stop cell-to-cell propagation.
Compete as a finalist for Battery Pack Innovation of the Year
for GORE MultiVent at the 2026 Battery Awards, with winners announced on Oct. 13
Present “Beyond Thermal Runaway: Advanced Materials and Venting Strategies for
Safer, Higher-Energy Battery Systems,”
with Steve Aubuchon, PhD, Head of Market Development for Batteries, on Thursday, Oct. 15
, from 11:00 to 11:45 a.m. EDT in the Battery Tech Theater (Booth 6050).
Visit Gore at Booth 6205 to see GORE MultiVent and talk with Gore engineers about your pack’s venting and thermal management requirements.

content:
Maxell Begins Mass Production of All-Solid-State Battery Backup Modules for Industrial Equipment
Power Supply Module Incorporating All-Solid-State Battery Helps Reduce Maintenance Workload and Improve Equipment Maintainability
BUSINESS WIRE
Maxell, Ltd.
(TOKYO: 6810) will begin mass production of its “
All-Solid-State Battery
Backup Module” incorporating the ceramic packaged all-solid-state battery, PSB401010H, and will start sales in Japan for industrial equipment applications in early November.
Maxell has been conducting field tests
of power supply modules incorporating its all-solid-state batteries in manufacturing equipment at customers’ factories since 2024, with the aim of reducing the workload associated with battery replacement at production sites. The tests confirmed stable backup performance under actual manufacturing conditions, and customers highly valued the modules for their ability to improve equipment maintainability. Based on these results, Maxell developed four models of the All-Solid-State Battery Backup Module.
The module is available with output voltages corresponding to those of ER batteries (3.6 V) and CR batteries (3.0 V), which are widely used as backup power sources. Two battery capacity options are available for each voltage type, offering a lineup of four models that can be selected according to the application. The all-solid-state battery incorporated into the module has an expected service life of more than 10 years
. As a result, the module is expected to reduce the labor associated with primary battery replacement and the risk of downtime caused by unexpected battery depletion. In addition, the module can operate at temperatures of up to 85°C.
Maxell will exhibit the module at Maintenance Munich 2026 (October 14-15, 2026; MOC – Event Center Messe München, Germany) and at other exhibitions in Japan.

title: Rivian and Redwood Materials Expand Partnership to Span the Lifecycle of the Battery - Batteries News
content:
Rivian and Redwood Materials Expand Partnership to Span the Lifecycle of the Battery
Redwood will now recycle Rivian’s battery scrap and end-of-life packs as well as provide energy storage for its manufacturing plant
IRVINE, Calif.–(
BUSINESS WIRE
)–American automaker Rivian (NASDAQ: RIVN) and energy technology company Redwood Materials today announced a major expansion of their partnership, establishing Redwood as one of Rivian’s key partners to enabling end-to-end energy solutions—recycling Rivian’s production scrap and end-of-life EV batteries, as well as providing stationary battery storage at its manufacturing plant in Normal, Illinois.
Through the partnership, Redwood collects Rivian EV battery packs through Rivian’s nationwide network of service centers when they are no longer suitable for in-vehicle use. Redwood then evaluates each battery pack to determine whether to repurpose it for energy storage—deployed directly at Rivian’s manufacturing facilities or at other locations—or to recycle it. Redwood will now also recycle battery scrap generated at Rivian’s manufacturing operations.
This new scope of the partnership builds on the existing work,
announced in April 2026
, that is deploying 10 megawatt-hours (MWh) of battery energy storage from repurposed Rivian battery packs at the automaker’s manufacturing plant in Normal, Illinois.
RJ Scaringe,
Rivian Founder and CEO, said:
Giving Rivian battery packs a second life in stationary storage is a massive unlock for the energy transition,
“By partnering with JB and the Redwood team, we’re turning retired EV batteries into a powerful tool to make the grid more reliable and lower energy costs for everyone.”
JB Straubel,
Redwood Materials Founder and CEO, said:
Every Rivian battery pack that comes back to us is a potential source of domestic grid energy storage in addition to critical materials,
“Redwood’s unique ability to integrate and redeploy Rivian batteries with our technology is an opportunity to enable fast, flexible and more cost-efficient energy storage. As the demand and cost for energy keeps rising, working with companies like Rivian is how we help meet these challenges.”
When EV batteries reach the end of their useful lives in vehicles, they often still have substantial useful energy capacity for second-life applications, such as stationary storage. Energy storage applications with repurposed batteries can ease stress on the grid during periods of high electricity demand, improving grid reliability while reducing energy costs for the user, as well as the grid at large. During periods of low demand or when low-cost renewable energy is most productive, these packs can store electricity for easy dispatch during periods of higher demand. When paired with Rivian—and other—EV battery packs, Redwood’s proprietary technology architecture offers an integrated system that can respond intelligently to the needs of the facility it is serving.
Once batteries are no longer useful in energy storage applications, or where scrap is generated during manufacturing, they can be recycled. Redwood’s advanced process is capable of recycling and recovering critical minerals like lithium, nickel, cobalt, and copper at rates exceeding 95 percent, encouraging the development of a circular, domestic supply chain for battery materials in the United States.
This expanded partnership reflects a broader shift underway in how American manufacturers source power. As grid connections take years to secure and conventional infrastructure remains supply-constrained, companies increasingly need partners who can solve more than one piece of the problem—recovering materials, managing recycling, and deploying storage as a single system rather than separate vendors. Rivian’s work with Redwood is a model for that approach: one partnership spanning the full lifecycle of a battery, built to move faster than the grid alone can.

Sakuu Corporation to Go Public via Business Combination With Pyrophyte Acquisition Corp. II
Advancing Mission to Transform Energy Storage Manufacturing Industry by Supplying Commercial-Scale Dry-Printing Equipment for Accelerated, Sustainable and Cost-Effective Battery and Supercapacitor Production
SAN JOSE, Calif. & HOUSTON–(
BUSINESS WIRE
Sakuu Corporation
(“Sakuu”), a Silicon Valley-based company that seeks to become a global leader in the production and supply of transformative dry-printing electrode manufacturing platforms, and
Pyrophyte Acquisition Corp. II
(“Pyrophyte”) (NYSE: PAII), a special purpose acquisition company, announced today that they have entered into a definitive Business Combination Agreement (“BCA”) for a business combination.
The terms of the Business Combination imply a pre-money equity value of $600 million for Sakuu. The proceeds from the Business Combination are expected to be used to support the continued development and commercialization of Sakuu’s Kavian
platform, its next-generation dry-battery printing platform, including preparations for anticipated commercial availability in the second quarter of 2027, and to support purchase-order fulfillment. Upon closing, Pyrophyte will be renamed Sakuu Corporation and is expected to be listed on the NYSE under the ticker symbol “
.” Unless otherwise specified, all amounts in this press release are in U.S. dollars.
Sakuu Overview
Founded in 2016, Sakuu develops the first known multi-material, multi-process additive manufacturing platform for energy storage production enabling electrode production in a fully dry process with proven electrode performance. It is the first company to 3D-print fully functional batteries in custom shapes and sizes with multiple materials, including metal-free composites, in a fully dry process.
For battery manufacturers, Sakuu’s process and Kavian platform save both CapEx and OpEx, as well as significantly reduce factory and carbon footprints compared to traditional wet process manufacturing, thereby potentially improving gross margins. Sakuu believes the platform offers the potential to provide:
100% elimination of toxic solvents and water;
40-60% potential overall manufacturing cost reduction;
50% smaller factory footprint; and
55% reduction of CO2 emissions.
Additionally, Sakuu’s polymeric current collector (PCC) technology and Kavian dry-printing manufacturing process enable the production of inherently safe batteries by dry-printing electrodes designed to mitigate the risk of thermal runaway associated with traditionally manufactured Li-Ion batteries.
Sakuu’s technology can produce batteries and supercapacitors for AI data centers tailored for rack integration close to the server, with much higher pack energy density, lower resistance, inherent safety and lower heat generation (meaning less need for cooling and safety investments).
Global energy-transition drivers, evolving regulatory and trade policies, and major investments in AI datacenter buildout are all expected to be significant catalysts driving demand for both batteries and supercapacitors and advanced production capabilities, creating a robust long-term growth outlook for Sakuu’s revolutionary technology.
Commentary
Sakuu Founder and Chief Executive Officer
Robert Bagheri
Sakuu’s technology enables energy storage manufacturers to meet the demands of the modern era,
“Kavian technology is not only the world’s first additive manufacturing solution to dry print high-performance battery electrodes at scale; it can also dry print supercapacitor electrodes customized for the growing power needs of AI data centers. It is the only known solution for producing heavily in-demand energy products that can be custom-printed rapidly, sustainably, and cost-effectively.”
Chairman of Pyrophyte,
Dr. Bernard J. Duroc-Danner
AI is a profoundly transformative technology.
”Energy is what makes that transformation possible. Sakuu brings transformative technology to energy storage manufacturing, a critical segment of the energy industry. Sakuu will improve the economics of AI infrastructure as well as more broadly the economics of energy storage in all its applications. It will also significantly improve the safety and the environmental footprint of AI data centers and more generally the electrification of the economy. Pyrophyte wanted to assist in bringing to market a company that makes a difference in the energy industry. After long years of technology development, Sakuu is such a company. We are proud to be part of their development path.”
Transaction Summary
The terms of the Business Combination imply a pre-money equity value of $600 million. New capital is expected to accelerate Sakuu’s delivery of next-generation dry-electrode printing technologies.
The Business Combination, which has been unanimously approved by the Boards of Directors of Sakuu and Pyrophyte, is subject to approval by Pyrophyte’s and Sakuu’s shareholders and other customary closing conditions. CEO Robert Bagheri and President and COO Arwed Niestroj will continue to lead Sakuu, supported by a deep bench of experienced operators. Pyrophyte’s leadership team is expected to support Sakuu by introducing relevant industry and capital-markets relationships.
Advisors
Cohen & Company Capital Markets, a division of Cohen & Company Securities, LLC, is acting as Exclusive Financial Advisor and Lead Capital Markets Advisor to Sakuu. Brookline Capital Markets, a division of Arcadia Securities, LLC, is acting as capital markets advisor to Pyrophyte. Nelson Mullins Riley & Scarborough LLP is acting as legal advisor to Sakuu. Ashurst Perkins Coie US LLP is acting as legal advisor to Pyrophyte.

title: NEU Battery Materials closes oversubscribed US$7,6 million funding round to scale LFP recycling and strengthen lithium supply chain resilience - Batteries News
content:
NEU Battery Materials closes oversubscribed US$7,6 million funding round to scale LFP recycling and strengthen lithium supply chain resilience
SINGAPORE, Oct. 13, 2026 /PRNewswire/ — NEU Battery Materials, a Singapore-based material security company focused on recycling lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries, announced the oversubscribed close of its US$7.6 million funding round co-led by Shift4Good, a global venture capital platform investing in the decarbonisation and resilience of transport and energy, and SGInnovate, a Singapore government-backed Deep Tech investor and ecosystem builder. The funding comes off the back of NEU’s newly commissioned 1,300-ton-per-year Singapore factory, marking a major step from technology development to industrial scale-up. The capital will support the ramp-up of producing battery-grade lithium from LFP feedstock such as cathode production scraps and end of life black mass, and the company’s international expansion.
The round saw participation from new investors including
Lotus Singapore Group and M7 Holdings,
as well as existing backers such as
Paragon Ventures I.
The funding comes as demand for LFP batteries surges globally, where
LFP accounts for over 90% of battery energy storage systems
worldwide, and
over 55% of all EV batteries,
according to the International Energy Agency. As battery deployments and manufacturing continue to grow worldwide, scalable recycling solutions are becoming increasingly important to strengthen industrial sovereignty and secure critical lithium supply chains.
Bryan Oh,
Co-founder and CEO of NEU Battery Materials, said:
Our vision is to build cleaner and more resilient lithium supply chains for the ongoing energy transition,
“The commissioning of our Singapore plant is an important milestone in that journey. The funding will catalyse the scale-up and deployment of our modular LFP recycling technology, enabling us to expand the production of vital battery-grade lithium, and at progressively lower costs to our customers.”
NEU has developed the world’s first patented electrochemical redox targeting technology designed specifically to close the loop on LFP batteries, making lithium recovery scalable, cost-efficient and more sustainable. Its process is driven by electricity and water, and uses regenerative chemicals generating less waste and reducing environmental impact compared with conventional recycling methods such as hydrometallurgy and pyrometallurgy, with emissions up to 83% lower.
Sebastien Guillaud,
Co-founder and Managing Partner at Shift4Good.
LFP battery recycling is both a decarbonisation and an industrial sovereignty imperative,
“NEU has developed a differentiated solution to recover battery-grade lithium from LFP feedstock and is now entering a new phase of industrial scale-up, thereby helping build more resilient supply chains.”
Hsien-Hui,
Head of Investments at SGInnovate, said:
NEU plays a strategic role in the battery value chain, and we remain committed to supporting its growth,
With the new capital and its newly commissioned plant, NEU will be focusing on scaling production, further reducing production costs, and expanding its network of partners. This next phase builds on an
R&D roadmap that has delivered key technical milestones ahead of schedule
, providing a strong foundation for the company’s international deployment and continued commercial growth.

title: American Battery Solutions Unveils Aventor, a Rugged, BABA-Compliant High-Voltage Battery Platform - Batteries News
content:
American Battery Solutions Unveils Aventor, a Rugged, BABA-Compliant High-Voltage Battery Platform
Next-generation 800-volt system combines class-leading energy density, U.S.-sourced cells and two purpose-built form factors designed to simplify OEM integration.
LAKE ORION, Mich. and DETROIT, Oct. 13, 2026 /PRNewswire/ — American Battery Solutions, Inc. (ABS), a leading U.S.-based provider of advanced lithium-ion battery systems for commercial and industrial electrification, today introduced
, its next-generation high-voltage battery platform, at The Battery Show North America (booth #5400). Developed for rugged, high-utilization commercial, industrial and specialty applications, the platform combines class-leading energy density, U.S.-sourced cells, advanced safety and intelligence, and flexible integration for demanding OEM electrification programs.
Designed, engineered and assembled in the U.S.A. with domestically sourced cells, Aventor is built to support
BABA-compliant
OEM programs. The advanced 800-volt architecture delivers class-leading 300 Wh/L volumetric and up to 200 Wh/kg gravimetric energy density, 113 kWh of energy and 358 kW of peak discharge power.
Subhash Dhar,
founder and CEO of ABS, said:
Aventor represents years of work across ABS and an exciting step forward in what we can offer our heavy-duty OEM customers,
“We set out to develop a battery platform that leads on energy density without any compromises in the safety, durability or performance these applications demand. The result is a highly capable platform that gives customers more energy, more uptime, more value and an excellent foundation from which they can scale electrification across their portfolios.”
A scalable common architecture supports two purpose-built form factors, helping OEMs integrate the platform across vehicle layouts and duty cycles:
Chassis-Integrated Pack
, the standard offering, is optimized for packaging efficiency and energy density. It can be installed between the frame rails, where many commercial vehicles already have protected availablespace, as well as in other constrained horizontal locations such as roof-mounted installations.
Hyper-Rugged Cube Pack
offers an even more rugged enclosure and load-path strategy for use in harsher mechanical environments that see the highest levels of vibration, shock, and utilization. This configuration is designed for multiple installation orientations and mounting faces.
Jeffrey Donaldson,
SVP engineering for ABS, said:
Safety, reliability and intelligence are central to the design,
The wire-free battery management system (BMS) reduces system complexity and improves reliability. Ultra-high-precision voltage and temperature measurement at every series element, together with a microprocessor and onboard data storage at every cell group, provide granular monitoring and diagnostics. The system includes cybersecurity protections, over-the-air update capabilities, active isolation monitoring, vent-gas detection and anti-propagation technologies.
Aventor is also designed to align with the functional-safety, regulatory and certification requirements important to commercial and industrial OEMs, including ASIL-C requirements under ISO 26262, FMVSS 305a, UL 2580 and ECE R100, among others. With ABS taking care of these requirements at the battery-platform level, the company is helping OEMs simplify integration, validation and compliance as they bring electrified products to market.
Donaldson
For high-utilization applications where charging time directly affects productivity, the platform supports fast charging from 10% to 80% in 42 minutes or less,
It is built and validated for up to 10 years of heavy-duty design life with the vibration, shock and environmental exposure common across commercial and industrial equipment. The standard enclosure is dust-tight and certified to both IP67 for immersion and IP69K for high-pressure washdown.
Aventor is being developed using ABS’ IATF 16949-certified quality management system and highest-quality battery engineering, validation and manufacturing processes. Together with U.S.-based engineering, cell sourcing and pack assembly, the platform gives OEMs a domestic battery option designed to meet their needs and the highest standards.
Customer samples are planned for 2027, with start of production planned for Q1 2028. Initial production capacity will be 6,000 battery packs annually, representing approximately 0.7 GWh.
Attendees at The Battery Show North America can visit American Battery Solutions at booth #5400 to learn more about Aventor and meet with the ABS team.

title: ACC unveils its 5 millionth ‘Made in France’ cell for electric vehicle batteries at the 2026 Paris Motor Show alongside the PFA - Batteries News
content:
ACC unveils its 5 millionth ‘Made in France’ cell for electric vehicle batteries at the 2026 Paris Motor Show alongside the PFA
ACC (Automotive Cells Company), Europe’s leading manufacturer of electric vehicle batteries, will be taking part in the 2026 Paris Motor Show at the ‘La Fabrique de l’Innovation’ stand, an area dedicated to the excellence and dynamism of the French automotive sector, organised by the Plateforme Automobile (PFA).
On this occasion, ACC will showcase its 5 millionth (5,000,000) lithium-ion cell produced at its Gigafactory in Billy-Berclau / Douvrin (Hauts-de-France), representing nearly 40,000 vehicles already fitted with ACC batteries; one of our batteries will also be displayed in a cutaway vehicle provided by the Stellantis Group.
Since the previous Paris Motor Show, in just two years, ACC has grown significantly and its industrial maturity has evolved considerably:
Its cells and modules power eight High Range electric vehicle models marketed by the Stellantis Group (Peugeot E-3008, E-5008, Jeep Compass, Lancia Gamma, DS N° 7, N° 8, Citroën C5 Aircross, Opel Grandland).
The first block of the Gigafactory is operating on a 5×8 shift pattern, 7 days a week, with scrap rates steadily approaching target levels.
The ramp-up is continuing; industrialisation and scaling up are now well and truly underway.
Module production volume for the month of September alone is close to the total production level achieved by ACC for the whole of 2025.
ACC is successfully supplying Stellantis in line with agreed production plans.
The second production block, with a capacity of 12.9 GWh, is scheduled to commence production in 2027 to power the Mercedes Group’s electric cars.
In a context shaped by geopolitical tensions, rising energy prices, economic uncertainty and climate imperatives, ACC offers a concrete European answer to the challenges of transport electrification. Building and mastering battery technology in Europe is critical to securing strategic supply chains, preserving industrial jobs and know-how, and strengthening the continent’s technological sovereignty.

Europe must now ensure that its industrial ambitions are supported by a framework that enables battery manufacturing to compete on a level playing field. Only a competitive European offering will be able to meet the demand for ‘Made in the EU’ production.’
ACC will continue to innovate and develop next-generation products offering best-in-class performance and real-world driving range. Combined with faster charging times, these technologies will help accelerate the transition to electric mobility while meeting consumers’ expectations.

title: ProLogium and Rimac Technology Advance Next-Generation EV Battery Development - Batteries News
content:
ProLogium and Rimac Technology Advance Next-Generation EV Battery Development
Paris, France, October 12, 2026
– ProLogium today announced progress in its collaboration with Rimac Technology on next-generation electric vehicle battery pack development. The companies signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) in September 2025 to develop a next-generation battery platform and have completed a battery pack concept mockup, which will be displayed at the 2026 Paris Motor Show. The next phase will focus on developing a functional battery segment to establish a basis for testing the thermal management and cell-integration concepts and support battery pack applications in the battery electric vehicle (BEV) market.
The collaboration combines ProLogium’s next-generation cell technology with Rimac Technology’s battery system development expertise, focusing on a pouch cell-to-pack architecture. Through a staged development path from concept mockup to functional battery segment, full-scale functional battery pack and in-vehicle testing, the companies will progressively evaluate cell and system integration approaches, connecting next-generation cell technology with automotive product development.
Vincent Yang,
Founder and CEO of ProLogium, said:
Since jointly announcing our collaboration with Rimac Technology at IAA in 2025, both teams have continued to advance the project, translating our shared technical vision into concrete engineering development work.
”What we are presenting at the Paris Motor Show is the baseline of that collaboration. Building on the completed concept mockup and the functional segments currently in development, we are preparing to move into the development and production of a functional battery progressing toward a full-scale battery pack and subsequent vehicle integration validation. Bringing next-generation batteries to the automotive market requires more than cell technology. It also takes the engineering expertise to integrate those cells into a battery pack with optimized architecture and thermal management. We look forward to combining our technical strengths through hardware development and testing to address the engineering challenges of automotive integration and translate the value of next-generation cell technology into solutions that can be adopted in vehicles.”
Daniel Kišić,
Principal Product Architect of Rimac Technology said:
Rimac Technology is developing a scalable cell-to-pack integration technology for solid-state pouch cells, designed to meet and exceed the requirements the automotive industry is expected to set over the coming decade.
”A wide range of integration solutions is currently being evaluated and tested in parallel on functional battery segments, covering thermal management, swelling management, cell integration and system-level design. Some of these solutions are oriented towards maximum energy density and reduced space and weight, while others are oriented towards delivering performance. The work starts from vehicle-level requirements and aims to improve every aspect of the battery design by reducing complexity, combining functions and reducing weight. It does so with cost in mind, while still delivering state-of-the-art charging times and power output. Once validated at vehicle level, the solution is expected to deliver significant weight savings, improving driving efficiency and extending range. OEMs could then choose between more energy on board at the same weight, a smaller and lighter battery for the same range, or any combination in between.”
A Clear Pathway to Full-Scale Battery Packs and In-Vehicle Testing
According to Rimac Technology’s current development roadmap, the functional battery segment currently in development is planned for display at CES 2027, with the full-scale functional battery pack identified as a development milestone for the second half of 2027. Subsequent targets include in-vehicle and public-road testing in the second half of 2028.These stages will progressively expand the scope of validation, from assessing integration concepts in a functional battery segment to a full-scale battery pack, followed by vehicle installation and road testing to evaluate system performance in an automotive environment. At the Paris Motor Show, the companies will present the concept mockup stage of the collaboration and outline the next steps in functional hardware development and integration validation. By combining cell technology with battery systems engineering, ProLogium and Rimac Technology will continue to advance next-generation battery integration technology development from concept design toward automotive applications.

title: BMW Confirms LFP Batteries For Some Neue Klasse Electric Cars - Batteries News
content:
BMW Confirms LFP Batteries For Some Neue Klasse Electric Cars
The company’s boss reveals certain EVs will get lithium-iron-phosphate (LFP) batteries, with China’s entry-level iX3 leading the way.
BMW is preparing to expand its battery portfolio as it rolls out the Neue Klasse generation of electric vehicles. While the company has started its latest EV offensive with nickel-manganese-cobalt (NMC) batteries, it will eventually add lithium-iron-phosphate (LFP) chemistry to the mix.
Speaking during BMW Group’s Q3 2026 earnings call,
CEO Milan Nedeljković
confirmed that LFP batteries are coming, though their use will depend on the vehicle type and its intended purpose. Responding to a question about the company’s battery strategy, the number one in Munich explained that BMW is starting with NMC chemistry and cylindrical cells because it currently considers this technology superior in the market. He pointed to the impressive range figures achieved by the new iX3 and i3, including in China, as evidence that the approach is working.
However, BMW isn’t ignoring the cost advantages of LFP batteries. The CEO acknowledged that this chemistry offers a different cost structure but also comes with different range capabilities. As a result, the company will be selective about where it introduces the technology rather than offering it across every segment.
NMC And LFP Batteries Will Coexist,
With Neue Klasse, we are starting with the NMC technology and the cylindric batteries, and this technology is now superior in the market.
”We see that our range we can offer with the iX3 and the i3 are deeply impressing also in China, and that is why we start on that level. At the same time, and you are right, the LFP technology offers a different cost structure, but also different range. So we will add the LFP technology in our vehicles, but we will be very specific in which vehicle and for which purpose. And so it will come, but it will not be a generic exchange or a generic offer in all segments.”
In other words, don’t expect BMW to replace NMC batteries with LFP packs across the board. The two technologies will coexist, serving different purposes within the lineup.
The differences between the two technologies explain why BMW wants to keep both options available. NMC batteries use nickel, manganese, and cobalt in their cathodes. Their main advantage is higher energy density, allowing automakers to store more energy in a compact, lightweight battery pack. That’s particularly important for larger, more expensive vehicles where customers expect longer driving ranges.
LFP batteries, meanwhile, use lithium iron phosphate for the cathode, eliminating the need for nickel, cobalt, and manganese. This makes them cheaper to manufacture, with production costs generally around 20% lower than comparable NMC batteries. They also tend to last longer, resist thermal runaway better, and degrade more slowly over repeated charging cycles.
There are trade-offs, though. LFP batteries have lower energy density, meaning they need more space and weight to store the same amount of energy. They can also charge more slowly in cold weather. Consequently, NMC remains an attractive choice for vehicles where maximum range and performance take priority over manufacturing costs.

title: POSCO Future M reaches a seven-year, 720,000-ton supply agreement with LG Energy Solutin - Expands cooperation to LFP cathode materials, synthetic graphite anode materials, and more - Batteries News
content:
POSCO Future M reaches a seven-year, 720,000-ton supply agreement with LG Energy Solutin – Expands cooperation to LFP cathode materials, synthetic graphite anode materials, and more
Speeds up high-nickel → LFP conversion of Pohang plant production lines… Will supply LFP cathode materials to LG Energy Solution in a timely manner from early next year
– Strengthens competitiveness by collaborating to develop future battery materials, such as materials for sodium-ion batteries, and responding jointly to global supply chain regulations
POSCO Future M is expanding its cooperation with LG Energy Solution to include LFP (lithium iron phosphate) cathode materials, synthetic graphite anode materials, and more.
On the 30th, POSCO Future M signed a Future Cooperation MOU with LG Energy Solution and agreed to strengthen the two companies’ cooperation framework to jointly respond to the rapidly changing EV and ESS markets and global trade environment.
The Future Cooperation MOU covers cooperation on the supply and technology development of LFP and synthetic graphite anode materials, which have recently become a focus of the secondary battery industry. It also extends this cooperation to ultra-high-nickel cathode materials and next-generation products such as sodium-ion batteries and silicon anode materials, among other areas. To respond to market changes, the two companies plan to work out how they will diversify their cathode and anode products and lay out a supply roadmap, then sign a formal contract within the year.
Under the agreement reached that day, POSCO Future M is expected to supply a total of 720,000 tons of cathode and anode materials to LG Energy Solution over seven years, from 2027 through 2033.
For the ternary NCM (nickel-cobalt-manganese) cathode materials POSCO Future M has been supplying to LG Energy Solution, the two companies agreed to pursue ways to further boost cost competitiveness by expanding the use of metals recovered from spent batteries over the mid to long term. They will also extend their cooperation to LFP cathode materials, demand for which has recently surged, driven by the expansion of AI data centers and growing sales of affordable EVs.
First, POSCO Future M plans to quickly convert the high-nickel ternary cathode material production lines at its Pohang cathode material plant into LFP lines and begin full-scale supply of LFP cathode materials to LG Energy Solution from early next year.
Going forward, the company plans to supply next-generation LFP cathode materials with further improved cost competitiveness and quality by developing a new process that uses POSCO Group’s lithium from salt lakes in Argentina.
In addition, POSCO Future M will produce synthetic graphite anode materials in Korea and Vietnam and supply them to LG Energy Solution. Demand for these materials has been rising steadily because they are well suited to improving batteries’ fast-charging performance and lifespan.
The two companies also agreed to cooperate on technology development and supply for future battery materials, such as materials for sodium-ion batteries (SIBs), ultra-high-nickel cathode materials, and silicon anode materials. They also agreed to stay ahead of changes in the trade environment, including by exploring joint measures when they anticipate or face global supply chain issues, such as the introduction of PFE (prohibited foreign entity) requirements in the US and the announcement of the IAA (Industrial Accelerator Act) in Europe.
In July, POSCO Group announced its future growth strategy, presenting a vision to build a Triple-Core system and grow into a “national supplier of critical resources.” The system spans industrial resources (steel), strategic resources (such as lithium, cathode and anode materials, and rare earths), and energy resources (LNG and renewable energy).
POSCO Future M plans to keep strengthening the competitiveness of its cathode and anode materials business based on POSCO Group’s in-house value chain, such as lithium salt lakes and graphite mines, and further solidify its position as a core strategic resources company within the group.

title: BMW GROUP LOCALISES SUPPLY CHAINS AND EXPANDS PORTFOLIO WITH SAMSUNG SDI AND LG FOR BATTERY CELLS FROM EUROPE AND THE US - Batteries News
content:
BMW GROUP LOCALISES SUPPLY CHAINS AND EXPANDS PORTFOLIO WITH SAMSUNG SDI AND LG FOR BATTERY CELLS FROM EUROPE AND THE US
Strengthening regional value creation and resilience with leading technology partners
A broad supplier portfolio for globally balanced sourcing
New battery cell partnerships with Samsung SDI in Europe and LG Energy Solution in the US
The BMW Group applies the “local for local” principle throughout its global supplier network, purchasing components close to where vehicle production takes place wherever possible. Targeted localisation of supply chains strengthens value creation in the key strategic regions of Europe, Asia and North America, reduces transport distances and increases supply security. A globally diversified supplier network also supports resilience and flexibility.
Further localisation of battery cell production: Samsung SDI in Europe and LG Energy Solution in the US
The high-voltage battery plays a key role in the global supplier and production network. As a core component of the electric vehicle, it influences essential properties, such as range and charging performance. The BMW Group sources the cells for its high-voltage batteries from world-leading manufacturers, combining regional supply chains with a globally diversified supplier network. The BMW Group has now contracted additional cell suppliers for its sixth-generation (Gen6) high-voltage batteries: Samsung SDI in Europe and LG Energy Solution in the US. These two battery cell manufacturers will supply the BMW Group from their established plants in the respective regions from the late 2020s onwards. “Local for Local” combines regional value creation with a global network of leading technology partners. In this way, the BMW Group is relying on a broad supplier portfolio with localised cell production – in close geographical proximity to its high-voltage battery and vehicle production facilities.
Nicolai Martin, Member of the Board of Management of BMW AG responsible for Purchasing and Supplier Network
Global purchasing strategy enhances resilience and competitiveness
With the latest nominations, the BMW Group will source battery cells produced in Europe from CATL, EVE Energy and Samsung SDI going forward. LG Energy Solution will also supply the BMW Group in the US in the future. “Our global partner network with leading cell manufacturers ensures that we have a resilient, flexible and competitive battery cell supply,” says Hendrik Lang, Head of Purchasing and Quality of High-Voltage Batteries at BMW AG. The “local for local” principle extends from the supplier network to the assembly of Gen6 high-voltage batteries, which takes place at five new production facilities worldwide that the BMW Group has built close to its vehicle plants: Irlbach-Straßkirchen (Lower Bavaria), Debrecen (Hungary), Shenyang (China), Woodruff (USA) and San Luis Potosí (Mexico). This strengthens regional infrastructure and existing facilities and helps secure jobs. The distances between suppliers, battery and vehicle plants remain short.
Supply chain localisation: Time and partnerships as key success factors
Competitive localisation of industrial value creation is a highly complex process, especially in the field of battery cell production. It demands significant investment and the development of effective supply chains with global technology leaders – as well as their willingness to establish operations locally. The BMW Group aims for long-term development of comprehensive regional battery ecosystems. This requires both attractive local conditions and feasible political regulations for the necessary industrialization periods.
Strong in-house expertise: Battery Cell Competence Centers in Bavaria
In addition to its diversified supplier network, the BMW Group also has comprehensive in-house expertise in the development, production and recycling of battery cells. “Our competence centers enable us to actively shape technological developments and meet our partners on an equal footing,” explains Lang. At the
Battery Cell Competence Center (BCCC)
in Munich, the BMW Group is exploring new cell technologies for future high-voltage batteries. The
Cell Manufacturing Competence Center (CMCC)
in Parsdorf examines how these battery cells can be produced in the highest quality and with maximum resource efficiency. Near-series battery cells are also manufactured and tested here. At the new
Cell Recycling Competence Center (CRCC)
in Salching, valuable raw materials are recovered using the innovative direct recycling concept developed by the BMW Group and reintegrated into the production process. While the Competence Center will be built and operated by Encory GmbH, the intellectual property for the recycling method is owned by the BMW Group.

title: Walmart Agrees to Expand Zipline Retail Drone Deliveries
content:
Walmart Agrees to Expand Zipline Retail Drone Deliveries
Prioritise Us
on Google
Families no longer need to leave the house in order to get essentials and groceries. Credit: Walmart
Walmart SVP Greg Cathey explains how a new multi-year agreement with Zipline will increase efficiency and add 300 drone delivery sites across the US
Walmart and Zipline have signed a multi-year agreement to add 300 drone delivery sites across the US. The retailer expects the expansion of delivery capabilities to increase the efficiency of fulfilment operations for staff and customers.
The new multi-year agreement expands the scope of Walmart's existing collaboration with Zipline. The two companies have been working together on drone deliveries since 2021.
This demonstrates the capabilities that technological advances can add within last-mile delivery options, showing how innovation can support growth.
Network collaboration
Walmart already has the largest network of delivery drones for retailers in the US, but is undergoing further expansion.
Its drone delivery programme has been used to deliver more than two million packages since it began. Drone delivery is seen as an
efficient and fast last-mile delivery option
, as it delivers the order to the destination in a short period of time.
Drone deliveries offer customers a fast way to receive their needed products, within minutes. This acts as an accessible option for customers, as they do not need to leave their house in order to receive their essentials.
“We see customers try drone delivery for the novelty and then continue to come back to it for the convenience when they need something in minutes,” says Greg Cathey, Senior Vice President, eCommerce Fulfillment Transformation at Walmart.
Greg Cathey, Senior Vice President, eCommerce Fulfillment Transformation at Walmart
“Walmart’s stores put us close to the communities we serve. With Zipline, we can build on that proximity and bring this fast delivery option to even more customers across the country.”
At a glance
Walmart has completed more than two million drone deliveries
The retailer is adding 300 new Zipline drone delivery sites
Its aim is to deliver essentials in as little as 30 minutes
Deliveries can weigh up to 8lbs depending on the vendor
Zipline also uses its drones for medical deliveries, saving more than 14,000 lives a year
Last-mile efficiency
Following the success of the drone programme, Walmart is bringing this capability to more communities across the nation. According to Walmart, tens of thousands of items are available for delivery in as little as 30 minutes.
Walmart’s physical presence is vast, with 90% of America living within 10 miles of a Walmart store. Through this, the retailer can build on its existing network to expand delivery.
It is seen as a more efficient and sustainable delivery option – there is no traffic for a driver to sit idly in,
there are fewer emissions
and costs are reduced significantly. Though the packages are of a limited weight, these deliveries are ideal for a forgotten item.
“​​​Five years ago, Walmart and Zipline made our first deliveries together. Back then, the idea of autonomous delivery seemed impossible to most people,” explains Keller Cliffton, CEO and Co-Founder of Zipline.
Keller Cliffton, CEO and Co-Founder of Zipline
“Today, customers order from us multiple times a day. When you can get what you need in 10-30 minutes it takes a huge amount of anxiety out of life. People can plan their lives around their loved ones, not errands. Now, with Walmart, we're going to expand this tech to homes throughout the country."
If their account is within the delivery range, customers will see drone delivery as an option online. They can track the items as they travel to the home, with real-time visibility and updates. It aims to position Walmart as the convenient retailer for customers across the US.
Advancing technology
Zipline is a quickly expanding organisation, currently the world’s largest service by miles flown. In total, it has 150 million commercial autonomous miles in its 10-year service, without a major safety incident, demonstrating its high capabilities.
The drone hovers approximately 330ft above the ground during delivery, with a descending pod containing the order. This ensures safety for the customer and the device, as well as efficiency, as it does not require landing and takeoff.
The company has also announced a US$1.5bn raise at a US$21.5bn post-money valuation. It is growing significantly, having also partnered with Uber to increase delivery capabilities. Zipline is using its increased capital to expand manufacturing capabilities in order to support its
growing drone delivery network
With Zipline, we can build on that proximity and bring this fast delivery option to even more customers across the country.
Greg Cathey, Senior Vice President, eCommerce Fulfillment Transformation at Walmart
The partnership helps consumers save time and provides reliable last-mile solutions. Credit: Walmart
Key partners
Walmart is America's largest retailer, founded by Sam Walton in 1962. Operating over 10,500 stores worldwide, it serves millions of customers daily with affordable groceries, electronics, and household goods. The company dominates through economies of scale, efficient supply chains, and competitive pricing. Recently, Walmart invested heavily in ecommerce, curbside pickup, and automation to compete with Amazon while maintaining brick-and-mortar strength.
Zipline is a drone delivery company founded in 2014, specializing in medical supply transport. Operating in Africa and the US, Zipline's autonomous aircraft deliver blood, vaccines, and medicines to remote healthcare facilities. The company has completed hundreds of thousands of deliveries, reducing delivery times from hours to minutes. Zipline demonstrates how drones can solve critical healthcare supply chain challenges.
Uber revolutionised transportation by launching ride-hailing services in 2009. Through its mobile app, Uber connects passengers with drivers, disrupting traditional taxi industries worldwide. The company operates in over 10,000 cities across 70+ countries, offering various services including UberX, UberEats food delivery, and freight logistics.
