title: New model helps robots learn tasks faster with less human programming
content: UC Berkeley researchers have developed an AI-driven approach that could significantly accelerate how robots are programmed and trained for real-world tasks. Called agentic robotics, the approach uses teams of AI agents to generate robot-control programs, test them in simulated environments, and refine their performance.The method could reduce the need for extensive training data and manual engineering, two major challenges that have slowed the development of capable robots.Early trials have demonstrated improvements in robotic task performance, pointing to potential applications in industrial automation and warehouse operations.Robots learn through AIThe new approach to robotic programming combines agentic AI, physics-based simulations, and modular control systems to help robots improve their performance without relying on enormous training datasets.Called agentic robotics, the approach allows teams of AI agents to generate robot-control programs, test them in simulated environments, identify failures, and revise their code before deploying it on physical machines.The technology could address two longstanding challenges in robotics: the extensive engineering required to program robot behaviors and the large volumes of real-world data needed to train robots through imitation learning.The team released an industry-standard benchmark for evaluating the performance of robots across industrial tasks, examples of which of shown here.Traditionally, roboticists have relied on two broad approaches. Model-based robotics involves engineers manually programming how machines perceive objects, plan movements, and control their actions. Model-free robotics uses demonstrations and imitation learning to teach machines how to perform tasks. While the former requires considerable engineering effort, the latter demands extensive datasets and lengthy training periods.Agentic robotics seeks to combine the advantages of these methods while reducing their limitations. The approach uses a framework called Graph-as-Policy, which divides complex robotic tasks into smaller, reusable skills. These include identifying objects, planning grasps, and moving robotic grippers without colliding with surrounding objects.AI agents connect these individual skills to construct complete robot-control programs. Using NVIDIA’s Isaac simulation framework, they test the programs under different conditions, identify problems, and repeatedly modify the code to improve performance. This allows robots to undergo multiple rounds of virtual testing before engineers deploy the resulting programs on physical machines.Accelerates robot programmingOne demonstration involved a robot using a sponge to wipe ink from a metal bar. Researchers supplied an AI system with a short video of the task and access to their simulation interface. Within an hour, the system generated and fine-tuned a physics simulation that reproduced the task, including realistic sponge deformations. The AI then used the simulation and Graph-as-Policy framework to generate a robot-control program. It repeatedly tested and refined the code before researchers transferred it to a physical robot.During one trial, the robot pushed over the metal bar because it had not accurately accounted for the object’s weight. The system used video of the failed attempt to update its simulation, revise the control program, and test a new approach. This feedback process allows AI agents to use failures during physical trials to improve simulations and refine subsequent attempts, potentially reducing manual engineering effort.The technology has also been tested in industrial logistics. A warehouse robotics company applied the methods to parcel sorting, analyzing production data and testing updates to robot behavior. The trials reportedly increased sorting capacity by more than 15,000 packages annually per robot. The company has since deployed the improvements across 30 percent of its U.S. fleet.The researchers are also releasing open-source code built around NVIDIA’s Isaac simulation framework, alongside an industrial benchmark for evaluating robot performance across different tasks.Initial applications are focused on industrial environments, where repetitive operations offer opportunities to test and refine robot behavior at scale. The approach could eventually make robotic systems easier to adapt to changing requirements without manually programming every movement or collecting extensive demonstrations for each new task.However, it does not mean robots can independently master arbitrary real-world activities. Its immediate potential lies in making robot programming, testing, and improvement faster and more adaptable, particularly in structured industrial settings.

title: World-first solar pavilion offers up to 62.64 kWh of home backup power
content: A California startup is turning the backyard deck into a home energy system. Outer Spaces will give its OS1 pavilion its first in-person showing at RE+ 2026, running November 16–19 at the Las Vegas Convention Center. The company bills it as the ‘world’s first’ combined solar pavilion and battery deck.The OS1 puts solar panels in the pavilion roof and batteries beneath the deck, giving homeowners a way to generate and store electricity without altering the roof of their house. A full-size unit at booth W17153 will give visitors a look at both components and the electrical wall that connects them. Solar above and batteries belowOuter Spaces will offer the OS1 in two sizes. The 12-by-12-foot model has about 2.5 kW of solar capacity, while the 12-by-24-foot version has about 5 kW. Beneath the floor, slim lithium iron phosphate battery modules lie flat in dedicated compartments, leaving the deck clear for furniture and appliances.Each module stores 7.83 kWh. Homeowners can configure the system with one to eight modules, for up to 62.64 kWh of storage. The pavilion’s electrical wall houses the hybrid inverter, the OS1 DC Hub, and the distribution equipment.“We designed OS1 around the battery from day one, so the cooling, waterproofing, and wiring live inside the frame. It’s modular and easy to assemble on-site,” said Jiake Liu, co-founder and CEO of Outer Spaces. Up to 11.4 kVA for home backupThe OS1 has a rated power output of up to 11.4 kVA. Outer Spaces said the system can start equipment with large motors, including air conditioners and heat pumps. Whether it can back up an entire home during an outage depends on how the system is configured and what equipment is connected.Owners can control the system through an app or a web portal. They can choose among modes for using stored power at home, managing electricity use around time-of-use rates, or keeping power in reserve for outages. The system is also designed to participate in virtual power plants where regional programs allow it, linking the batteries with other distributed energy resources.Southern California rollout planned for 2027The pavilion is assembled on-site, with a licensed electrician handling the final connection to the home. Outer Spaces plans to meet with builders and installers at RE+ as it recruits its first Southern California partners for 2027.The company launched in October with $8 million in pre-seed funding led by Upfront Ventures, with participation from Unlock Venture Partners, Mucker Capital and Genius Ventures. Liu founded the company with Terry Lin and Robin Liao. The three also started the outdoor furniture brand Outer.Sales are expected to begin in 2027 in Southern California and select markets elsewhere in the U.S. Outer Spaces plans to sell the pavilion online and through installers, builders, and developers.  The company has yet to disclose what either size will cost and expects to announce pricing in early 2027.

title: Ionic liquids help scientists precisely shape metal-organic frameworks
content: Researchers at the Tokyo University of Science have developed a method to shape porous materials called metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) into microscopic patterns without destroying delicate structures.Previously, carving these materials into tiny components for advanced electronics or chemical sensors required expensive liquid-nitrogen cooling to prevent them from collapsing under energy beams. Liquid ionic filler soaks into the MOF’s microscopic pores, strengthening the structure so it can absorb heat and clear electrical charges during standard room-temperature etching.This low-cost, scalable technique makes it much easier to incorporate over 100,000 known MOF variations into practical technologies like high-sensitivity sensors and micro-catalysts.Ionic liquid treatmentScientists building microscopic electronics have faced a major challenge: their best raw materials crumbled under the tools meant to shape them.Now, a team of Japanese researchers has unlocked a way to sculpt these delicate crystals using a technique as simple as filling a sponge with liquid.MOFs are widely considered important for modern materials science. Discovered in 1974 by Professor Richard Robson at the University of Melbourne, these custom-engineered materials link metal ions with organic molecules to create hyper-porous structures. Imagine a microscopic cage where a single gram offers thousands of square meters of internal surface area. The material’s tiny pores can store gases, trap environmental pollutants, and catalyze complex chemical reactions.Engineers have long eyed MOFs for next-generation chemical sensors and micro-electronics. Translating that potential into practical hardware required carving the material into precise micro-scale patterns.Standard semiconductor manufacturing relies on dry etching, blasting materials with high-energy ion beams to strip away microscopic layers. MOFs, however, are far too fragile for such high force.Striking a standard MOF crystal with an ion beam causes the delicate lattice to collapse into giant, ruined cavities. Until now, the only way to shield these fragile architectures during etching was to freeze them with liquid nitrogen. This has been a costly process that requires specialized cryogenic equipment.Led by Assistant Professor Yumeng Zheng and Professor Kentaro Kinoshita, the team devised a room-temperature solution. And soaked a copper-based MOF in an ionic liquid, filling 50 percent to 60 percent of its internal pore volume. The liquid acts like a microscopic structural reinforcement.High-tech future applications Blasting the treated samples with a focused beam of gallium ions revealed a dramatic difference. The ionic liquid absorbed the thermal heat of the beam while redistributing electrical charges across the material. Hardness tests confirmed that all liquid-treated samples became tougher, while thermal analysis showed the material resisted breakdown at much higher temperatures.Interestingly, the MOF retained its structural integrity. It etched precise shapes into the material at room temperature, including micro-pillars, a 5 × 5 µm² square, and even a Chinese character with line widths as narrow as 130 to 300 nanometers.The findings could finally clear the path toward mass-producing MOF-powered technology. Manufacturers can now shape these materials with existing microfabrication machinery because they no longer need cryogenic cooling.“We can foresee applications in high-sensitivity sensors, separation and analysis devices, and catalytic devices. This technology has the potential to become a foundational technology for bridging the exceptional material functionalities of MOFs with their use in practical devices,” concluded Prof. Kinoshita. The findings were published in the journal Communications Materials.

title: NVIDIA's GR00T 2 lets robots learn tasks from humans, not machines
content: NVIDIA has introduced a new generation of robot foundation models that can transfer skills demonstrated by humans to machines that have never practiced those tasks.Called GR00T 2, the world-action model predicts future video and robot movements together. This allows it to learn how physical interactions unfold and work out the actions needed to complete a task.The model is designed to work across different robot bodies, including parallel-gripper arms, dexterous five-fingered hands and humanoids. NVIDIA says it can learn from human videos, handheld grippers, and demonstrations collected using other robots.In tests involving 50 tasks that were not demonstrated on the target robot, GR00T 2 achieved a 40 percent average success rate without task-specific training. Providing five demonstrations for each task raised the average to 95 percent following a 30-minute fine-tuning session on a single NVIDIA RTX 5090 graphics card.The demonstrations required less than three minutes of robot data per task.Robots learn from human demonstrationsNVIDIA calls the approach cross-adaptation, or X-Adapt. It allows a robot to transfer skills from demonstrations performed using a different body or device.In one experiment, researchers showed a robot how to line a laboratory funnel with filter paper and wet it using a wash bottle. The demonstration was performed only by a human, without teleoperating the target robot. The five-fingered robot completed the task successfully in 65 percent of trials.In another test, a handheld Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI) gripper demonstrated how to assemble a toy dump truck. A different robot arm, called YAM, then completed the assembly in 60 percent of trials, despite never receiving a task-specific demonstration.Researchers also used a wearable device that mirrors the movements of a person’s fingers to teach a robot hand two-handed tasks. These included preparing banana yogurt and scooping granola, as well as striking a match to light a lamp.The model’s training combines 402,730 hours of first-person human video, 10,184 hours of handheld-gripper demonstrations and 23,500 hours of robot teleoperation data. NVIDIA says 100,000 hours of its Human-1M dataset are openly available.Reasoning models direct robot actionsGR00T 2 can also work with reasoning models that break complex tasks into steps, monitor progress, and direct the robot through an application programming interface.In tests involving three toy assemblies, this approach completed at least 97 of 100 trials for each toy. The system could recover from errors and interruptions during the process.A visual-steering feature also lets a reasoning model mark where a robot should grasp and release an object. This raised success on short tasks involving what to move and where from 40 percent to 92 percent on YAM.NVIDIA has also developed GR00T 2 Turbo, a smaller version designed for faster execution on a humanoid. It runs directly on the Unitree G1 using an onboard Jetson Thor processor, with each prediction taking 124 milliseconds.Through a whole-body controller, the humanoid completed popcorn-serving tasks in all 48 trials and cleared a table of different objects in 93 percent of trials.NVIDIA introduced GR00T 2 at the Conference on Robot Learning in Austin, Texas, on November 9. The company says the model is intended to help robots move beyond narrowly trained actions towards more adaptable manipulation in industrial and everyday settings.

title: US Army's reusable 24-rocket pod system aces third flight test
content: Raytheon has completed a third successful flight test of a new reduced-range rocket system designed to make U.S. Army training more affordable. The DeepStrike JR3 system could replace the Army’s existing Reduced Range Practice Rocket, offering a reusable launch container and a lower-cost rocket for repeated exercises.The test took place at Yuma Proving Ground in Arizona. Raytheon fired multiple rockets in rapid succession, demonstrating several features intended to support the Army’s growing training demands. The results also move the system closer to a formal qualification process, although additional flight testing remains ahead.Reusable pods reduce costsOne of the system’s central features is its reusable launch pod container. Instead of treating the entire launch assembly as disposable equipment, the design allows crews to reuse and maintain the container across multiple training exercises.Raytheon also demonstrated the pod’s maintainability during the Yuma trials. This approach could help the Army manage training expenses by reducing the need to replace launch hardware after every exercise.The JR3 rocket fits inside the Multiple Launch Rocket System Family of Munitions (MFOM) pod. Each pod can accommodate 24 rockets, giving the system compatibility with an established launch architecture.That capacity could make the DeepStrike JR3 useful across different Army training operations. It also gives the service a way to practice rocket artillery procedures without relying exclusively on more expensive operational ammunition.The test evaluated more than the launch system’s physical design. Raytheon examined the rocket’s range, flight trajectory, and accuracy during the demonstration. Engineers also assessed the visibility of its marking solution, which helps personnel identify where training rounds land.Commercial suppliers support productionRaytheon developed the JR3 rocket through a rapid prototyping initiative. The program also brings together established defense contractors, smaller technology suppliers and government production facilities.Its industrial partners include Combined Systems Inc., Corvid Technologies, L3Harris Technologies and Northrop Grumman. Letterkenny Munitions Center also contributes to the production effort.This arrangement draws on existing manufacturing capabilities and commercially available technologies. Raytheon wants the approach to shorten production timelines while controlling manufacturing costs.The company’s strategy also addresses a practical challenge for military training programs. A replacement training rocket must offer dependable performance without introducing the expense associated with operational weapons.Brian Burton, Raytheon’s vice president of Precision Fires & Maneuver, said the JR3 combines expected training performance with lower costs and reduced complexity. He also pointed to the reusable pod as a key part of the system’s design.More flight tests aheadThe third successful demonstration gives Raytheon another opportunity to evaluate the rocket before qualification. The company plans additional flight tests to establish further evidence of the design’s maturity.Those trials will help determine whether the JR3 can meet the Army’s technical and operational requirements. Its ability to support repeated launches, maintain consistent accuracy, and simplify training logistics will remain important evaluation points.The Army’s existing Reduced Range Practice Rocket provides a training alternative to operational rocket ammunition. A replacement could help preserve valuable live-fire training opportunities without requiring the service to expend its full-capability munitions.DeepStrike JR3 is not yet a qualified replacement. However, its latest flight demonstration provides another milestone toward that goal, with affordability and reusable launch hardware at the center of its development.

title: Google expands chipset lineup with 80% better inference performance
content: Google has added two specialized systems to its eighth-generation Tensor Processing Unit (TPU) lineup, targeting secure AI computing and workloads requiring massive memory capacity. The expansion gives Google four distinct TPU configurations in one generation, reflecting the growing demands of enterprise AI infrastructure.The new systems, TPU 8tx and TPU 8i Max, address challenges emerging as businesses deploy autonomous AI agents. One prioritizes confidential computing for sensitive workloads, while the other targets models handling enormous amounts of contextual information.Google says its TPU business now serves nearly 100 customers. These include AI research labs, financial trading firms, retailers and universities. Customers can also deploy TPUs directly inside their own data centers.Two systems, two prioritiesTPU 8tx targets organizations that process sensitive information or operate under strict regulatory requirements. Google has integrated hardware-level confidential computing into the system, protecting data and model weights during active processing.Typically, processors must decrypt information before working with it. That creates potential exposure even when storage systems and network connections use encryption.Today, we're expanding our eighth-generation TPU portfolio with two new systems built specifically for the agentic era — bringing our total to four distinct eighth-generation TPU systems launched in a single year.TPU 8i Max was built for massive context windows and the highest… pic.twitter.com/Ljj622Z5zL— Google (@Google) November 9, 2026Google addresses this vulnerability through hardware-based isolation. TPU 8tx uses the same silicon as TPU 8t, paired with fifth-generation AMD EPYC CPU hosts. It also incorporates Google’s low-latency Boardfly networking technology.The configuration delivers up to twice the latency reduction compared with TPU 8t, according to Google. Performance penalties from its additional security protections remain minimal.Organizations can also fine-tune proprietary models using private datasets. They can distill larger models into smaller versions without transferring sensitive information between separate computing clusters.TPU 8i Max tackles a different limitation: memory bandwidth. Large AI workloads increasingly require processors to access enormous amounts of information without waiting for data transfers.Google combines two TPU 8i chips within a single package to address that bottleneck. The resulting system doubles compute capacity, on-chip SRAM, and high-bandwidth memory bandwidth.It also fits twice the silicon within the existing rack footprint. That allows data centers to accommodate more computing capacity within the same physical space.Four accelerators for AIThe expanded lineup now covers different stages of AI development and deployment. TPU 8t handles large-scale model training, while TPU 8i focuses on low-latency inference and reasoning.TPU 8tx adds confidential computing capabilities. TPU 8i Max targets applications requiring extensive context windows and greater compute density.Google originally introduced TPU 8t and TPU 8i at Cloud Next in April. The company reported up to 2.7 times better training performance for TPU 8t. TPU 8i offered up to 80 percent better inference price performance against the previous generation.Making TPUs easier to useHardware improvements represent only part of Google’s broader strategy. The company is also trying to reduce the software expertise required to deploy workloads on its accelerators.Its open-source TorchTPU project brings native PyTorch support to the platform. Developers can run existing PyTorch code and Hugging Face models without rewriting their applications.Google has also introduced TPU development agents compatible with Claude Code, Cursor and Google Antigravity. These tools can automate onboarding, identify performance bottlenecks, and optimize custom kernels.Another addition, TPU Sync, creates a unified memory architecture across TPU memory, host memory, and shared storage. Google says it can reduce key-value cache transfer latency and time to first token by more than 90 percent.The company is also expanding its infrastructure management tools. Cloud Pathways and GKE dynamic slicing help developers coordinate large TPU clusters and reconfigure computing resources more efficiently.Google’s broader bet is that AI infrastructure must evolve beyond faster individual processors. As autonomous agents handle increasingly complex tasks, memory, networking, and security will play equally important roles.

title: US approves first high-temperature gas reactor permit in 60 years
content: The US Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) has issued a construction permit for a four-reactor nuclear power facility in Texas, marking the first approval for a high-temperature gas-cooled reactor (HTGR) in nearly 60 years.The Long Mott Generating Station, planned for Calhoun County, Texas, will feature four Xe-100 small modular reactors (SMRs) developed by US-based X-energy. The project is being developed by Long Mott Energy, a wholly owned subsidiary of chemical manufacturer Dow, for its Seadrift Operations site.The facility is designed primarily to supply high-temperature steam for industrial processes at Dow’s site. It will also generate electricity, with surplus power exported to the grid.The construction permit marks a significant milestone for advanced nuclear technology in the US. It is the third advanced reactor construction permit issued by the NRC in 2026 and the agency’s first approval of a multi-module advanced reactor facility.Four reactors supply industrial steamThe four Xe-100 reactors will have a combined thermal capacity of 800 megawatts (MWth) and an electrical capacity of 320 megawatts (MWe). Each module is designed to generate approximately 80 MWe of electricity while also supplying heat for industrial applications.Unlike conventional nuclear power plants that primarily generate electricity, the Long Mott facility is designed around the energy requirements of an industrial site. High-temperature steam can support energy-intensive manufacturing operations, potentially replacing conventional fossil-fuel-based heat sources.The Xe-100 is a high-temperature gas-cooled reactor that uses helium as a coolant and graphite pebbles containing tri-structural isotropic (TRISO) fuel particles. Its pebble-bed core allows fuel to be added during operation, rather than requiring the reactor to shut down for conventional refueling.The NRC’s approval also marks several regulatory firsts. These include its first construction permit for a pebble-bed reactor, its first approval of a reactor design featuring online refueling, and its first review of an HTGR under its risk-informed, technology-inclusive Licensing Modernization Project framework.Permit clears construction pathThe NRC completed its comprehensive safety evaluation in October, ahead of its scheduled timeline. It had already issued an Environmental Assessment and Finding of No Significant Impact in May.The agency said its review was completed within an 18-month schedule, demonstrating its ability to assess advanced reactor designs while maintaining its safety requirements.“Today, the new NRC is issuing America’s first construction permit for a high-temperature gas-cooled reactor in more than half a century,” NRC Chairman Ho K. Nieh said.The permit authorizes Long Mott Energy to construct the facility in accordance with the approved design. However, it does not allow the company to load nuclear fuel or operate the reactors. A separate operating license from the NRC will be required before the plant can begin generating power.Dow has also clarified that receiving the permit does not constitute a final investment decision to proceed with construction. The company still needs to complete engineering and design work and secure approval from its board. If it proceeds, construction could begin later this decade, with the facility expected to start operating in the early 2030s.The project is being developed under the US Department of Energy’s Advanced Reactor Demonstration Program, which supports the development and deployment of next-generation nuclear technologies.

title: Boston Dynamics' Atlas robot performs a 360-degree jump on wheels
content: Boston Dynamics has given its Atlas humanoid robot an unusual upgrade: a pair of wheels replacing its feet. The experimental setup lets engineers test how the humanoid handles sustained high-speed movement and heavy loads. It also offers a demanding environment for testing the robot’s motors and machine-learning-based control systems.The wheeled Atlas isn’t a planned commercial product. Boston Dynamics developed it as a research platform to investigate how accurately simulation-trained controllers can operate real hardware. The project also explores what happens when engineers push the robot’s actuators close to their physical limits.Simple hardware conversionThe engineering behind the modification was surprisingly straightforward. Boston Dynamics attached standard electric scooter wheels to Atlas using a custom adapter. The adapter connects directly to the robot’s existing ankle actuators.No other major hardware changes were necessary. Engineers also avoided rebuilding the robot’s software model from scratch. They simply replaced the simulated feet with wheels capable of continuous rotation.That simplicity reflects Atlas’ modular hardware design. Boston Dynamics developed the humanoid with manufacturing scalability and easier maintenance in mind. The same design principles also made this experimental conversion relatively uncomplicated.Wheels offered another advantage during testing. They forced the motors to deliver considerable torque while maintaining high rotational speeds. Every acceleration, turn, and stop placed sustained demands on the actuators.Teaching Atlas to rollThe experiment also gave engineers an opportunity to explore reinforcement learning (RL). The technique trains a robot through repeated simulations, allowing its control system to discover effective movements.However, transferring those learned behaviors to physical hardware presents a significant engineering challenge. A simulated motor might behave differently from its real-world counterpart. That mismatch can produce movements that work virtually but fail on the actual robot.Boston Dynamics addressed the problem by refining its simulated motor models. Engineers conducted physical experiments to measure actuator behavior. They then adjusted simulation parameters to reflect the hardware’s actual performance.The team also modified existing reinforcement-learning frameworks. Changes to training commands, reward functions, and posture controls helped Atlas develop smooth rolling movements.The results demonstrated why accurate motor simulations matter. A controller trained against realistic hardware behavior has a better chance of performing reliably outside simulation.Wheels unlock new movementsSome of Atlas’ movements drew inspiration from human motion-capture recordings. Engineers selected examples featuring substantial foot sliding to explore how wheels could reproduce similar movements.Sideways dashes offered an interesting example. Instead of dragging its feet across the ground, Atlas learned to steer its wheels and roll sideways.The robot also performed a 360-degree jump using a trajectory-tracking controller. The system followed recorded human movement data and completed the maneuver on its first attempt.Its approach differed from the foot-based Atlas configuration. Before jumping, the robot rolled its lower body into position to prepare for takeoff. The behavior showed how reinforcement learning could discover new ways to exploit available traction.Boston Dynamics says the findings will influence development of Atlas’ standard configuration. Engineers want to combine accurate actuator models with whole-body learning to improve reliability and expand the humanoid’s capabilities.The wheeled experiment ultimately provided something beyond an entertaining demonstration. It offered engineers a demanding test environment for understanding how motors and learned controllers behave together under extreme conditions.

title: OpenAI launches Control Room with a 35-second kill switch for agents
content: OpenAI has deployed a centralized control system called Control Room to stop potentially risky AI model workloads across its research infrastructure, with the system designed to halt further model output within 35 seconds of a decision to intervene.The system is intended to strengthen safeguards as increasingly capable AI models introduce greater safety and security risks. It connects research workloads, including agent-based model training, evaluations, and data-processing jobs, to a central service that controls whether they can continue generating outputs.Unlike conventional monitoring systems that primarily flag suspicious behavior, Control Room can actively prevent a research workload from obtaining additional model outputs. It works alongside OpenAI’s existing systems for monitoring potentially misaligned model behavior.The company said Control Room is already deployed across its research infrastructure, where the need for intervention is greatest. Its external model-serving infrastructure is more centralized and already has operational mechanisms to take down model deployments when necessary.How shutdown worksControl Room connects three main components: the research workload, the inference engine, and the central Control Room service.A workload is a research job, such as a reinforcement learning experiment, an evaluation, or a high-volume data-processing task. Each research workload that performs agentic inference must be associated with an approved safety case.When a researcher starts a job, its code requests a unique job ID from Control Room. This identifier is then attached to requests sent to inference engines, which run models directly on GPUs and generate their outputs.We built Control Room, a central system to track model workloads across our research infrastructure and stop them quickly when safety or security concerns arise.It connects every research inference workload, including agentic sampling for model training and evaluation, data…— OpenAI (@OpenAI) November 9, 2026Before fulfilling an inference request, the engine checks with Control Room to confirm that the associated job is still authorized to run.If a researcher or monitoring system has instructed Control Room to stop that job, the service denies the next inference request. The engine then refuses to generate further model output for that workload.Importantly, the research process itself does not necessarily terminate. Its code may continue running, but it can no longer obtain additional model outputs through the authorized inference engines.This approach also avoids relying on researchers’ workload code to implement safety checks correctly. OpenAI places the critical authorization mechanism in the inference layer, which has fewer and more centrally managed code paths.Fails closed if system failsControl Room is designed to remain effective even when other infrastructure components malfunction. Its fail-closed mechanism also prevents inference requests if the Control Room service itself becomes unavailable.This means a technical failure, deliberate disabling, or potential tampering with the central service will cause inference engines to deny requests until the system returns to normal operation.OpenAI said the maximum delay between receiving a stop instruction and preventing further progress is 35 seconds. This delay comes from a caching layer used to handle the volume of inference authorization requests. The company is working to reduce the interval to zero.The system also integrates with automated monitoring. OpenAI said all its frontier reinforcement learning jobs run with a separate model-based monitor that examines model behaviour and can raise alerts when it detects potential problems.If an alert warrants intervention, the monitoring system can instruct Control Room to terminate the associated job. The service then blocks subsequent inference requests across any model or engine used by that workload.The company cited a recent DNS-related incident, in which a monitor detected an agent attempting to reach an external chatbot, as an example of why such safeguards matter.Control Room is one part of OpenAI’s broader approach to securing frontier model development. The company said it will continue strengthening its monitoring systems and safeguards against misaligned behavior and security breaches.

title: Meta unveils Muse Ember, its smallest model yet for cheaper AI agents
content: Meta has unveiled Muse Ember, its smallest model yet, designed to handle repetitive coding and reasoning tasks performed by AI agents while keeping operating costs low.The compact model is built for everyday agent workloads, including tool calls, coding subtasks, information extraction, request routing, and parsing lengthy documents. Meta says Muse Ember delivers more intelligence per dollar than Anthropic’s Claude Haiku 5.5 and OpenAI’s GPT-6 Luna across reasoning settings.According to Artificial Analysis, Muse Ember scores 36 on its Intelligence Index, matching Claude Haiku 5.5 while costing approximately $0.14 per task. This is nearly three times cheaper than Haiku’s estimated $0.41 cost at the same score.The model also compares favorably with Meta’s larger Muse Spark 1.3. Artificial Analysis estimates that Muse Ember costs $0.14 per Intelligence Index task, compared with $2.39 for Spark, which scores 37 on the index.Built for everyday agent tasksMeta designed Muse Ember to handle the numerous smaller operations that agents perform during extended workflows rather than focusing exclusively on complex reasoning problems.It can execute business workflows from start to finish by retrieving records, making sequential tool calls, and updating information across applications. The model also comes with a 1-million-token context window and can generate up to 512,000 output tokens, allowing it to process entire codebases or large document collections in a single call.In evaluations, Muse Ember scored 37.8 percent on AutomationBench-AA, which measures end-to-end business workflows. This compared with 20.2 percent for GPT-6 Luna and 13.9 percent for Claude Haiku 5.5.It also achieved 61.6 percent on Agents’ Last Exam, narrowly exceeding Luna’s 57.1 percent and Haiku’s 57 percent. On the Personal Superintelligence Index, Meta’s internal measure of personal and knowledge work, it scored 46.8 percent, ahead of Luna’s 37 percent and Haiku’s 36.1 percent.Its coding performance was similarly competitive. Muse Ember scored 40.9% on Terminal-Bench 4.0, compared with 39.2 percent for Haiku and 16.4 percent for Luna. However, Haiku performed better on FrontierCode 2.0-AA, scoring 34.9 percent against Muse Ember’s 27.2 percent.Multimodal capabilities and availabilityBeyond coding and agent execution, Muse Ember can process text, images, audio and video. This allows it to interpret screenshots, charts and scanned documents, as well as voice recordings and video content.On OSWorld 2.1, which measures computer-use capabilities across desktop applications, Muse Ember scored 69.5% using partial-credit scoring. It also achieved 80.6 percent on PerceptionBench, which evaluates fine-grained visual understanding with tools.Meta said the model underwent safety evaluations covering chemical and biological risks, cybersecurity, and loss-of-control scenarios. The company reported that Muse Ember remained below its framework’s high-risk thresholds.The model is available through Muse Code and the Meta Model API as muse-ember-1.0. Pricing starts at $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.50 per million output tokens, while cached input costs $0.004 per million tokens.Muse Ember is the first model Meta says was trained using Muse Wonder Full. It joins Muse Wonder, designed for the hardest reasoning problems, and Muse Spark, aimed at coding and agentic workflows.Meta’s broader goal is to make advanced capabilities affordable enough to run across everyday products and services, with Muse Ember targeting the repetitive workloads that agents handle at scale.

title: Nuclear submarine maker eyes 200-acre hub for reactor parts, defense
content: Rolls-Royce Submarines, which develops nuclear reactors for the UK’s Royal Navy, has struck a deal to produce nuclear reactor, aerospace, and defense components at a 200-acre technology park.The Rolls-Royce subsidiary announced the partnership with Derby-headquartered Infinity on Friday, November 6. The advanced manufacturing company is currently building a 200-acre technology park to speed up both research and production of nuclear and aerospace components. The sprawling site, roughly the size of 151 American football fields, is expected to bring together advanced manufacturing, testing, digital engineering, as well as prototyping hubs. The deal aims to accelerate production, cut material costs, and improve access to critical components. The announcement comes as Rolls-Royce expands its work on nuclear-powered submarines. The company also plans to provide nuclear reactors for Australia’s future submarines under the AUKUS defense agreement. A new innovation hubInfinity revealed that the site will unite manufacturers, suppliers, universities, and training providers at a single site. It will further include 3D printing, power beam welding, and hot isostatic pressing (HIP), a method that involves applying high temperatures and pressure to materials to boost their strength and remove any internal defects.Power beam welding, on the other hand, relies on concentrated energy beams to join metal components. These processes could improve the production of large and complex parts used in nuclear reactors, aerospace equipment, and defense systems.This could provide manufacturers more control over how critical components are made. The site already houses the Rolls-Royce Nuclear Skills Academy, a first-of-its-kind facility that trains workers for the nuclear industry.Lee Warren, Rolls-Royce Submarines engineering and technology director shared that exploring new manufacturing methods is essential. “As our business grows to meet the demand for our naval nuclear propulsion work, including increasing our manufacturing drumbeat and providing reactors to Australia as part of the AUKUS agreement, we need to ensure we are continually exploring new technologies,” he said. A fresh nuclear chapterRolls-Royce Submarines develops, produces, and maintains the nuclear reactors that have powered the Royal Navy’s submarine fleet for decades. Its first PWR1 reactor entered service in the 1960s, starting with the Valiant-class submarines. The newer PWR2 reactors provide propulsion for the Vanguard-class and Astute-class submarines. Meanwhile, the PWR3 reactor is intended for the upcoming Dreadnought-class submarines, with an enhanced version planned for future AUKUS-class vessels operated by the UK and Australia.“For over 65 years we have designed, developed, manufactured, and maintained the reactors that power the UK’s fleet of nuclear submarines and we have done this by balancing consistent delivery with exploring future innovations,” Warren said in a press statement. The company currently employs over 5,500 people. Warren said that the deal will allow the company to explore new manufacturing methods at the park while continuing production at its Raynesway site. The park could also serve other industries, as UK Fusion Energy recently partnered with Infinity to advance the UK’s STEP fusion power plant in Nottinghamshire.Gary Jones, PhD, Infinity chief executive, said the collaboration will strengthen the domestic manufacturing for the defense industry. “I am very proud to announce our partnership and look forward to working with Rolls-Royce Submarines,” he concluded. The wider technology park is expected to create about 17,500 skilled jobs in the East Midlands.

title: Claude Fable 5.2 builds a working OS with 1,000 agents in eight days
content: Anthropic’s newest Claude models have taken on engineering challenges that typically demand extensive human expertise and months of work. Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 have demonstrated significant improvements across software development, robotics, mathematics, and theoretical physics.During internal testing, Fable 5.2 coordinated more than 1,000 agents to build a working operating system. The model also helped researchers tackle two previously unresolved problems involving black holes. In another experiment, it completed a computer-verifiable formalization of Fermat’s Last Theorem in just 30 hours.These results suggest the models can handle increasingly complex technical assignments. Anthropic says both versions share the same underlying architecture. However, Mythos targets vetted cybersecurity and biomedical research organizations.Working operating systemOne of the more striking experiments involved building an operating system from scratch. An Anthropic engineer gave Fable 5.2 a basic prompt and an empty project folder.The model coordinated more than 1,000 subagents over eight days. They wrote code, tested components, and reviewed their work throughout the process.The resulting operating system could boot on a laptop. It included its own kernel, hardware drivers, and permanent file storage. It also featured a graphical interface, login screen, installer, and built-in Claude functionality.Introducing Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2, designed to tackle the most daunting technical challenges.They’re capable collaborators on ambitious projects in many fields, and show improvements in areas like coding, reasoning, and vision. pic.twitter.com/jP0AutLxXb— Claude (@claudeai) November 9, 2026Software engineering wasn’t the only area where Fable 5.2 demonstrated its capabilities. Anthropic also tasked it with designing three electronic devices.These included a home voice-assistant hub, a USB speakerphone, and a handheld virtual pet. The model selected components from US distributors and designed circuit boards. It also created 3D-printed enclosures and wrote the required software.All three devices worked without electrical modifications. Their circuit boards reached manufacturing readiness in less than a day.Anthropic also reported a striking result from an internal software migration. A team of agents moved a critical production service from Python to Rust. The resulting service now starts approximately 26 times faster.Stronger robotics and securityFable 5.2 also demonstrated substantial improvements in controlling physical robots. On the RoboDojo benchmark, it achieved a 64.9 percent success rate.That represents a significant jump from Fable 5.1’s 27.6 percent score. It also outperformed GPT-6 Astra, which recorded 29.8 percent on the same evaluation. Opus 5.5 reached 39.4 percent.The benchmark tests how models control a simulated two-arm robot using camera images. Demonstrations included solving puzzle cubes, opening bottle caps, and drawing pictures.Cybersecurity results offered another notable performance gain. Anthropic’s specialized Mythos 5.2 model achieved an 89.6% score on its CVE Rediscovery evaluation.That represents a 10.2 percent improvement over Opus 5.5. It also marks an 11.3 percentage-point increase over Mythos 5.1, which scored 78.3 percent.A separate security company found that other tested frontier models missed one in six confirmed vulnerabilities identified by Mythos 5.2.Faster performance, fewer blocksAnthropic says Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 generate outputs up to 30 percent faster than their predecessors. Their standard pricing also starts at $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens.An optional fast mode increases token generation speeds by up to 2.5 times. However, it doubles the standard pricing.The company also reports improvements to its safety classifiers. Fable 5.2 produces approximately 55 percent fewer unnecessary blocks than Fable 5.1. Cybersecurity-related blocks fell by 60 percent, while biology-related blocks declined by 40 percent.These changes should make the models less restrictive during legitimate work. Mythos 5.2, however, remains available only to vetted organizations pursuing approved cybersecurity and biomedical research.

title: UK startup turns spent EV batteries into 400 kW fast charger
content: UK startup Allye (pronounced like ally), has put spent batteries from electric vehicles (EV) back into use and built a 400 kW fast charger from them. The approach lets sites deliver fast charging to cars without requiring a grid upgrade to accommodate new charger installations.The EV industry is delivering on its promise of longer-range cars and a charging infrastructure owners can rely on. However, there is a bigger problem that we will soon face, one where a large number of EV batteries will come to their end of life. These spent batteries may not be suitable for a car but definitely have enough juice in them that does not warrant them being destroyed.London-based Allye has found the right solution to this problem. Using spent EV batteries to charge other EVs. The biggest advantage of this approach is that such chargers can be installed in any location and use their existing electricity supply to offer charging services. This avoid high upfront costs for a connection upgrade to the grid to install a new EV charging service.Short of powerThe rollout for EV charging for large fleets is painstakingly slow. The common hurdle in the process is lack of grid capacity that can handle a large number of chargers at once. Allye, however, argues that what charging stations lack is not energy but power to deliver it.Once range anxiety was addressed, users also wanted their EVs to be quick to refuel like their gasoline-powered counterparts. It is perfectly okay if the car needs the whole night to charge at home, but when you are on the road, chargers can’t take hours to get your vehicle ready. Charging must happen in minutes, and this is where spent batteries can help.Even in their second life, EV batteries work sufficiently well to charge over slow connections. When an EV comes in, a battery pack can quickly transfer its charge to a drained battery and resume charging. This is exactly what Allye is doing with its battery-buffered chargers and does so in two different forms.MAX300 and MEVAllye built the MAX300 from repurposed batteries to charge vehicles directly where they are. This is much like a mobile diesel generator, which takes energy to the place where it is needed the most. The company has more than 20 installations of this portable charger that can be moved around by a pickup truck and delivers 400 kW of fast charging with its integrated charger.Mobility is not the main use case for EV chargers. Allye also built a fixed charger on the same concept. Called MEV, the charger is designed to charge two vehicles at once and can have a larger storage capacity, much like an underground fuel tank at a pumping station.Allye’s biggest challenge is that the batteries it uses are not at the same level. To overcome this, the startup gives power control and battery management to each pack, so that even batteries of different chemistries or ages are working together, they work as one unit.The MEV is available in two variants, not based on the capacity of the battery pack but on the power outlet available at the site. Reusing old batteries saves anywhere between 15 and 24 tonnes of CO2 per MEV, when compared to new cells. However, using existing power outlets can save the facility hundreds of pounds by deferring an upgrade to the grid.Deliveries of the MEV are expected in Q2 2027.

title: Fast-charging lithium-metal battery holds 94% capacity past 100 cycles
content: South Korean scientists have just unveiled a new liquid-crystal polymer separator, which, when tested in a lithium-metal battery, retained 94 percent of its capacity after 100 charge-discharge cycles at a 4C charging rate.The separator was built by the a research team at the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST). It could reportedly improve battery stability and charging speed, meaning drivers could charge their EVs in just 15 minutes.The study was led by Dong Ki Yoon, PhD, and Hye Ryung Byon, PhD, professors at KAIST’s Department of Chemistry. “Lithium metal batteries can store more energy than conventional batteries,” they stated. “However, during charging, lithium can accumulate in sharp, branch-like structures known as ‘dendrites.'”For the separator, the researchers used liquid-crystalline polymers to control how the lithium ions move inside lithium-metal batteries. Both Yoon and Byon believe that their find could address slow ion transport and dendrite formation.A highway for lithium ionsLithium-metal batteries can store more energy than conventional ones. However, during charging, lithium can accumulate on the electrode surface and, as a result, form dendrites. These tiny needle-like metallic crystals grow on the anodes, and they can damage the separator between the electrodes, which could cause short circuits and increase the risk of fires. To address this problem, the team created a porous separator made from liquid-crystalline polymers, which have an ordered structure like solids. They also share some properties with liquids. For the project, the team incorporated polyethylene glycol (PEG) chains into the material to facilitate lithium-ion transport.The scientists then monitored the alignment of the liquid-crystal molecules and arranged them either vertically or horizontally to examine how their orientation affected ion movement. The vertically aligned separator created direct pathways for lithium ions to travel toward the electrodes.In contrast to the horizontally aligned separator, it reduced the tortuosity (winding nature), of the ion transport pathways by about 2.5 times. This allowed the lithium ions to move faster and more uniformly. What’s more, it suppressed the dendrite formation and improved the battery stability.Longer battery lifeUltimately, the researchers tested the separator in a working lithium-metal battery to evaluate its performance. To their massive surprise, the cell retained 94 percent of its initial capacity after 100 charge-discharge cycles at 4C. In simple terms, a 4C charging rate means a battery can fully recharge in 15 minutes. According to the team, controlling how molecules are arranged could potentially make batteries charge faster and last longer without compromising safety. Yoon emphasized the significance of this finding for future battery development.He said that molecular alignment plays a key role in battery performance. “We expect this approach to contribute to the development of high-energy-density next-generation battery technologies, for which long driving ranges and rapid charging are essential,” he concluded in a press release.The scientists believe the approach could contribute to the development of high-energy-density batteries for future EVs, where rapid charging and longer driving ranges are essential. Further tests will, however, show whether it works in larger batteries as well.The study has been published in the journal ACS Nano.

title: US robot builds space structure without human assistance for first time
content: Caltech researchers have developed a robotic system that has successfully built a structure in space without human intervention for the first time.The autonomous truss builder uses a robotic manipulator to collect structural struts and joints from nearby dispensers and assemble them into identical sections.The technology was developed as part of the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency’s (DARPA) Novel Orbital and Moon Manufacturing, Materials, and Mass-efficient Design (NOM4D) program.According to the team, the demonstration marks a step toward enabling robots to autonomously construct large structures in space without requiring astronauts.Autonomous Orbital ConstructionThe robotic system is capable of assembling a structure in space without direct assistance from astronauts. The autonomous builder constructed a section of a truss structure in low Earth orbit, marking the first demonstration of its kind.Called Autonomous In-Space Tensioned Reflector Assembly (ASTRA), the technology uses a robotic manipulator to collect structural components from onboard dispensers and repeatedly assemble sections, known as bays, of a perimeter truss. Its components include composite fiber tubes, aluminum joints, and a reflective surface made from a perforated Kapton film.The system is intended to construct a 1.4-meter-diameter (4.6-foot-diameter) reflector antenna. Although the demonstration did not complete the entire antenna, it successfully assembled a third truss bay in orbit, establishing the feasibility of the autonomous construction approach.ASTRA combines a robotic arm, motorized component dispensers, an assembly plate, and an onboard computer within a payload approximately 1 cubic meter (35 cubic feet) in size.The payload was launched on March 30, 2026, from Vandenberg Space Force Base aboard Momentus Inc.’s Vigoride 7 orbital vehicle. The vehicle carried ASTRA as one of 10 payloads on SpaceX’s Transporter-16 mission.Before launch, the system contained two preassembled truss bays and the components required to construct additional sections. Once in orbit, ground controllers instructed the onboard computer to release the launch restraints and deploy the two existing bays.The robotic manipulator then began assembling the third bay. It picks up individual struts and joints from nearby dispensers, positions them on an assembly plate, and connects them to form the required structural section.After a bay is assembled, the system attaches a net-like reflective film to the truss. The design uses two reflective cable nets prestressed against each other with springs. Once prepared, the completed section is pushed outward into space, allowing the manipulator to repeat the construction sequence.ASTRA’s planned configuration consists of 11 bays connected to the reflective surfaces.One of the technology’s important features is its lightweight reflective material, co-developed by Caltech researchers and collaborators at the University of Pennsylvania. Unlike conventional knitted metallic mesh used in deployable reflectors, the perforated film requires less prestress. This could help engineers build lighter structures while maintaining the required reflective surface.Beyond rocket limitationsOperating the system in space presented several challenges that were not encountered during laboratory testing on Earth. The team had to repeatedly adjust commands and troubleshoot unexpected problems using images transmitted by the spacecraft.Communication opportunities were limited to approximately seven or eight windows of around 15 minutes each day. Researchers therefore tested potential solutions using a flight spare of ASTRA maintained in Pellegrino’s Caltech laboratory before sending revised instructions to the orbital system.The project represents the third phase of DARPA’s NOM4D program. During the first two phases, researchers developed the assembly concept and demonstrated its operation in laboratory conditions.The program aims to enable the construction of structures hundreds of meters or even kilometers in size. Current space structures are constrained by rocket fairing dimensions, requiring engineers to either fold components for deployment or assemble sections delivered through multiple launches.Autonomous orbital manufacturing could provide another approach by allowing structural components to be assembled directly in space.Although ASTRA was unable to complete its planned reflector before the demonstration’s December mission-end deadline, the results provide a starting point for refining the technology.Future applications could include large space telescopes, radio-frequency antennas, communications infrastructure, and solar arrays for collecting energy in orbit. Such structures could eventually exceed the dimensions of systems that can be transported or deployed using conventional spacecraft.

title: Something Unusual Is Swirling around the Monster Black Hole at the Center of Our Galaxy
content:
A colorful infrared view of the Milky Way’s galactic center reveals dense clouds of gas, dust, and stars surrounding Sagittarius A*, the supermassive black hole at the heart of our galaxy. Credit: NASA, ESA, SSC, CXC, STScI
Webb’s measurements of metal-rich gas offer clues to the processes that fuel our galaxy’s supermassive black hole, which consumes material more slowly than others.
The gas circling the Milky Way’s central black hole is rich in metals, probably supplied by stars that exploded and released material into its surroundings over time. Researchers at McGill University’s Trottier Space Institute uncovered chemical enrichment around Sagittarius A* (Sgr A*), offering clues to the origins of the material available for the black hole to consume.
For astronomers, “metals” means every element heavier than hydrogen and helium. The category includes carbon and oxygen as well as iron and gold.
Gas and stars may share an origin
Sgr A* is closer to Earth than any other supermassive black hole, making it easier to observe. The team studied its surroundings using data from the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), launched five years ago. The telescope measures infrared light across a wide range of wavelengths with unprecedented spectral and spatial resolution. Those capabilities allowed the researchers to distinguish the heat signatures of multiple gas clouds orbiting near the black hole and precisely measure each cloud’s metal composition.
The gas also turned out to have a composition similar to that of many stars orbiting Sgr A*. That resemblance suggests the gas and stars may have formed together. The researchers said the findings could help explain how metals are distributed around supermassive black holes in more distant galaxies, as well as the processes that supplied Earth with many of these elements.
Three views of the center of our Galaxy in infrared light, with the location of the black hole Sagittarius A* marked by a white star. From left to right, the images zoom in and show the region at different wavelengths. Credit: JWST, NASA, STScI, CSA, ESA, ESO/VLT. Additional image data courtesy of Rainer Schödel (Dinh et al., 2024)
Metals influence how black holes feed
Chemical composition also affects what happens to the gas. Metals influence how quickly it cools, which in turn influences how readily the black hole can draw it in.
“We know there’s a black hole at the center of our galaxy pulling material into itself, but we see that it’s eating a lot less material than other supermassive black holes, and more slowly,” said Nicole Ford, the study’s lead author and a PhD student in Professor Daryl Haggard’s research group in McGill’s Department of Physics. “Part of understanding why this is happening means looking at the properties of the materials available for it to consume, including gas, dust and the stars orbiting around it.”
Gas swirling around the center of our Galaxy. The animation shows the gas at different infrared wavelengths, demonstrating how it moves around the black hole Sagittarius A*, marked by a white star icon. Credit: JWST, NASA, STScI, CSA, ESA, ESO/VLT.
Gas offers no reliable record of outbursts
The findings complement a recent study led by Banting Postdoctoral Fellow Mayura Balakrishnan, which examined whether the surrounding gas retained evidence of earlier bursts of energy from the black hole. That study found that local conditions shape the light emitted by the gas, making the black hole’s influence difficult to isolate. The results do not rule out past outbursts. They show that the surrounding gas cannot provide a reliable history of the black hole’s activity.
Ford said understanding how Sgr A* attracts material will require comparing these observations with simulations of how gas evolves over longer timescales.

Ford, Mayura Balakrishnan, Sebastiano D. von Fellenberg, Daryl Haggard, Joseph M. Michail, Yuzhu Cui, Joseph L. Hora, Joey Neilsen, Giacomo Principe, Tamojeet Roychowdhury, Nadeen B. Sabha, Howard A. Smith, Zach Sumners and S. P. Willner, 19 October 2026,

title: Scientists Discover a Strange Form of Iron on the Moon That Shouldn’t Be There
content:
Tiny iron particles found in lunar soil may hold clues to the Moon’s ancient magnetic past. Credit: Shutterstock
Scientists examining lunar soil collected by China’s Chang’e-6 mission have discovered an unexpected form of iron preserved within microscopic impact glass.
Tiny particles of iron trapped inside lunar glass may preserve evidence of the Moon’s ancient magnetic history. Scientists studying soil returned by China’s Chang’e-6 mission have identified face-centered cubic γ-Fe, an unusual form of metallic iron never before confirmed in natural lunar samples.
The discovery is particularly unexpected because γ-Fe normally exists only at high temperatures and changes into a different crystal structure as it cools. Yet researchers found that this phase of iron had survived inside microscopic glass particles formed during impacts on the lunar surface.
How an Unusual Form of Iron Survived on the Moon
Researchers led by Prof. Haifeng Du of the High Magnetic Field Laboratory at the Hefei Institutes of Physical Science (HFIPS) of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS) examined impact glass containing numerous nanoscale iron particles. Using focused ion beam preparation, transmission electron microscopy, and chemical analysis, they confirmed that γ-Fe was the dominant iron phase in the two glass samples studied. Their findings were published September 16 in the
Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS)
Lunar topography and magnetic anomalies. Credit: Image by Li Long
Under normal conditions, γ-Fe transforms into α-Fe as temperatures fall. The team proposed that the extreme conditions created by lunar impacts could prevent this transformation. Rapid cooling of molten material, small amounts of carbon and other elements, and the surrounding glassy matrix may have helped preserve the unusual crystal structure at the lunar surface.
Microscopic Iron Particles May Record Ancient Magnetism
The scientists also investigated whether these particles could retain magnetic information. Using off-axis electron holography, a technique that can map magnetic fields at extremely small scales, they examined the magnetic structure of individual γ-Fe nanoparticles. Relatively large particles displayed a stable single-vortex magnetic state, with their magnetization arranged in a circulating pattern. They also maintained a stable magnetic response when exposed to an external magnetic field.
“This tiny magnetic fossil may help us better understand the Moon’s ancient magnetic history,” said Dr. Long Li of HFIPS, a member of the research team.
New Evidence Hidden in Lunar Impact Glass
Although the Moon no longer possesses a global magnetic field, its rocks and soils contain magnetic minerals that can preserve information about past conditions. The newly identified γ-Fe expands the range of materials scientists can investigate when reconstructing that history.
Because γ-Fe and α-Fe develop under different physical conditions and exhibit distinct magnetic properties, they may retain records from different stages of lunar impact events. Further research will be needed to determine how reliably these minerals preserve ancient magnetic signals and what they can reveal about the evolution of magnetism on the Moon.
Reference: “Magnetic vortex state of natural lunar γ-Fe” by Pengfei Liu, Ziliang Jin, Zheng Gong, Long Li, Kang Wang, Xiandi Zeng, Jing Liu, Dongsheng Song, Haifeng Du, Kelei Zhu, Chuanxin Yan, Jinhua Li, Keke Zhang, Wyn Williams and Ann M. Hirt, 16 September 2026,
Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
DOI: 10.1073/pnas.2608395123

title: High-Tech Drones Reveal Long-Hidden Aboriginal Rock Art Shelters in Australia
content:
One of three previously unregistered Aboriginal rock shelters identified during archaeological surveys in the Blue Mountains, NSW. Drone-mounted LiDAR helped researchers locate potential sites, which were then investigated on the ground. Credit: University of Sydney
Drone-mounted lasers helped locate three unregistered Aboriginal rock art shelters in Australia, offering communities another way to document and protect their cultural heritage for future generations.
In Australia’s Blue Mountains, rugged terrain and dense bushland make searching for Aboriginal cultural sites slow, difficult, and expensive.
More than 200 rock shelters containing cultural and archaeological evidence have been recorded there, but only an estimated 10 percent of the region has been surveyed, according to Dr. Amy Mosig Way, a research archaeologist at the University of Sydney and the Australian Museum.
Three shelters enter the archaeological record
Researchers from the two institutions, working alongside the Dharug Custodian Aboriginal Corporation, used drone-mounted lasers to help narrow that search. The technology, called LiDAR, short for Light Detection and Ranging, uses laser pulses to create detailed three-dimensional maps of the landscape, helping researchers detect features hidden beneath bushland and tree cover.
Dr Jacob Bongers and a DJI M350 drone with a YellowScan Explorer V2 LiDAR sensor. Credit: University of Sydney
After the drone surveys identified potential rock shelters, Way led teams of students and volunteers into the field to verify their locations and assess whether they contained cultural material. The work confirmed the locations of six registered shelters and identified three previously unregistered ones. The newly recorded shelters contain stone artifacts and rock art, including red hand stencils.
“One of the most rewarding aspects of the Gulamada Project has been creating opportunities for students to gain hands-on experience in cultural heritage research in a community-centered project,” Way said.
Archaeologists Dr Amy Way and Wayne Brennan, a rock art specialist, at one of the Aboriginal rock shelters surveyed in the Blue Mountains, NSW, as part of research using drone-mounted LiDAR to help locate potential archaeological sites. Credit: University of Sydney
The research, published in
Remote Sensing
, also produced much more accurate shelter coordinates than those listed in the official New South Wales sites register, the
Aboriginal Heritage Information Management System
(AHIMS).
“This work is exciting because it offers an efficient and accurate way to locate sites in rugged environments, which are notoriously arduous, expensive and time-consuming to survey,” said Dr. Jacob Bongers, lead author of the drone research and a digital archaeologist at the University of Sydney. He is also a former AMF/AMRI Visiting Research Fellow at the Australian Museum.
Dr Jacob Bongers flying a drone with a LiDAR sensor in the Blue Mountains. Credit: Lauren Roach/University of Sydney
Caring for Country through shared knowledge
The surveys form part of the
Gulamada Project
, co-directed by Way and
Wayne Brennan
, an Indigenous rock art expert at the University of Sydney. Built on the principle of walking side by side, the project brings scientific knowledge and First Nations cultural knowledge together to better understand and care for Country. At the confirmed shelters, Brennan and
Erin Wilkins
, of the Dharug Custodian Aboriginal Corporation, led the rock art recording.
“From the outset, our vision for the Gulamada Project has been to create a true nexus of science and culture. This work highlights the importance of listening, learning and working together,” Brennan said.
Rock art specialist and archaeologist Wayne Brennan with University of Sydney students at an Aboriginal rock shelter in the Blue Mountains, NSW, during archaeological fieldwork. Credit: University of Sydney
Susan Templeman, the Federal Member for Macquarie, which includes the Blue Mountains, said, “This project demonstrates the power of bringing together First Nations knowledge and new technology to better understand and protect Australia’s rich cultural heritage. I’m proud that the Australian Government’s First Nations Heritage Grants program is supporting important projects like Gulamada here in the Blue Mountains, already renowned for the extraordinary natural and cultural significance within our rugged landscapes.”
Faster searches could help protect heritage
The team says the approach allows Aboriginal communities, archaeologists, and heritage managers to search vast areas of challenging terrain much faster than traditional ground surveys. Used alongside existing knowledge and cultural practices, it could help communities locate, document, manage, and protect cultural sites before they are affected by development, erosion, bushfires, or other threats.
A drone equipped with LiDAR scans the rugged terrain of the Blue Mountains, NSW, helping archaeologists identify potential Aboriginal cultural heritage sites beneath dense vegetation. Credit: University of Sydney
“Importantly, our methodology is helping expand the record of Aboriginal cultural sites in the Blue Mountains and has the potential to be applied in other regions,” Bongers said.
The researchers plan to work with Aboriginal communities to test and adapt the approach in different environments, including the tropical savannas of western Arnhem Land and the semi-arid landscapes of western New South Wales.
Reference: “LiDAR-Assisted Survey Locates Unregistered Rock Shelters in the Blue Mountains, Australia” by Jacob L. Bongers, Wayne Brennan, Erin Wilkins, Lauren Roach, Emily Nutman, Joseph W. Lehner and Amy Mosig Way, 11 October 2026,
Remote Sensing
DOI: 10.3390/rs18203495
The project “The Gulamada Project: Walking side by side: A Nexus of Science and Culture” was funded under the 2023-24 First Nations Heritage Grants program (Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water (DCCEEW) – grant no. FNHI000045 ($248,610), awarded to Amy Mosig Way & Wayne Brennan (the University of Sydney) in collaboration with Erin Wilkins (Dharug Custodians Aboriginal Corporation).
