title: How Archaeologists Risked Their Lives To Save 30,000 Ancient Treasures From ISIS
content:
An ancient statue from the site of Mari, dating to the second millennium BCE. Credit: Yaarob Abdullah
Syrian archaeologists rescued roughly 30,000 artifacts from a museum threatened by ISIS, highlighting how protecting human history can depend on trust built before a crisis.
A narrow, highly vulnerable corridor was the Deir ez-Zor Museum’s only connection to the military airport. Access to the Syrian city was severely restricted, and the Islamic State of Iraq and Syria (ISIS), also known as Daesh, threatened to capture it. Archaeologists trying to move the museum’s collections to safety had to act amid active fighting.
During the summers of 2014 and 2015, Syrian archaeologists risked their lives to rescue approximately 30,000 artifacts. Maamoun Abdulkarim, Professor of Archaeology and History at the University of Sharjah, examines the operation in a study published in
Museum Management and Curatorship
. He oversaw the rescue as Director-General of Syria’s Directorate-General of Antiquities and Museums (DGAM).
An ostrich egg with decorated opening from Tell Terqa, dating to the second millennium BCE. Credit: Yaarob Abdullah
ISIS’s advance forced urgent decisions
Deir ez-Zor sits on the Euphrates River near Iraq’s border and is the capital of the province of the same name. The region contains some of Syria’s most important oil and gas fields, which made it a fiercely contested battleground during the conflict. As ISIS expanded its control across large parts of Syria and Iraq in 2014, the danger to cultural collections became increasingly clear. Abdulkarim describes the period that followed as “an important example of the sort of looting, destruction, and illicit trafficking of sites and museums that took place in this context.”
“This period formed a critical juncture, as it coincided with the fall of Mosul in Iraq, the looting of its civilizational museum, and the destruction of antiquities from Nineveh and Assyria,” he writes. “These occurrences compelled Syrian antiquities authorities to promptly reevaluate protection policies and expedite emergency measures in cities that were at risk of siege or collapse.”
Evacuation of boxes from a storage in the museum of Deir ez-Zor. Credit: Yaarob Alabdullah
Before the civil war began in 2011, Syria had 35 archaeological museums. Deir ez-Zor’s was not the largest, but it ranked among the country’s most valuable. Many of its collections came from renowned Mesopotamian civilizations and sites, including Halaf, Dura-Europos, and Mari.
“The 30,000 objects rescued from Deir ez-Zor represent more than just museum pieces; they hold thousands of years of human history and are part of the identity and memory of the communities in the Euphrates region.”
For Abdulkarim, leading the rescue meant making necessary decisions at the right moment, even when none of the choices was easy.
“My foremost priority was the protection of cultural heritage, and I was prepared to bear whatever personal and professional risks and consequences those decisions might entail,” he explains.
“There is rarely a perfect moment to act during an armed conflict; often, delaying a decision in search of greater certainty poses a greater danger than acting under uncertainty.”
About 300,000 artifacts moved to safety
The Deir ez-Zor evacuation was part of a much larger effort. During Abdulkarim’s tenure as DGAM’s Director-General from 2012 to 2017, approximately 300,000 museum artifacts were rescued and relocated to secure sites across Syria.
“The artifacts accounted for the overwhelming majority of the country’s museum collections,” he said. “This included approximately 30,000 objects from the Deir ez-Zor Museum.”
An agate bead necklace from Tell Terqa, dating to the second millennium BCE. Credit: Yaarob Abdullah
Those rescue figures do not provide a complete accounting of the war’s toll. The study gives no precise estimate of how many artifacts were looted during the civil war, which lasted nearly a decade and a half. It also does not specify how many of Syria’s 35 museums escaped destruction or preserved their collections intact.
Even the extent of Syria’s archaeological heritage remains uncertain. Modern-day Syria forms part of the broader Mesopotamian cultural sphere, where some of the world’s earliest and most influential civilizations flourished. There is no official estimate of the country’s total number of archaeologically significant sites. Its antiquities department is said to have records for about 10,000, primarily places that have been excavated or identified through visible remains on the surface. With large areas still archaeologically unsurveyed, the actual number may run into the tens of thousands.
Abdulkarim views responsibility for this heritage as extending beyond the borders of the countries where it is found.
“We did not rescue 30,000 objects simply to save 30,000 museum pieces. We were protecting thousands of years of memory that war threatened to erase,” he said.
Museum rescues require preparation and trust
His account treats a rescue during active hostilities as more than a logistical operation. “It fundamentally involves decision-making, institutional resilience, trust, and the ability to adapt rapidly to changing circumstances,” he explained.
Opening storage in Deir ez-Zor Museum for evacuation of the objects. Credit: Yaarob Alabdullah
He identifies competent personnel, effective institutions, meticulous inventories and documentation, and trusted colleagues on the ground as essential to protecting endangered collections. These resources help determine whether an organization can respond when its usual procedures are no longer workable.
“The most valuable resource during a crisis is not always money or technology,” he noted. “Sometimes it is trust, the trust between colleagues who can make the right decision when there is no time left for normal procedures.”
Abdulkarim presents Deir ez-Zor as a case study for heritage professionals confronting war and crisis elsewhere. Museums and archaeological sites in countries including Iraq, Libya, Sudan, and Yemen have also suffered destruction, looting, and illicit trafficking amid war and civil unrest. His analysis emphasizes the timing of decisions alongside the resources available to carry them out.
“In a cultural emergency, waiting for perfect conditions can become more dangerous than acting under uncertainty,” he stressed. “Heritage protection during war is not only about what we save. It is also about when we decide to act, whom we trust, and how quickly we are prepared to adapt.”
The study argues that museum and heritage professionals should make risk management part of their everyday work, rather than introducing it only after an emergency begins.
“The relationships, documentation, professional capacity, and trust required for effective emergency action must be established during periods of stability,” Abdulkarim concluded. “They should not wait until a crisis erupts before taking action. These foundations cannot be built overnight.”
Reference: “The rescue of the Deir ez-Zor museum collections during the Syrian conflict: cultural emergency management, multi-level governance, and lessons for heritage protection” by Maamoun Abdulkarim, 15 August 2026,

title: A 4,000-Year-Old DNA Mystery Is Rewriting the Origins of the English Language
content:
Rock art in the King’s Grave at Kivik (Kiviksgraven) in southern Sweden, an exceptionally large Bronze Age burial monument dating to c. 1500 BCE, coinciding with the expansion of East Scandinavian Bronze Age ancestry. From left: Hugh McColl, lead author; Eske Willerslev, senior author. Credit: Nicolas Delgado Clausen
Ancient DNA is uncovering forgotten migrations that may have shaped the origins of English, German, and Celtic languages, challenging what researchers thought they knew about Europe’s linguistic history.
How can researchers trace a language back thousands of years when no one knows exactly what its earliest speakers sounded like? Although DNA cannot reveal the words ancient people used, it can show where they traveled, offering clues to how the languages we recognize today first spread.
That approach is helping scientists reconsider the origins of English, German, Dutch, and the Scandinavian languages. Spoken by hundreds of millions of people today, these languages share Germanic roots that researchers have long believed reached Northern Europe about 5,000 years ago. New evidence suggests a major part of that history may have unfolded roughly 1,000 years later.
In two studies published in
, an international team led by the University of Copenhagen and Leiden University examined DNA from more than 4,500 ancient individuals, including 712 genomes sequenced for the first time. Comparing these genetic records with archaeological and linguistic evidence allowed the researchers to reconstruct population movements that had previously gone unnoticed.
Nordic Bronze Age ship and axe rock art at Järrestad in southern Sweden. Carving at the site began around c. 1500 BCE, coinciding with the expansion of East Scandinavian Bronze Age ancestry. From left: Hugh McColl, lead author; Eske Willerslev, senior author. Credit: Nicolas Delgado Clausen
“These studies show what becomes possible when genetics, archaeology, and linguistics are brought together. Questions that have remained unresolved for generations can now be addressed with a level of evidence that was previously impossible,” says Kristian Kristiansen, professor of archaeology at the University of Gothenburg.
A forgotten migration challenges Germanic history
One of the clearest discoveries was a previously unknown migration into Scandinavia around 4,000 years ago. The newcomers likely arrived from areas around the Baltic Sea and spread rapidly, leaving a lasting genetic influence on the region. Researchers believe they may have brought an early ancestor of today’s Germanic languages.
“For over a century, scholars have debated when and from where the Germanic languages arrived in Northern Europe. What is exciting is that we can now test some of these ideas directly. We discovered a previously unknown migration that occurred at exactly the time and place where we would expect the earliest form of Germanic to be spreading,” says Hugh McColl, assistant professor at the Globe Institute at the University of Copenhagen and lead author of the study.
Celtic languages may have eastern roots
The findings also shed light on a separate mystery involving Celtic languages. Although these languages now survive mainly in Ireland, Wales, Scotland, and Brittany, they were spoken across much of Europe around 2,500 years ago. Their origins have been disputed for more than a century, with competing theories pointing to the Atlantic coast or central Europe.
Ancient DNA revealed that people migrated westward from central Europe around 3,000 years ago, reaching France, Britain, Ireland, and the Iberian Peninsula. Researchers consider this the simplest explanation for the spread of Celtic languages, challenging the influential theory that they originated along the Atlantic coast.
Ales stenar (Ale’s Stones) in southern Sweden, a monumental Iron Age stone ship-setting overlooking the Baltic Sea, dating to c. 600–1000 CE and broadly coinciding with the period of back-migration into the region. From left: Eske Willerslev, senior author; Hugh McColl, lead author. Credit: Nicolas Delgado Clausen
“The question of where Celtic languages came from has been debated for more than 100 years. Ancient DNA gives us an entirely new way to evaluate competing theories and brings important new evidence into the discussion,” says Guus Kroonen, associate professor of comparative linguistics at Leiden University and the University of Copenhagen.
The Vikings’ unexpected Anglo-Saxon connection
The genetic evidence also revealed an unexpected connection between the Vikings and Anglo-Saxons. Around 1,500 years ago, several centuries before the Viking Age, people from what is now northern Germany migrated into Denmark and southern Sweden. In some areas, particularly Zealand, they became a major part of the population.
Their arrival coincided with the emergence of Old Norse, the language later spoken by the Vikings. Many Danish and Swedish Vikings appear to have inherited much of their ancestry from these newcomers, who were closely related to populations that also contributed to the Anglo-Saxons in Britain. That connection may help explain similarities between their languages and artistic traditions.
“This migration came as a real surprise. Archaeologists and linguists had not predicted it, but it helps explain several cultural and linguistic connections between Scandinavia and Britain that have puzzled researchers for a long time,” says McColl.
The researchers caution that migration alone cannot establish which language a population spoke. Their conclusions depend on how the genetic evidence fits with decades of archaeological discoveries and linguistic research.
“DNA sequences do not tell us directly which language people spoke. But by combining ancient DNA with linguistic and archaeological evidence, we can begin to trace how languages spread and changed over thousands of years,” says Eske Willerslev, senior author of the studies and professor at the Globe Institute at the University of Copenhagen.

title: Dinosaurs May Have Eaten Far More Fruit Than Scientists Ever Thought
content:
In this scientific illustration reconstruction of a Late Cretaceous forest, a small mammal and a horned dinosaur eat the fleshy fruits of flowering plants. The scene is based on fossils found together at a single site in New Mexico. In this scientific illustration reconstruction of a Late Cretaceous forest, a small mammal and a horned dinosaur eat the fleshy fruits of flowering plants. The scene is based on fossils found together at a single site in New Mexico. Credit: Illustration by Brian Engh
An exceptionally preserved 74-million-year-old forest in New Mexico is revealing unexpected details about ancient plant life.
Dinosaurs may have been eating a much wider variety of fruits than scientists once believed. Fossils from a 74-million-year-old forest in New Mexico show that some flowering plants were already producing surprisingly large fruits millions of years before the asteroid impact that ended the age of non-avian dinosaurs.
The findings, published in the journal
, challenge the longstanding theory that larger fruits and more complex seed dispersal strategies evolved primarily after the extinction event 66 million years ago. They also suggest that dinosaurs and other prehistoric animals may have helped spread the seeds of flowering plants much earlier than previously thought.
A Prehistoric Forest Preserved in Volcanic Ash
The research centers on an exceptionally preserved fossil forest near Truth or Consequences, New Mexico. James Saulsbury, a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Kansas Biodiversity Institute and Natural History Museum, helped collect, classify, and analyze the plant fossils discovered there.
“This paper focuses on a fossil forest in New Mexico and the preserved fruits, seeds and other reproductive structures of the plants that lived there,” Saulsbury said. “These fossils change how we understand the way flowering plants became modern in terms of their reproductive ecology.”
The forest was buried beneath volcanic ash that eventually hardened into rock. The preserved deposit stretches more than a kilometer (about 0.6 miles), capturing plants from approximately the same period and retaining evidence of how they were arranged across the ancient landscape.
“The New Mexico fossil site is exceptional,” Saulsbury said. “My co-authors have referred to it as a ‘botanical Pompeii’ because of its remarkable preservation. The site contains a layer of volcanic ash preserved as rock, known as tuff, that stretches for more than a kilometer. The deposits formed at essentially the same time, preserving many plants where they lived and died. It provides a snapshot of a forest from about 74 million years ago and even preserves aspects of its spatial arrangement.”
Ancient Fruits Challenge a Longstanding Theory
Flowering plants first appeared approximately 136 million years ago, but researchers have traditionally believed that their reproductive strategies remained relatively simple throughout much of the Cretaceous Period. Early flowering plants generally produced small seeds and fruits, with wind and other non-animal mechanisms thought to play major roles in seed dispersal.
“For much of their early history, they were relatively small, weedy plants that did not dominate forest canopies,” Saulsbury said. “Although they gradually diversified and occupied more ecological niches, it was thought their seeds and dispersal structures remained small and were primarily dispersed by wind or without fleshy fruit.”
Many early flowering plant seeds were thought to have ranged from dust-sized particles to roughly the size of poppy seeds. By contrast, the New Mexico fossils include fruits approximately as large as modern grapes. Such fruits are much larger than those previously expected from flowering plants of that age.
“The prevailing view has been that this more diverse reproductive ecology emerged only after the end-Cretaceous extinction,” Saulsbury said. “Our study suggests that transition began much earlier. The largest fruits in our fossil flora are about the size of a grape. That may not sound especially large today, but it is remarkably large for flowering plants of that period.”
Hundreds of Fossils Reveal an Unusual Ancient Ecosystem
The team examined hundreds of fossilized seeds, sorting them according to their physical characteristics. Because fossil material often lacks the features necessary to identify an exact species, researchers organized specimens into groups based on their shapes and structures.
“We sorted hundreds of fossil seeds into what we call morphotypes,” Saulsbury said. “These are groupings based on form rather than confirmed species because it is often impossible to determine whether similar-looking fossils represent one species or several.”
The fossil assemblage contains an unusual diversity of fruits, seeds, and reproductive structures. Although the exceptional preservation helped researchers recover this material, Saulsbury believes the forest itself differed from many other known Cretaceous environments.
“However, we don’t believe these findings are simply the result of preservation bias,” he said. “It appears to represent a genuinely unusual forest.”
How Fruit Size Connects to Ancient Forests
Fruit size can provide information about the environments in which plants evolved and how their seeds may have spread. Today, many flowering plants produce fleshy fruits that attract animals, which can transport seeds away from the parent plant after eating the fruit.
“Large fruits tend to occur in moist environments with densely packed forests,” Saulsbury said. “Our findings indicate that modern-looking forest structure and reproductive ecology were developing earlier than previously believed. The diversification of flowering plant reproductive strategies did not have to wait until after the end-of-Cretaceous extinction.”
The discovery also complicates an established explanation for the evolution of fruit-bearing plants. Scientists had proposed that large, fleshy fruits became more widespread as mammals diversified following the extinction of non-avian dinosaurs, creating new opportunities for plants to disperse their seeds through animals.
“As mammals expanded into newly available ecological niches, flowering plants were thought to have diversified their seed dispersal strategies in response,” Saulsbury said. “Our findings suggest that story began earlier. If diverse, large fruits already existed in Cretaceous forests, they were likely being dispersed not only by early mammals but also by large dinosaurs and other animals.”
Reference: “Diversification of angiosperm reproductive strategies predated the end-Cretaceous extinction” by Jaemin Lee, Dori L. Contreras, James G. Saulsbury, Garland R. Upchurch and Cindy V. Looy, 25 June 2026,

title: A New Iron Age? Scientists Uncover a Potential Game Changer for Clean Energy
content:
Technology
Iron dust flame at lab scale. For presentation purposes, the photo has been rotated by 90 degrees. Credit: Janik Hebel
Scientists are exploring how iron powder could transform renewable energy storage and transportation while giving aging coal power plants a new purpose.
Iron powder could help transform old coal power plants into a source of climate-neutral electricity, according to a new study from the
Karlsruhe Institute of Technology (KIT)
. Researchers found that this recyclable fuel could help keep Europe’s power supply stable during extended periods of weak wind and sunlight, particularly in regions where other forms of energy storage are limited.
The process relies on a cycle in which iron powder is burned to generate heat, producing iron oxide, commonly known as rust. Hydrogen produced using renewable energy can then remove the oxygen from the iron oxide, restoring the metal so it can be used again. “This works in a cycle that emits no carbon dioxide or environmentally harmful substances,” said Julia Schuler from KIT’s Institute for Industrial Production (IIP).
Turning Coal Power Plants Into Iron-Fueled Facilities
One potential advantage is that iron powder could be used in existing coal power plants without replacing all their equipment. “When burned, iron powder behaves very much like coal. We wanted to find out whether it was possible to repurpose existing coal power plants to iron-firing,” said Schuler.
According to Schuler, most modifications would involve the equipment responsible for generating heat. Other major components, including steam turbines, generators, and connections to the electricity grid, could remain in service. Germany may be particularly well suited to this approach because of its large fleet of coal power plants and the possibility of retaining existing heating networks and other infrastructure.
Transporting Renewable Energy Without Hydrogen Pipelines
Iron powder could also provide a practical way to move renewable energy across long distances. Electricity generated by coastal wind farms or solar facilities in desert regions could be used to produce hydrogen, which would convert iron oxide into iron. The resulting powder could then be transported to another location and burned to recover the stored energy.
Unlike hydrogen, which requires specialized pipelines, import terminals, and underground storage facilities, iron powder is relatively straightforward to transport and store for extended periods. This could reduce the infrastructure investment needed to move renewable energy between regions. Surplus renewable electricity generated within Europe could also be used to regenerate iron locally through an intermediate hydrogen production step.
Computer Models Reveal Where Iron Could Be Most Useful
To investigate the technology’s potential, KIT scientists built on findings from the Clean Circles research project. In a study funded by Stiftung Energieforschung Baden-Württemberg (Baden-Württemberg energy-research foundation), they expanded the established PERSEUS energy model to include iron-fueled power plants, facilities for regenerating iron, and the infrastructure needed for storage and transportation.
The researchers then simulated the development of a climate-neutral European energy system through 2050, comparing iron with competing technologies such as batteries, hydrogen storage, and hydrogen power plants. Iron-fired power plants appeared in the lowest-cost energy system across every scenario examined, although the results did not suggest that iron would replace hydrogen.
The greatest benefits emerged in countries with limited hydropower resources or few suitable locations for underground hydrogen storage. In these regions, iron could help maintain electricity supplies during prolonged shortages of wind and solar generation. It could also reduce demand on hydrogen pipelines and import facilities when their capacity becomes constrained.
The Challenges That Could Determine Iron’s Future
“Iron might play a very special, but economically meaningful role for reaching climate-neutrality and in reliably making renewables available,” said Schuler.
Whether a new “iron age” emerges in electricity generation will depend largely on two unresolved technical and economic questions: how extensively existing coal power plants must be modified and how efficiently iron oxide can be converted back into reusable iron. The simulations indicate that iron could complement hydrogen in a climate-neutral energy system, but its practical competitiveness will depend on how these processes perform outside the model.
Reference: “A new iron age? The potential role of iron fuel in Europe’s clean energy transition” by Julia Schuler, Armin Ardone, Viktor Slednev and Wolf Fichtner, 8 June 2026,

title: Is Einstein Wrong? Deep-Sea Neutrinos Put the Laws of Physics to the Test
content:
Neutrinos are tiny, nearly massless subatomic particles that rarely interact with matter. Produced by nuclear reactions in stars, radioactive decay, and powerful cosmic events, trillions pass through your body every second without you noticing. Credit: SciTechDaily.com
Scientists are testing whether one of Einstein’s most fundamental principles holds true throughout the Universe.
A neutrino telescope deep in the Mediterranean Sea has put one of Einstein’s fundamental principles to a new test. After analyzing 5,828 atmospheric neutrino candidate events, scientists found no evidence that Lorentz invariance, a cornerstone of relativity, had been violated. Their findings place new restrictions on theories suggesting that the laws of physics might behave differently under certain conditions.
The international KM3NeT collaboration conducted the study using KM3NeT/ORCA, an underwater detector designed to investigate neutrinos and their unusual behavior. Published in the
Journal of Cosmology and Astroparticle Physics
(JCAP), the research establishes the first direct experimental limits on certain possible violations involving muon and tau neutrinos, two types of these elusive particles.
Could Spacetime Have a Hidden Structure?
Lorentz invariance requires the fundamental laws of physics to remain unchanged for observers moving at different constant velocities or facing different directions. Some theories of quantum gravity, which attempt to unite general relativity with quantum physics, suggest that this principle might not hold perfectly at extremely small scales.
One possibility is that spacetime is not truly continuous but consists of tiny, discrete units. If such a structure exists, it could produce subtle deviations from the predictions of relativity.
View from inside a detector building block of detection units. Clearly visible the yellow buoy of a nearby detection unit. Credit: Edward Berbee/Nikhef
“We still don’t know whether our spacetime is continuous or might be discrete,” explains Alba Domi, a researcher at the Erlangen Center for Astroparticle Physics (ECAP), Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg, and one of the study’s corresponding authors. “Looking for violations of Lorentz invariance is one way to investigate this possibility.”
Why Neutrinos Are Ideal for Testing Einstein’s Physics
Neutrinos are exceptionally difficult to detect because they interact so weakly with matter. Vast numbers pass through Earth without leaving a trace, allowing them to travel enormous distances with little interference.
These particles also possess an unusual ability: they can transform between different types, or “flavor” (this is the term used by scientists), as they travel. Known as neutrino oscillation, this phenomenon follows mathematical predictions that scientists can test against observations. Unexpected changes in these oscillations could indicate previously unknown physical effects, including violations of Lorentz invariance.
To search for such discrepancies, the researchers examined 1.4 years of observations collected by KM3NeT/ORCA. At the time, the telescope was operating with only six detection units. The team compared the neutrinos’ measured energies and arrival directions with theoretical predictions to identify potential departures from established physics.
Underwater Observations Set New Limits on Physics
The analysis revealed no evidence of Lorentz invariance violation. However, it established tighter constraints on certain possible effects, including those that could influence oscillations between muon and tau neutrinos.
Despite relying on an early version of the detector, the results were competitive with measurements from established experiments such as IceCube and Super-Kamiokande, which have collected neutrino data over much longer periods.
Optical module attached to the Dyneema ropes of the detection unit. Credit: KM3NeT Collaboration
“These results show the potential of KM3NeT/ORCA to test fundamental principles of physics, even with a relatively small detector,” says Lukas Hennig, a PhD student at ECAP and the study’s other corresponding author. “With more data and an expanding detector, we will be able to search for even smaller effects.”
The Next Frontier: Neutrinos From Deep Space
As KM3NeT/ORCA expands toward its full planned configuration, researchers expect to improve their sensitivity to possible deviations from relativity. They also hope to extend these investigations to KM3NeT/ARCA, a detector designed to study much higher-energy neutrinos originating from distant astrophysical sources.
Some proposed violations of Lorentz invariance could become more pronounced as neutrino energy increases or as particles travel across greater distances. Neutrinos arriving from distant cosmic sources may therefore offer a way to test effects too small to detect with atmospheric neutrinos.
“ARCA could be particularly well suited to this kind of research, but we don’t yet have enough astrophysical neutrino events to perform such an analysis,” explains Domi.
Reference: “Atmospheric neutrino constraints on Lorentz invariance violation with the first six detection units of KM3NeT/ORCA” by O. Adriani et al., 4 November 2026,
Journal of Cosmology and Astroparticle Physics

title: Scientists Discover a Hidden Weakness in Prostate Cancer That Could Transform Treatment
content:
The graphic conceptualizes PBITE-1, shown in blue, binding to ERG. Credit: Jessica Johnson
A newly identified vulnerability in a cancer-driving protein could pave the way for a different approach to treating prostate cancer.
Researchers at the
University of Michigan
have identified a potential way to target a protein that helps drive prostate cancer but has long been considered beyond the reach of drugs. Their experimental compound, PBITE-1, interfered with the protein’s cancer-promoting activity in laboratory models, offering a possible starting point for more targeted treatments.
The protein, known as ERG, becomes abnormally active when two genes,
, fuse together. This genetic rearrangement occurs in roughly half of prostate cancer cases among patients of European ancestry and promotes tumor cell growth and migration.
Scientists Discover a Hidden Target in ERG
For years, ERG has been considered “undruggable” because it appeared to lack the molecular pockets where medications typically attach. In the new study, published in the
Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
, researchers discovered an accessible pocket in a region called the PNT domain, which helps regulate ERG’s interactions with other proteins.
After screening more than 1,600 compounds, the team identified a promising molecule and refined it into PBITE-1. In experiments involving prostate cancer cell lines and laboratory models of human and mouse prostate tissue, the compound inhibited ERG activity, triggered cancer cell death, and reduced the ability of cancer cells to invade surrounding tissue.
“Although we were the first to identify the gene fusion as a driver of prostate cancer, it was challenging to find a drug target for ERG,” said Arul Chinnaiyan, M.D., Ph.D., S.P. Hicks Professor of Pathology and member of the Rogel Cancer Center.
Why Current Prostate Cancer Treatments Have Limitations
Most existing prostate cancer therapies focus on androgen receptors, proteins that respond to hormones such as testosterone. These receptors can activate the
TMPRSS2-ERG
fusion, helping fuel tumor growth. Drugs that block androgen signaling can slow the disease, but tumors often develop resistance, and treatment can cause side effects that affect quality of life.
Targeting ERG directly could provide an alternative approach for patients whose tumors carry the gene fusion, rather than relying exclusively on treatments that interfere with hormone signaling.
“This work shows that instead of treating all prostate cancer as one disease, we have the potential to personalize therapy for subtypes of prostate cancer.”
An Early Step Toward More Precise Treatments
PBITE-1 remains an experimental research tool, and its effects have not been established in patients. Further research will be needed to determine whether compounds targeting ERG can be developed into safe and effective medicines.
“Although it is unlikely that PBITE-1 is ready to become a drug any time soon, this study shows that ERG is a druggable target,” Chinnaiyan said.
“It is exciting that we now have a path forward to target ERG in prostate cancer.”

title: A New Approach Could Eliminate “Zombie” Cancer Cells That Survive Chemotherapy
content:
Researchers have identified proteins that allow damaged cancer cells to persist after chemotherapy and potentially promote tumor recovery. Credit: Shutterstock
Some cancer cells survive chemotherapy by blocking their own self-destruct system, but researchers have found a way to switch it back on and kill those cells.
Chemotherapy can leave behind cancer cells that have stopped dividing but remain alive and capable of helping a tumor recover. These survivors can draw support from an unexpected source, the immune system, by activating responses that normally help the body repair damaged tissue.
This “zombie-like state,” called “premature senescence,” involves dramatic changes. Within a few days of exposure to chemotherapy, senescent cells can grow to almost ten times the size of a normal cell and increase the activity of genes associated with wound healing. Their ability to release inflammatory mediators, molecules that attract immune cells, also increases greatly.
Cancer exploits the body’s repair system
The danger lies in the range of jobs the immune system performs. Alongside protecting against infection, it coordinates the repair and replacement of damaged tissue. During wound healing, it stimulates cell division to replace cells lost through injury and triggers the growth of blood vessels that deliver extra oxygen and nutrients. Normally, this complex, carefully coordinated process ensures that new cells appear only where and when they are needed.
Senescent cancer cells stained for a ‘Death Receptor’ protein that is highly upregulated in response to chemotherapeutic treatment. Credit: Professor Seamus Martin, Trinity College Dublin
Cancers can exploit those repair functions by masquerading as damaged tissue. Instead of destroying malignant cells, the immune system can then help them divide and obtain more oxygen and nutrients. That behavior has led cancers to be described as “wounds that do not heal,” although how they activate the immune system’s wound-healing capabilities remains poorly understood.
Proteins shield cancer cells from chemotherapy
Research newly published in
Science Advances
identifies a mechanism that helps cancer cells survive chemotherapy and enter senescence. Scientists at the Smurfit Institute of Genetics at Trinity College Dublin found that molecules called Inhibitor of Apoptosis Proteins, or IAPs, can protect tumor cells from the killing effects of commonly used chemotherapy drugs. The team was led by Professor Seamus Martin, Smurfit Professor of Medical Genetics, and Dr. Gokhan Gunay, a postdoctoral research fellow.
The researchers found that DNA damage caused by chemotherapy switched on molecules called “Death Receptors,” which can trigger a cell’s self-destruct program. IAPs neutralized their cell-killing effects. That protection allowed surviving tumor cells to enter senescence, where they could coordinate wound-healing responses that benefit the tumor and help it recover after treatment.
Reactivating cancer cells’ self-destruct program
But the cells’ continued survival also depended heavily on IAPs, creating a vulnerability. In the study, compounds called IAP antagonists neutralized these proteins and reactivated the Death Receptor self-destruct program, selectively eliminating the senescent cells. The same proteins that helped the cells escape chemotherapy thus remained essential to keeping them alive afterward.
Dr Gokhan Gunayh and Professor Seamus Martin in the lab in Trinity College Dublin. Credit: Professor Seamus Martin, Trinity College Dublin
Senescent cells are also relevant beyond cancer treatment. They accumulate in tissues as people age, and that buildup is thought to contribute to age-related inflammation and declining normal function in many tissues.
For cancer treatment, the findings identify both an escape mechanism and a possible way to target the cells that use it. Tumors that evade chemotherapy remain a major challenge for clinicians, and improved treatments could offer patients better survival and quality of life.
Professor Martin said, “Discovering how tumors can evade the cell-killing effects of chemotherapy and enter senescence is an important and challenging problem.
“These new findings suggest ways in which we may be able to lower the defenses of tumors by neutralizing IAPs after the delivery of chemotherapeutic drugs, which should block their entry to senescence and kill more cells of the tumor.”

Mielke, Sarah L. Doyle, Sabrina L. Spencer, Matthew Campbell, Conor J. Kearney, Hamid Kashkar and Seamus J. Martin, 23 October 2026,

title: Hidden Brain Signals Could Predict Alzheimer’s Years Before Symptoms Appear
content:
Brain waves are rhythmic patterns of electrical activity produced by the coordinated firing of neurons. These patterns change with sleep, attention, memory, and other mental processes, offering scientists valuable clues about how the brain functions. Credit: Shutterstock
Subtle differences in brain activity may reveal who is most vulnerable to Alzheimer’s disease and who could remain mentally sharp well into old age.
Distinct patterns of brain activity may predict Alzheimer’s disease years before memory problems or hallmark brain changes appear.
Stanford Medicine
researchers have developed a scoring system that identifies people at greater risk of cognitive decline while also recognizing those whose brains show unusual resilience to aging.
The study, published November 4 in
Science Advances
, found that these patterns could predict future cognitive decline more effectively than several established risk indicators, including genetics and Alzheimer’s biomarkers.
Identifying the Brain’s Hidden Patterns
Researchers analyzed resting-state functional MRI scans from 180 “super agers,” adults aged 75 and older with memory abilities comparable to those of typical 45-year-olds, and 110 similarly aged people diagnosed with Alzheimer’s disease.
“Normal, cognitively unimpaired individuals are pretty heterogeneous in terms of their biological abnormalities,” said Yu Zhang, PhD, assistant professor of psychiatry and behavioral sciences at Stanford Medicine. “Simply comparing super agers with such a heterogeneous population makes it challenging to define what is critical in terms of resilient or vulnerable brain patterns.”
The team identified distinct patterns of activity across brain networks and developed the Alzheimer’s resilience-vulnerability connectome (ARC) score. The system distinguished super agers from people with Alzheimer’s with approximately 85% accuracy.
Predicting Alzheimer’s Before Symptoms Appear
The researchers tested the ARC score in more than 1,300 cognitively healthy adults aged 55 to 70. Although participants initially showed no clear differences in cognitive performance, their brain activity patterns predicted different outcomes over follow-up periods extending as long as 12 years.
People with more Alzheimer’s-like activity experienced faster cognitive decline and were more likely to develop amyloid-beta plaques or receive an Alzheimer’s diagnosis. Those with super-ager-like patterns generally maintained stronger cognitive abilities.
“We used the ARC score to make a prediction of how likely this patient will convert into mild cognitive impairment or Alzheimer’s disease,” said Kanhao (Alex) Zhao, PhD, a Stanford postdoctoral scholar and lead author.
Going Beyond Traditional Biomarkers
“We want to address a major challenge in the Alzheimer’s field nowadays — most studies are looking at well-known Alzheimer’s disease biomarkers, such as amyloid-beta or tau. But those are observable at relatively late stages of the disease,” Zhang said. “What we really care about is defining early markers that can detect earlier signs of cognitive decline and potentially help us deliver timely interventions to people.”
The ARC score performed as well as or better than existing biomarkers at predicting progression toward Alzheimer’s, while offering information at an earlier stage. Combining the score with traditional biomarkers improved predictions further.
“We compared the ARC score with existing biomarkers in predicting people converting to Alzheimer’s disease,” Zhao said. “Our model shows comparable or better prediction ability, and it can do so at an earlier time point. And if we combine our score with the existing biomarkers, the prediction performance improves.”
The researchers also found a relationship between ARC scores and brain age, a broader measure of aging derived from functional MRI data.
“I’m excited we established a signature that can help us better understand the difference between people who can maintain excellent cognitive performance and people who show cognitive decline,” Zhang said.
Could Brain Activity Be Changed to Prevent Decline?
ARC scores are not diagnostic, and they do not determine a person’s future. Brain activity can change with aging, injuries, and neuropsychiatric conditions. Researchers hope that targeted interventions might eventually shift vulnerable brain patterns toward greater resilience.
Potential approaches include cognitive training and transcranial magnetic stimulation, which uses magnetic pulses to influence brain activity. However, these interventions have not been shown to prevent cognitive decline by changing ARC patterns.
“There are two main components: One is to know which part of the brain to target, the other is how we should change it,” Zhang said. “That’s why identifying the super-ager brain resilience pattern is a critical component — so we know what a good pattern should be.”
Zhang’s team is planning a trial to examine whether cognitive training can alter ARC scores.
“But the critical part is that we have to intervene at an early stage,” Zhang said. “That’s why we focus on the cognitively unimpaired population to identify super-ager-like versus Alzheimer’s-like individuals. If we can precisely identify such as early indicator, I’m optimistic that we can reverse or prevent this process through advanced intervention technologies.”
Reference: “A functional connectome identifies vulnerability to cognitive decline and Alzheimer’s disease progression” by Kanhao Zhao, Hua Xie, Gregory A. Fonzo, Nancy B. Carlisle, Tovia Jacobs, Ricardo S. Osorio, Arpana Church, Feng Vankee Lin, Yu Zhang and Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative, 4 November 2026,

title: Smithsonian Scientists Built a Virtual Universe 1.5 Billion Light-Years Across
content:
A rendering of the cosmic web, about 650 million light-years across, produced by the Lumina simulation. The fine filaments represent dark matter, and the warm orange and yellow tones highlight where gas is moving the fastest between galaxy clusters. Credit: Oliver Zier, Center for Astrophysics | Harvard & Smithsonian
Scientists have recreated the universe’s first 2 billion years in a record-breaking simulation that could reveal new secrets about the Big Bang and the birth of galaxies.
Scientists have recreated the universe’s first 2 billion years in extraordinary detail using one of the world’s most powerful supercomputers. The enormous simulation, called “Lumina,” allows researchers to explore how the earliest stars and galaxies formed, how dark matter influenced their development, and how radiation transformed the young cosmos.
Developed by researchers at the Center for Astrophysics | Harvard & Smithsonian, Lumina is among the largest and most sophisticated simulations of the early universe ever produced. It provides a virtual record of cosmic evolution that scientists can compare with observations from the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) and the Nancy Roman Space Telescope.
The research, published in
Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society
, could help answer fundamental questions about what happened after the Big Bang. By recreating the interactions between ordinary matter, dark matter, and radiation, scientists can test whether their current theories accurately describe the early universe or whether surprising telescope discoveries point to physics that remains unexplained.
The cosmic web structure as simulated by Lumina, showing where helium has changed to its modern form in the early universe (cyan regions). Credit: Oliver Zier, Center for Astrophysics | Harvard & Smithsonian
Recreating the Universe to Test Cosmic Theories
Astronomers have spent centuries studying the sky and developing theories to explain the origins of stars, galaxies, and the enormous structures that fill the universe. Modern supercomputers have added a powerful new approach by allowing scientists to simulate how the cosmos should develop if those theories are correct.
These simulations act as virtual laboratories. Researchers can start with conditions in the young universe, apply the known laws of physics, and calculate how matter and energy evolve over billions of years. The results can then be compared with actual telescope observations.
If the simulated universe resembles what astronomers observe, it strengthens confidence in the underlying models. But if important differences emerge, those discrepancies could reveal missing pieces in our understanding of cosmic history.
“With JWST, the early universe has become an exciting new frontier in astrophysics,” said lead author Oliver Zier, an ITC Fellow at the Center for Astrophysics | Harvard & Smithsonian. “To understand what we are seeing with this telescope, we need to translate our theories into detailed predictions. After several years of work, with plenty of ups and downs, it is incredibly rewarding to see the simulation results and watch our predictions come to life in video.”
A Virtual Universe 1.5 Billion Light-Years Across
Lumina sets a new benchmark for a particular class of cosmological simulations known as radiation hydrodynamics simulations. These models calculate how gas, dark matter, and radiation influence one another as the universe develops, making it possible to investigate the processes responsible for creating the earliest galaxies.
Dark matter is an invisible form of matter whose gravitational influence helps shape galaxies and other cosmic structures. Meanwhile, radiation from stars and other luminous objects affects the surrounding gas, changing its temperature and physical state. Capturing these interactions is essential for understanding how the early universe evolved.
Lumina follows these processes across the first 2 billion years of cosmic history, revealing how young galaxies formed and how their light gradually altered the enormous clouds of gas that filled the space between them.
The simulation’s scale is particularly remarkable. It encompasses a cube of space approximately 1.5 billion light-years along each side, representing more than 100 times the volume covered by previous comparable simulations. That enormous region is similar in scale to the volumes of the universe astronomers can investigate with today’s most advanced telescopes.
Capturing a Crucial Transformation in Cosmic History
One of Lumina’s most important advances involves a process called reionization, which fundamentally changed the gas that filled the early universe.
As the first generations of luminous objects emerged, their radiation stripped electrons from atoms of hydrogen and helium, transforming much of the surrounding gas into an ionized state. This transition helped establish the conditions found throughout the universe today.
Lumina is the first simulation of its kind to model helium reionization as it happened while allowing the resulting changes to immediately affect other processes unfolding within the simulated cosmos.
“We feel incredibly fortunate to be building simulations like Lumina,” said Aaron Smith, an assistant professor of physics at the University of Texas at Dallas and an author on the paper. “For the first time, we can follow along as both hydrogen and helium changed into their modern form across such an enormous volume of the universe, while still resolving the galaxies and other luminous objects driving that transformation.”
The Frontier supercomputer at Oak Ridge National Laboratory in Tennessee, where scientists used more than 15,000 graphics processors to recreate the universe’s first 2 billion years in extraordinary detail. Credit: Carlos Jones/Oak Ridge National Laboratory, U.S. Dept. of Energy
More Than 15,000 Processors Recreate Billions of Years
Building such an enormous and detailed virtual universe required extraordinary computing power.
The team used Frontier, a supercomputer at Oak Ridge National Laboratory in Tennessee that ranks among the fastest machines in the world. More than 15,000 graphics processing units worked together to perform the immense number of calculations needed to produce Lumina.
That processing power made it possible to simulate a much larger region of the early universe than previously comparable models while preserving enough detail to investigate individual galaxies, stars, and black holes.
This combination of scale and precision is especially valuable because cosmic evolution involves processes operating across vastly different distances. Changes occurring around individual galaxies can influence the gas between them, while the overall distribution of matter helps determine where galaxies form.
A New Tool for Uncovering the Universe’s Mysteries
Lumina is designed to do more than recreate the past. It gives astronomers a way to investigate competing explanations for how the universe developed and to make predictions that can be tested against real observations.
Future research will examine how gas travels between galaxies, how radiation left over from the Big Bang influenced cosmic evolution, and how regions of particularly intense star formation emerged and changed over time.
As observations from JWST, Roman, and other telescopes provide increasingly detailed views of the distant universe, Lumina will help researchers interpret what they find.
Reference: “Introducing the lumina project: large-volume radiation-hydrodynamic simulations of the epochs of hydrogen and helium reionization” by Oliver Zier, Aaron Smith, Xuejian Shen, Rongrong Liu, Rahul Kannan, Sonja M Koehler, Volker Springel, Rüdiger Pakmor, Mark Vogelsberger, Teodora-Elena Bulichi and Lars Hernquist, 26 October 2026,
Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society
DOI: 10.1093/mnras/stag1469

title: Anputai New Energy gets new investment for space-grade perovskite-silicon tandem cells
content:
Anputai New Energy gets new investment for space-grade perovskite-silicon tandem cells
Shanghai Anputai New Energy
, a developer of space-grade perovskite tandem solar cells, has received tens of millions of yuan (several million US dollars) in new investment, according to an announcement on Nov 9, 2026. Songjiang State-owned Investment, Shanghai Rongtai Fund and Bozheng Capital are the new shareholders. The company says the main equipment for its 20 MW space-grade perovskite tandem production line in Songjiang, Shanghai, has arrived, and that it is adapting the equipment and preparing the plant. The line is nearing completion, and the company plans to produce its first batch of cells by the end of November.
Anputai, a spin-off of Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics founded in 2023, is developing perovskite-silicon tandem cells for commercial satellites. It has worked with the Shanghai Institute of Space Power-Sources on space perovskite tandem cells since the end of 2023, and the two have built a joint lab. Reports say that samples have passed electron irradiation, thermal shock and reverse-bias tests, and that the company is planning verification across particle radiation, UV exposure, temperature cycling and vacuum cycling. No efficiency or lifetime figures have been disclosed.
In July 2026, the company reported a Series A round of nearly 100 million yuan (about US$14 million), led by Shanghai Kechuang Intellectual Property with Chengzhu Capital and Chuanghehui. It said the money would go toward an engineering production line, space environment testing, product iteration and team expansion.

title: Slot-die-coated perovskite module reaches 22.70% efficiency, with devices retaining 97.76% after 1,300 hours
content:
Slot-die-coated perovskite module reaches 22.70% efficiency, with devices retaining 97.76% after 1,300 hours
Researchers from Dalian Jiaotong University, the University of Chinese Academy of Sciences and Liaoning Normal University have developed a combined additive strategy that widens the processing window for slot-die coating of perovskite films in ambient air. Slot-die coating is seen as a scalable deposition route for perovskite devices because it makes efficient use of material and is compatible with continuous manufacturing. The researchers say the technique is limited by a narrow window between deposition and annealing, and by inhomogeneous ink distribution, both of which hold back device performance.
The team introduced rubidium thiocyanate (RbSCN) and formamidinium thiocyanate (FASCN) together. According to the researchers, the two additives regulate nucleation kinetics and phase evolution at the same time. They say an in situ coordination mechanism lowers the energy barrier for the δ-to-α phase transition and suppresses the formation of non-photoactive phases.
This leads to uniform crystallization over a time window of more than 100 seconds, the team reports. The resulting α-FAPbI₃ films are dense and large-grained, with a smaller vertical compositional gradient and reduced residual strain. The researchers also report fewer defects, longer carrier lifetimes and better energy-level alignment, which they say supports efficient charge extraction and less nonradiative recombination.
Using the strategy, the team deposited large-area films and fabricated perovskite solar modules with an efficiency of 22.70%. Unencapsulated devices retained 97.76% of their initial efficiency after 1,300 hours under the ISOS-L-3 protocol. The researchers describe the approach as a generalizable way to decouple crystallization kinetics from processing constraints.

CREC 2026
多议题深度研讨，凝聚行业共识
大会同期将举办2026 新能源产业生态大会、分布式光伏 + 储能会议、中欧新能源项目对接会、零碳园区建设与运营培训大会、长三角充换电设施建设运营研讨会、算电协同发展研讨会等系列高端论坛。围绕产业生态构建、光储融合、跨境项目合作、零碳园区落地、充换电网络建设、算力与电力协同等热点方向，汇聚政企、科研、产业代表深度交流，碰撞前沿观点、对接资源商机，为新能源高质量发展献策赋能。
共话能源生态，聚焦ESG投融资
11月12日下午，主论坛“2026新能源产业生态大会暨ESG与投融资领袖峰会”在君来世尊酒店梅花厅举行。将围绕政策趋势、绿色资本与全球市场三大主线展开。
汇聚院士专家、头部企业、金融机构及国际行业代表，打造高规格产业交流平台。论坛设置重磅主题分享与两大高端对话环节，聚焦ESG价值转型与新能源投融资创新、算力中心产业机遇、“一带一路”光储市场布局、新能源产业出海风险防控等行业核心热点，深度剖析产业发展新趋势与商业模式。活动现场还将举行“2026十大分布式光储品牌”颁奖仪式，树立行业标杆，助力新能源产业高质量规范化发展。
破解绿电与算力融合命题
11月11日率先启幕的绿电算力融合——算电协同发展研讨会，是本届大会前瞻布局的特色专场。
现场将举行无锡市能源集团与无锡数据集团、广盈集团的签约仪式；围绕绿电直连关键问题、AI算力电力一体化实践、苏南电网支撑算力布局、东西部算力中心标杆案例展开深度分享；圆桌对话聚焦柔性可调算力负荷市场、AIDC节能降碳、电力市场交易收益分配、新型储能应用四大核心命题，打通“绿电-电网-算力”全链路实践路径。
无膜电解的技术路线
首次增设的CREC-GHF 2026国际可再生能源制氢会议，于11月13日举办，以全英文论坛为特色，汇聚欧、以、加、荷等多国技术力量，是本届大会国际化程度最高的专场之一。
最大亮点来自以色列H2Pro公司，其首席技术官带来无膜解耦水电解（DWE）技术深度分享。该技术通过分时产氢产氧适配可再生能源波动，摆脱传统隔膜依赖，是绿氢技术路线的重点方向之一。论坛同步覆盖高温电解、PEM制氢、AEM阴离子交换膜、氢脆防腐涂层等多路线技术，探讨绿色氢氨产业化、氢能早期投资孵化路径。
直击行业痛点的技术方案
第十三届分布式光伏+储能会议聚焦“市场价值重构”，于11月13日举办，精选一批针对具体问题的技术：
- 板块互联组件技术：实现无热斑、高发电量，针对组件的能效与可靠性；
- 源侧直流直储方案：直流侧直接充放，破解限电弃光、电站低效难题；
- AI智驭配储系统：叠加智能算法，适配负电价环境，重塑工商业储能收益模型。
从有线到无线的场景迭代
长三角充换电基础设施建设运营高质量发展专题会议于11月12日下午举办，跳出传统基建讨论，聚焦重卡换电、液冷超充、移动能源、磁共振无线充电等新形态。其中磁共振无线充电技术亮相会场，指向不需要线缆的能源补给方式。
CREC 2026
头部企业联袂参展，共展硬核实力
本届展览会，十一科技、无锡市能源集团、国联集团、威孚、通威、远东、中国电信、上能、奥特维、爱旭、极电、萨科特、朗新科技、国网公司、CPVT、氢测科技、亿能电力、红翼安防、航天国器、牧羽天、数字鹰科技、等多家知名企业将集中亮相、展览展示。
专精特新企业同台集结，带来全产业链前沿产品、创新技术与系统解决方案，搭建高效的供需对接、商务洽谈、技术交流平台，共探新能源及低空产业发展新机遇。
CREC 2026
组团采购，精准匹配合作需求
带着清单来的采购团
11月14日上午，中欧新能源（光储）项目投资对接会在君来世尊酒店12号会议室举行。
本次会议汇聚多家欧洲光储企业组团来华，角色覆盖EPC、项目开发、系统集成、光储批发、EMS、资产运营与跨境供应链。与一般参观不同，这些企业明确列出了采购与考察重点，目标清晰。不仅如此，欧洲企业与机构代表的关注点也正在从“采购产品”进一步转向建立长期技术合作关系：公用事业规模储能的下一代技术、氢能的系统级应用、开放架构与系统集成、电网容量约束下的综合方案，以及装备电动化带来的储能新需求。
标杆集结，共拓分布式光储新局
经过筛选评审，本次活动遴选出来自上海、广东、山东、河北、河南、浙江、江西、江苏、湖北、安徽、云南等多地100余家分布式光伏服务商，业务覆盖投资、开发、安装、分销、运维、设计等全链条。企业以技术筑基、以服务赋能，依托创新实践助力行业稳步前行。
全国各地优秀服务商整装待发，将亮相11月12-13日第十八届无锡国际新能源展览会（CREC2026），期待这批行业标杆齐聚无锡，引领分布式光储产业迈向高质量发展新台阶。
CREC 2026
百变“新能”，应用纷呈
本届展会集中展示太阳能光伏、储能、氢能、交能融合等领域新产品、新技术和新应用。钙钛矿、BC、HJC等光伏组件产品、超级充电桩、氢燃料电池系统、新能源智能化装备以及低空经济区等特色产品将精彩亮相。让我们看一看有哪些百变多样的新能源应用形式吧~
CREC 2026
现代科技与传统艺术融合
光伏，是划破能源迷雾的科技之光，是人类对蔚蓝星球的绿色诺言。硅片将阳光转化为流动的能量，光伏板在天地间铺展科技图景，定格成东方美学的画卷。这是一次科技与艺术的跨界对话，是光伏人用东方美学书写的绿色宣言。2026年11月12-13日，无锡太湖博览中心第十八届无锡新能源展览会（CREC2026）A馆专区，杨智平先生光伏画展将重磅亮相。
CREC 2026
脱下西装，光伏老男孩的绿茵对决
平日里，他们是行业里运筹帷幄的企业高管、协会负责人、技术专家，在光储赛道上攻坚破局；脱下西装、卸下头衔，光伏行业的从业者们，拥有另一片属于自己的战场 —— 绿茵足球场。踏上草坪，他们即将化身为前锋、后卫、门将，只为奔赴一场属于光伏人的四年之约。

合作揽才双发力｜面向全球邀伙伴、纳贤才
依托本次无锡新能源展平台，远东股份带来前沿线缆与储能整体解决方案，面向行业寻求项目合作，可提供产品供货、联合投标等多种合作模式，诚邀行业伙伴洽谈对接。

content:
11月10日，国网新能源云公示了辽宁省2027年机制竞价结果。
光伏项目机制电量规模1028633.547兆瓦时，机制电价水平0.2000元/千瓦时，项目9055个；风电机制电量规模1879765.028兆瓦时，机制电价水平0.3000元/千瓦时，项目30个。
根据竞价文件，本次竞价纳入机制的电量总规模为53.08亿千瓦时。其中，风电为39.56亿千瓦时，光伏为13.52亿千瓦时。风电、光伏竞价上限均为0.3元/千瓦时，竞价下限均为0.18元/千瓦时。
由此可见风电项目为竞价上限出清，电量只用48%。光伏则逼近下限出清，与2026年0.3元/度，价格下降33%。

title: Envision Energy and ju:niz Energy strengthen partnership with BESS project
content:
Envision Energy and ju:niz Energy strengthen partnership with BESS project TGS 4C | 4C Offshore News
Envision Energy and ju:niz Energy strengthen partnership with BESS project
Envision Energy and ju:niz Energy have expanded their partnership with
a battery energy storage project in Bavaria, Germany.
The 442 MWh Smareg 13 project is expected to support Germany's growing
renewable energy sector by increasing energy storage capacity as demand
for clean power continues to rise.
Smareg 13 is the third project completed by the two companies. It combines
ju:niz Energy's expertise in the development and long-term operation of
large-scale battery storage projects with Envision Energy's battery energy
storage system (BESS) technology and project delivery capabilities.
According to the companies, the project will strengthen energy storage
capacity in the region through the deployment of Smarteg 13, which will
utilise Envision Energy's Gen 8 BESS platform. The system offers four hour
energy storage duration, advanced battery technology and grid forming capabilities,
while its low noise design makes it suitable for a wide range of operating
environments.
Henry Peng, Senior Vice President of Envision Energy and President of its
Europe and Latin America regions, said: "With Smareg 13, we are bringing
together our Gen 8 BESS technology and expanding local capabilities in
Germany to help build the flexible, resilient energy infrastructure required
for the country's next phase of renewable energy growth."
Vural Oezcan, Chief Operating Officer of ju:niz Energy, added: "The
project combines a very advanced stage of development with four-hour storage
technology and will make an important contribution to flexibility and system
stability."

title: UK and Japan sign offshore wind industrial compact

content:
The UK and Japan have strengthened their long-standing offshore wind relationship
through the signing of an Offshore Wind Industrial Compact, which aims
to provide a framework for increased cooperation between the two countries.
According to the announcement, the agreement will leverage both nations'
strengths, combining the UK's experience in offshore wind policy and project
delivery with Japan's extensive industrial capabilities and manufacturing
expertise.
The compact will be implemented through the UK government's Department
for Energy Security and Net Zero and Japan's Ministry of Economy, Trade
and Industry.
The arrangement aims to support the development of fixed-bottom, floating
and deepwater offshore wind projects, while strengthening supply chains,
encouraging investment and enhancing energy security in both countries.
The agreement also underscores the UK and Japan's ambition to become global
leaders in floating and deepwater offshore wind. To support this goal,
the partners plan to develop an aligned technical roadmap and establish
a pathway for reducing project costs.

title: 3t and Ørsted partner on offshore wind training hub
content:
Safety-critical training provider 3t has partnered with Ørsted to launch
a new training facility for wind turbine technicians at Ørsted's new Hub
in Grimsby.
The facility is expected to open in summer 2027 and will feature a specialised
wind turbine training simulator that replicates the internal and external
structure of a wind turbine generator.
The simulator will provide hands-on training designed to equip technicians
with the skills and knowledge needed to carry out work safely in offshore
wind environments.
Under the agreement, the partners will deliver Global Wind Organisation
(GWO) accredited safety and emergency response courses, including Basic
Safety Training and Advanced Rescue Training.
Jamie Purves, managing director of 3t Training Services UK, said: "This
partnership builds on a longstanding relationship we've built with Ørsted
over the years, and we're delighted to embed our training expertise within
their East Coast Hub operations."
Chris Reed, competent development specialist senior lead at Ørsted, said:
"The new training rig will help equip our people with the skills and
practical experience needed to safely operate and maintain our offshore
wind farms."
According to the announcement, the partnership reinforces the long-term
relationship between the two companies. Initially, the facility and training
programmes will support Ørsted employees and contractors working across
its offshore wind operations.

title: Saitec Offshore joins Castelló PortLab innovation commission
content:
Saitec Offshore Technologies has joined the External Innovation Commission
of Castelló PortLab, an initiative established to promote innovation and
new opportunities within the port sector.
The company said it will contribute experience gained through the DemoSATH
floating wind project while exploring opportunities for collaboration within
Castellón's industrial ecosystem.
In their announcement they have referenced reports by Offshore Renewable
Energy Catapult and the Global Wind Energy Council (GWEC) which have highlighted
the importance of port infrastructure, industrial capability and early
investment planning to support the floating offshore wind industry.
Saitec Offshore said port requirements have influenced the development
of its SATH floating wind technology. The platform requires around 10 metres
of water depth, enabling manufacturing activities to be undertaken at a
broader range of ports.
The Port of Castellón is seeking to establish itself as a floating offshore
wind manufacturing hub in the Mediterranean. Backed by €50.8m secured
through the IDAE PORT-EOLMAR programme back in June 2026. The funding was
provided through the EU's NextGenerationEU initiative.
"We want to get to know the innovative companies working around the
port, understand what they are developing and see where it makes sense
to work together,” said David Carrascosa, CEO of Saitec Offshore Technologies.

title: Mosaic Raises Funds for Robotic Surgery
content: Anthropic said on Tuesday that it has launched its roadshow, a 7 to 10 day period ahead of an IPO in which a company pitches prospective institutional investors like mutual funds, pension funds and hedge funds. Interestingly, the tentative valuation the Claude-maker set, of between $1.26 trillion to $1.4 trillion, was slightly lower than what investors initially expected. (And, it’s also around the $1.25 trillion valuation that OpenAI recently raised $11 billion at, despite the fact that Anthropic generates more revenue. That’s likely for several reasons, including that Anthropic likely wants its stock to have some wiggle room to trade up after its IPO.) Meanwhile, the largest pure-play robotics company in the world by revenue and market cap is Intuitive Surgical , which makes the da Vinci Surgical System , a multi-armed contraption that human surgeons use on a remote-control basis to perform a variety of operations. But da Vinci was first unveiled over 25 years ago, and a new generation of robotics companies is aiming to further automate surgery by harnessing the latest advances in AI. One such startup, Mosaic Intelligence Labs , has raised $47 million across two rounds of seed funding led by 8VC and Fundomo , the one-year-old company told The Information exclusively. Mosaic is developing a semi-autonomous catheter that can “find its own way” through a patient’s blood network during a surgery, said co-founder and CEO Ileana Pirozzi. As a human surgeon feeds the catheter into the body, the tip of the catheter will bend in different directions to travel down the correct veins and arteries. Eventually, Mosaic plans for its catheters to work mostly autonomously. In the meantime, the company also aims to provide surgeons with better maps of their patients’ circulatory systems—a strategy that Pirozzi says helps provide a product roadmap that doesn't require full autonomy in order to be valuable. Currently, surgeons steer their catheters based on a snapshot of the patient’s body taken days before the operation, as well as two-dimensional X-rays taken periodically during the operation. Mosaic aims to provide a 3D map of the patient’s circulatory system that updates in real time during the surgery, based on sensor data from the catheter inside the body, as well as the surgeon’s hands. “When you talk to the world’s best surgeons, they tell you that they can see themselves inside the catheter,” said Pirozzi. “What Mosaic does instead is that we take that image, we take that 3D world that they're making in their heads, and we put it on a screen.” To generate such 3D maps, Mosaic is drawing on data that is generated in computer simulations. That is a longstanding technique in robotics, but historically simulations have been best suited for tasks involving rigid objects. Computers have struggled to simulate squishy and deformable objects, such as a person’s veins. For that reason, when Mosaic started, Pirozzi says she was skeptical that simulations would be able to model the circulatory system in high enough fidelity. She was surprised to find that models trained on synthetic data outperformed models trained on real data alone. Thanks to that synthetic data, it’s as though Mosaic’s catheters have traveled through many more blood vessels than they actually have. Mosaic uses simulation software from Nvidia and collaborates closely with the chip giant, said Pirozzi, who met her co-founder Alison Mackanic while the pair were earning their PhDs at Stanford University . Mosaic is already collaborating with HonorHealth , an Arizona healthcare system. It is only the second AI and robotics company that has reached that stage, said Hasan Aldailami , the network director of vascular and endovascular surgery at HonorHealth and professor of surgery at Arizona State University . Aldailami said he receives a pitch from a new tech company about every other week. “The emails, the LinkedIn messages, they don't stop,” he said. Many of those requests to collaborate aren’t very exciting because they tend to focus on narrow aspects of care, said Aldailami. For Mosaic, on the other hand, “what they're proposing is a complete shift—and a paradigm shift, I would say—in the way we approach vascular disease and manage it,” he said. Mosaic also demonstrated deep knowledge of vascular disease and the limitations of current tools, he added. Mosaic’s technology could eventually make surgeries more efficient, allowing surgeons to see more patients in a given day, and make surgeries safer by reducing errors, Aldailami said. Longtime roboticist Rodney Brooks , who has founded multiple robotics companies, including the one behind Roomba vacuums and warehouse robotics startup Robust.AI , is an advisor with equity options in Mosaic. “The mission grabs me,” said Brooks. Currently, patients and clinicians get exposed to X-rays during operations. “The goal is to get rid of all that X-ray, ultimately, which is just much healthier for the patient and the doctors,” he said. AI Deep Dive: How to Secure a Data Center Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's romantic relationship with a Chinese businesswoman recruited as a spy by China’s top intelligence agency has thrown the tech industry into a tizzy in the past couple days. Based on what I learned in the most recent episode of AI Deep Dive , I doubt it will be the last instance of potential espionage involving AI companies. It is “pretty likely” that there are other spies in U.S. AI companies, said Lisa Thiergart , co-founder and CEO of Security Level 5 , a startup that works with AI companies and the intelligence community to secure AI data centers. Thiergart’s comment was in reference to the OpenAI employee who allegedly left a recording device in an officer conference room, but the comment looks especially prescient in light of the revelations concerning Huang. But spies are hardly necessary for other countries to obtain sensitive information about AI companies, and even their AI models, she said. No AI data center today could withstand a cyberattack by another country, especially a high-priority attack involving hundreds of employees—at least the data centers that are publicly known, said Thiergart. Even the security standards the government has typically followed for its data centers are not quite up to scratch when it comes to designing facilities to train and run AI models, she said. Here’s what else is going on… Court Watch President Donald Trump said in an impromptu press briefing Monday that the Federal Bureau of Investigation is looking into Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang ’s romantic affair with Alice Huang , a Chinese business executive whom other U.S. officials suspected of providing information to Chinese intelligence authorities. Overheard Anthropic’s outside counsel in Canada late Monday ​sent banks an updated prospectus for its initial public offering and then retracted it, saying some of the details are incorrect, The Information reported . The counsel in Canada first sent ​a copy of a filing, earlier reported by Reuters, that showed Anthropic aimed to raise up to $70 billion by selling about 867 ​million shares in a price ‌range ⁠of $70 to $80 per share. Anthropic’s counsel told the banks that some of the details were inaccurate and it ⁠would update the filing later. Nominal , which uses AI to test hardware designs for uses including defense and robotics, raised $240 million in a Series C funding round led by Lightspeed Venture Partners and Insight Partners. newmo , which develops self-driving taxis using its own AI, raised ¥20.8 billion (about $131.7 million) in a Series B funding round led by KDDI. Mavria , which mass-produces modular data centers for AI, has raised $130 million to date across pre-seed and seed rounds, with its latest round valuing the company at $1 billion and led by Paradigm. UniX AI (优理奇机器人), which builds general-purpose embodied-intelligence robots, raised RMB 500 million (about $75 million) in a Pre-A funding round from investors including returning backers Xienuo Capital , Yonghua Capital and Keli Sensing Technology. Spines , which is building an AI to automate book publishing, raised $64 million in growth capital, combining a $29 million Series A-1 funding round led by Zeev Ventures. SRTD Biotech , which uses AI to design precision mRNA therapies, raised €31.5 million (about $35 million) in an oversubscribed seed funding round led by Mérieux Equity Partners , NRW.BANK and Boehringer Ingelheim Venture Fund. Coframe , which uses AI to improve company websites, raised $35 million in total funding, including a $25 million Series A funding round led by Khosla Ventures and Hanabi Capital. geniosAI , which gives financial institutions AI-powered analysis tools, raised $19.1 million in combined seed and Series A funding, with the Series A led by FactSet. Vudoo , which embeds shopping into AI-powered media and content, raised A$22 million (about $15.1 million) in a Series B funding round led by Blue Sky Capital.
