title: Google Grapples With AI’s Hit to Its Ads Juggernaut
content: Cleverly CEO Nicholas Verity, whose Los Angeles business has advertised on Google for seven years, noticed an unusual pattern in Google search advertising about eight months ago. Part of the roughly $2,000 a day he set aside for Google was going unspent because not enough people were seeing or clicking on the ads to use up the budget. He believes that’s a result of more people researching the web on AI chatbots instead. “I want to give Google more money, but there’s that search traffic I think is going to people doing their own research in [large language models],” he said. For over two decades, Google has run one of the most profitable advertising businesses in history, thanks to the dominance of its search engine and the automated ad system built into it. But its push into AI is now cutting into that business, dragging down growth while Meta Platforms’ ad revenue is rising more than twice as fast as Google’s search advertising and OpenAI is entering the ad market. Alphabet shares fell nearly 13% on October 29, the day after it reported annual search advertising growth slowed to 12% in the third quarter from 17% in the second quarter. Chief Business Officer Philipp Schindler attributed part of the slowdown to lower monetization in AI Mode, the company’s ChatGPT-like version of Google search. Google doesn’t disclose how much advertising revenue comes from AI features versus traditional search, but the slowdown suggests Google isn’t making as much money from people using AI Mode as it does from regular search. The quarterly update followed an aggressive rollout of its AI summaries and chat as an alternative to regular search as it continues to experiment with how it places ads in these features. Other companies have had similar experiences with new products. Meta in February 2022 reported a hit to advertising growth when it expanded its TikTok-like Reels on Facebook, only to see advertising revenue growth start to pick up the next year as the company became better at monetizing Reels . Google could experience the same bounceback in advertising growth as use of AI Mode and AI Overviews accelerates. Google executives have sought to reassure investors and advertisers by highlighting the opportunity AI holds. Google is using AI to determine which searches trigger an ad, pick the webpages users land on after clicking on an ad and write versions of ads automatically. Behind the scenes, the company is striking partnerships and exploring possible acquisitions to make ads in AI features more useful. Still, some advertisers have grown frustrated and are moving their dollars elsewhere—including to Meta, say six advertisers and agencies. Like Google, Meta offers automated creative tools to drive sales, but its new AI products—such as its Muse agent—don’t show ads that compete with its main social feeds, which show ads next to video clips and social posts. “This year, there are real alternatives to Google such as ChatGPT ads and Meta, and we’re going to reallocate budgets based on which are doing better,” said Farhad Divecha, CEO of marketing agency AccuraCast, which buys ads for brands. Seismic Shift Google rolled out AI Overviews, AI-generated summaries that appear above search results, in May 2024. Nearly a year later, it added AI Mode, and it introduced advertising a few months after each product’s launch. Unlike ads in its regular web search, ads in AI Overviews and AI Mode no longer appear next to keywords but alongside longer prompts and conversations. Advertisers can’t buy ads specifically for Google’s AI search features or opt out of ads placed in the AI features. The AI summaries and chatbots represented one of the biggest shifts in search history since the desktop-to-mobile transition in 2016, raising the prospect that AI could cannibalize its $224.5 billion a year search advertising business. Still, for several quarters, Google’s revenue from search advertising showed little sign of faltering. As use of Google’s AI features has picked up, however, search revenue growth has slowed. The slowdown partly reflects the company’s decision to avoid alienating people using AI search with too many ads or with formats that don’t jibe with users. And it partly reflects the growing pains of a new product, as Google works out how to place and charge for ads in conversations rather than against keywords. “We’re taking a deliberate approach [to] building the best user experience first, which creates a durable foundation for our customers and our business,” said a Google spokesperson in a statement. “Our ads experiments in AI Overviews and AI Mode have shown promising results, and we’re now scaling monetization with formats that drive proven [return on investment] for advertisers.” One of the main challenges facing Google’s advertising business is that people are using its AI features differently than they did its web search. Their queries in AI Mode are about three times longer than queries in traditional search, says Google. They’re also richer in context and deeper than was typical for Google web searches. For instance, a person may search “what is the best tent to buy for a weeklong backpacking trip in the Sierras in September,” instead of simply asking for a tent. This browsing habit means they’re often not ready to buy a product, and so they’re less likely to click on an ad or to make a purchase after a click, says Fred Vallaeys, who worked for nearly a decade on Google’s ad products and is now CEO of Optmyzr, which makes software for managing Google ad campaigns. Vallaeys estimates that the share of clicks on Google ads that led to a sale fell 1.4% in the third quarter from the second quarter across Google’s major products, including search. Return on ad spend, the revenue advertisers get back from each dollar spent, fell 2.9%, its second quarterly decline after a 3.8% drop in the second quarter, Vallaeys estimates. He based his estimates on 21,000 accounts, many of them small businesses, managed through Optmyzr. As Google tries to proceed carefully with introducing ads to its AI features, the company is showing fewer advertisements in AI Mode than in the rest of search, advertisers say. This has driven the cost of each click higher over the past year, they say. With less ad space to purchase but just as many buyers, prices set by Google’s automated auction rise. The ascent of new ways to search has also created new challenges. As people research products on ChatGPT and other AI chatbots, it’s become far more difficult to figure out what led to a purchase made through Google, according to advertisers and agencies that place ads. Before the rise of chatbots, shoppers typically searched on Google, clicked an ad and bought the product, meaning advertisers could credit the sale directly to that ad. Complicating the outcome for advertisers, Google reports ad performance in AI Overviews and AI Mode together with the rest of search, so advertisers can’t tell how ads perform specifically in AI features. They also can’t see much about where and when their ads appear or why the AI chose to show them, according to advertisers and agencies. Google says it doesn’t offer separate reporting for AI Overviews and AI Mode since it’s still ramping up AI features. To answer some of the advertisers’ concerns, it added a reporting feature to their accounts in September that shows them the search terms people typed that prompted an ad, and other features. Google has also released creative tools such as Asset Studio, which generates ad images and videos with its Gemini Omni and Nano Banana models. “These are features that basically play into the changing nature of search” due to AI’s influence, said Nick Stoltz, chief strategy officer at Measured, an ad measurement firm that works mostly with large retailers. Meanwhile, advertisers are giving Google more information about their products, such as richer product descriptions, so its AI knows which conversations to show their ads in, according to Victor Batista, global search lead at Jellyfish, a London-based digital marketing agency. Many advertisers are now focusing more on impressions—how many people have seen the ad—than click-throughs, says Batista. “Because the value is shifting from clicks to impressions and some searches end without a click, brands are competing to be recommended in the AI’s answer,” he said. Google’s corporate development team has also explored acquiring AI tools for creating ads, according to a person with direct knowledge of the matter. Even though Google offers advertisers AI tools for making ads, these now increasingly compete with AI-powered apps such as Higgsfield, Runway and Typeface, which have seen growth rise as more businesses tap these tools in lieu of human ad agencies. Meanwhile, Google has been striking partnerships that make its ads more useful to advertisers. For instance, Google is paying Hightouch to move advertisers onto the startup’s tools for sharing customer data, according to a person with direct knowledge of the matter. Partnerships aim to solve a problem that AI has magnified: Google often doesn’t know what its advertisers’ customers have already purchased before it shows them an ad, because smaller advertisers often don’t use its tools to send that information, said a person with direct knowledge. Google has also inked partnerships with companies including Adswerve, CustomerLabs, Datahash, Fifty-five, Jellyfish, Lytics, Tealium, Treasure Data and Zapier to help advertisers connect their data to its tools.

title: How Jensen Huang’s Yearslong Ties to Alice Huang Enabled $7 Billion-Plus Nvidia Chip Sales to China
content: The relationship between Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and Alice Huang, the woman that the U.S. government reportedly identified as a Chinese intelligence asset, dates back to at least 2023, and the two have built a rapport that facilitated the shipment of at least $7.5 billion worth of Nvidia chips through Chinese companies since then, according to two people who know her. Alice Huang, her sister and her husband have built a labyrinth of companies spanning China and Singapore to acquire Nvidia chips, according to the people who know Alice Huang and corporate registration records. At the center of that corporate network is Shanghai Century Litong, a China-based company that was founded in June 2023 and, by October, was added to Nvidia’s list of preferred cloud partners, a status that comes with priority access to Nvidia’s chips. Century Litong was established around the same time as Megaspeed, a Singapore-registered company that U.S. law enforcement has been reportedly probing for smuggling Nvidia chips from Southeast Asia to China. Alice Huang, whose Chinese name is Huang Le, held an executive position at Megaspeed, which was linked to Century Litong, according to the two people who know her and corporate registration records in Singapore and China. Between 2023 to 2025, Megaspeed’s Nvidia imports totaled about $4.6 billion, according to a Bloomberg report in 2025 . Some of them have been used in data centers in Southeast Asia, while others went to Century Litong, which also secured Nvidia chips from other channels. Century Litong rents out computing capacity and operates data centers that host Nvidia graphic processing units, including those that have been banned from sale to China, according to the two people. Some of the chips that Century Litong acquired eventually ended up in data centers serving Alibaba, Tencent and smaller Chinese AI labs, the people added. The New York Times reported that U.S. officials had evidence that Alice Huang is a Chinese spy. In an email to Nvidia employees Sunday, Jensen Huang admitted that he had been unfaithful to his wife, after the Financial Times reported that he had a romantic relationship with Alice Huang. Nvidia’s board on Sunday said it’s launching an investigation into the matter, while saying it has no reason to believe that either U.S. national security or Nvidia secrets have been compromised. Jensen Huang has spent the past two years lobbying the Trump administration to loosen U.S. export controls on sales of advanced AI chips to China, arguing that continuous supply of Nvidia hardware in China is key to ensuring American AI leadership. Nvidia, meanwhile, has repeatedly denied knowledge of its chips being smuggled into China. The length of Alice Huang’s relationship with Jensen Huang, and the involvement of another major company connected to her family, haven’t been previously reported. It sheds light on the extent to which Alice Huang has been leveraging her access to Jensen Huang to get Nvidia chips into China. “We sell our data-center GPUs primarily to well-known partners, including [original equipment manufacturers], system builders, integrators, and [original design manufacturers], who work with us to ensure that all sales comply with U.S. export control rules,” an Nvidia spokesperson said in a statement in response to detailed questions about The Information’s reporting. “We apply the same standard to all transactions, large or small, and expect our partners to do the same.” “Our due diligence has helped identify suspected attempts to circumvent U.S. export controls, leading to federal prosecutions. Our work with law enforcement has led to prosecutions,” the statement added. Alibaba and Tencent didn’t comment. Megaspeed didn’t reply to a request for comment. Alice Huang could not be reached for comment. How the two Huangs met While images and videos circulating on social media documented two occasions where the two Huangs hung out together in large groups in Taipei in 2024 and 2025, their relationship goes back further. It couldn’t be determined precisely when they met. But one person who knows Alice Huang and her husband, Kang Wei, for over a decade recalls Kang saying that he met Jensen Huang in the 2010s. Kang was then a private equity investor and did a series of acquisitions of videogame companies, a sector that was the biggest market for Nvidia’s GPUs before the AI boom. Kang could not be reached for comment. Alice Huang, who had spent her career in the media and financial industries, had no background in AI prior to 2023, when Megaspeed and Century Litong were established. But, according to the people who know her, she quickly established her credibility by boasting about her chuminess with Jensen Huang. She regularly posted photos of her and Jensen on her WeChat feed, and showed colleagues and customers additional photos of them together, and bragged to those people that Jensen Huang celebrated her birthday every year by having dinner with her or sending her gifts, according to the people who know Alice Huang. She is also a familiar face to Nvidia’s China sales team, attending the company’s annual gathering for local partners in China, according to an Nvidia China sales employee. While she talks freely to business partners about Jensen Huang, she’s vague about exactly what her job is. And she’s cautious about signing documents and leaving her names in paper trails, the two people who know her said. Century Litong Century Litong was established in June 2023 by a founding shareholder that at the time was ultimately controlled by Alice Huang’s sister, Huang Yu. The company Huang Yu controlled exited Century Litong in 2024. Four months after Century Litong was established, its major shareholder, listed in Shanghai Stock Exchange, disclosed that Century Litong had earned the credential as an Nvidia preferred partner for cloud services—a designation it continues to hold, according to Nvidia’s website . Nvidia typically doesn’t sell its hardware directly to customers . Instead, its chips are sold with servers made by companies such as Dell Technologies and Super Micro Computers through layers of distributors. To help potential end users of its chips verify the credibility of Nvidia’s distributors, the company devised a cloud partner system that it discloses on its website. The system has different tiers for cloud partners. To qualify as a “preferred” one, a company has to show that it has sufficient training in handling and running Nvidia hardware and generates revenues at a certain level, and in return, it receives preferential supply allocation. Century Litong’s addition to Nvidia’s preferred list couldn’t have happened at a better time. Two weeks prior, Washington had extended its export ban to the A800 and H800, the chips Nvidia had engineered for China after the more powerful A100 and H100 were barred from exporting to China in 2022. While the additional bans stopped immediate shipments to China, the A800 and H800 that were already sitting in distributors’ warehouses could still be sold to China. Century Litong, as a preferred Nvidia cloud partner, was able to secure large volumes of them from Nvidia distributors. When a shipment of banned Nvidia chips could not be obtained from Nvidia’s distributors, Alice Huang stepped in, one of the people who knows her said. Her role was to secure the chip orders when they got stuck in the supply chain. She told some colleagues and customers that she could always get the supply, citing her close relationship inside Nvidia and with its distributors, another person who knows her said. Of the 240,000 banned Nvidia chips Alice Huang helped move into the country, most were the H100 and H200 systems, released in 2022 and 2023, respectively, the two people said. In 2022, an H100 was sold for roughly $25,000 to $40,000 in the U.S. Some of the chips were A100s, which were allowed to be sold to China until 2022, the two people said. Century Litong’s clients were China’s largest technology companies, which cannot buy restricted Nvidia chips themselves. That made the company the go-to supplier for Chinese tech firms racing to develop their own AI systems. “Whatever chips that the U.S. and Chinese governments don’t allow for sale, Litong has them,” said a person who has done business with the company, when describing the critical role that Century Litong played to supply chips to China. In an emailed statement to The Information, Century Litong said the company secured Nvidia’s partner qualification “through its professional expertise and compliant channels.” “All business resources of our company are obtained in compliance with applicable laws and regulations,” the company said. “Our company has no business dealings with Ms. Huang,” the company added. Supply Dried Up Alice Huang served as managing director at Megaspeed from March to November 2023, and the company’s owner was a British Virgin Islands entity bearing her Chinese name, Huang Le Limited. The Singapore-registered company also traces its roots to gaming. It was incorporated in 2015 as 7Road International, the Singapore arm of Shenzhen-based gaming company 7Road Holdings, until changing its name to Megaspeed in 2023, according to corporate records in Singapore and stock exchange filings in Hong Kong. According to people familiar with Century Litong’s business, Megaspeed procured Nvidia chips and either rented them out remotely from data centers in Southeast Asia to Chinese customers, or physically shipped them into China. But in a similar fashion to how Alice Huang left no trace to her ties with Century Litong, she also quickly removed herself from Megaspeed. In November 2023, Megaspeed’s ownership changed from Huang Le Limited to Swiftdata, another Singapore company. In February 2024, Megaspeed set up a Malaysian subsidiary, Speedmatrix. Some of the hardware that Speedmatrix bought from Nvidia subsequently reached Century Litong, two people familiar with its business said. Between June 2024 and June 2025, Speedmatrix received more than 200 shipments of Nvidia hardware worth roughly $2 billion, much of it traced back to a subsidiary of Inspur, a Chinese server maker on the U.S. Entity List, according to the New York Times. But the trade has largely ground to a halt, after U.S. and Singaporean authorities launched separate probes into Megaspeed over the last two years. The crackdown on chip smuggling has shot up the blackmarket prices for Nvidia’s hardware since late last year. After Washington and Singaporean authorities zeroed in on Megaspeed, Jensen Huang defended his interactions with Megaspeed as “completely normal” in an interview with Bloomberg and said Nvidia had “studied all their deployments of our GPUs and counted every one.” Jensen Huang has been called to a close-door congressional briefing next week to answer questions about whether he has endangered U.S. national security.

title: There Are Likely More Spies at AI Companies, Says Security Executive Lisa Thiergart
content: Other countries likely haven’t yet stolen AI models from leading U.S. companies—but only for a lack of trying, said Lisa Thiergart, co-founder and CEO of Security Level 5, a startup that works with AI companies and the intelligence community to secure AI data centers. “If a nation state really wanted to steal the weights right now, they could. However, I think that they have cheaper ways to get what they need,” she said on the latest episode of AI Deep Dive. (The full episode is available here .) The episode was recorded shortly after OpenAI accused one of its employees, a Saudi national, of hiding a recording device in an office conference room. In the interview, Thiergart said it is “pretty likely” that there are other spies in U.S. AI companies—a suspicion buttressed by recent reports from the New York Times and the Financial Times that some U.S. officials believed Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had a romantic relationship with a Chinese businesswoman recruited as a spy by China’s top intelligence agency. The name Security Level 5 refers to a data center that could resist a priority attack from another nation, similar to the effort the attacking country might spend tracking the position of a nuclear submarine. Such an effort could involve up to 1,000 staff working for a year to hack the data center, Thiergart said. Her company has purchased a small data center, which it is turning into a prototype of such a high-security facility. One of the challenges with designing such a data center is that it has to prevent both outsiders breaking in and AI agents breaking out. “Unlike standard computing payloads, this time we’re handling a much more unknown—well, intelligent—payload, where we need to be thinking about the AIs as insider threats themselves, and this kind of changes how you go about designing your data center,” she said. The notion that AI agents should be treated as insider threats, akin to foreign spies, has been catching on in the AI industry in the months following OpenAI’s hack on Hugging Face and related incidents in which AI agents took unauthorized actions to gain internet access. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella wrote an essay on the topic last month titled “Models as Insider Risks in the Super Intelligence Era.” Thiergart also discussed why government data centers are not currently secure enough to train AI models, why neoclouds have especially weak security and why AI could weaken cryptography. The following transcript of the conversation has been lightly edited for clarity. Drew: Welcome back to the Information’s AI Deep Dive. On this show, we get to the bottom of the hardest technical problems in AI. I’m your host, Rocket Drew. My guest today is Lisa Thiergart. Lisa is the co-founder and CEO of Security Level Five, an organization that works with AI companies and the intelligence community to secure AI data centers. Lisa, welcome on the show. Thiergart: Thank you so much for having me. I’m excited to inform the public more about SL5. Drew: Yeah, I’m really excited about this too. I feel like security in general is really on people’s minds right now with AI. But you’re looking at such a specific and interesting section of security that I think we should dig into a lot more. Thiergart: Yeah, that’s right. SL5 is specifically about defending a narrow set of the critical assets of AI labs, such as model weights and all the code that touches those model weights from priority nation state level espionage and sabotage. So we’re especially interested in the most frontier, the most capable models that could pose a danger to the public, and we want to avoid other nation-state adversaries being able to steal those models, or those models being able to escape from the data centers themselves and take unintended actions out in the wild. Drew: There’s a lot to get into there that I’m really excited to talk about, but I want to start with something that was in the news recently. I’m sure you saw that an OpenAI employee has been arrested for planting a secret listening device in a conference room, basically a microphone wrapped up in toilet paper, tucked behind a TV in a conference room that executives were using, presumably to discuss secret topics. As someone who thinks about security a lot, what did you make of that incident? Thiergart: Yeah, it’s rough. It was not surprising. I think that defending against insider threats in the way that companies operate right now is really, really tough. I do think they need to do better. I think I’m glad that they at least caught it on the timeline that they did, but I think especially if we’re defending against priority nation states, insider threats is what they’re extremely good at, and so I think really it’s kind of hopeless to protect all of your secrets from them. But I think what companies do have a shot at is triaging their secrets and protecting the most valuable ones with a lot of resources. Drew: Protecting them, including maybe like not saying them in certain conference rooms? Thiergart: Yeah, I think especially making sure that you very strictly reduce the number of people that have access to that information or that could access a resource or a room where that information would be shared. Drew: So you weren’t surprised that this happened. I mean, would you wager that there are other spies at AI companies right now? Thiergart: I think that’s pretty likely. Drew: Really? What do you expect to see in the next year or so? Do you expect more incidents like this to come to light? Thiergart: Yeah, I think that’s likely. I mean, I think that AI labs are aware of this threat and probably gearing up to try and defend against this as best possible, but I would say this is one of the hardest things to get right. And I would say the best shot they have is just reducing the number of people that can access the information, and also moving towards something that is kind of closer to government-style clearance for their staff. And my organization has actually published a framework for how that could be achieved in the [private] industry. It’s called Sensitivity Levels, and outlines sort of a path on how to cover this window where we are in the stage where we’re still working with a high number of staff that need to access things, and we need to kind of triage who is how trusted to access what information, but with having a very international staff. Drew: Okay, yeah, a very international staff. One of the things that surprised me about this incident was that the employee in question was a Saudi national. I guess when I think of insider threats—OpenAI has done some trainings, it’s been reported for their employees where they caution their employees against honeypots, basically espionage by—I guess the typical example is like beautiful Chinese women will come to you and they’ll try to get your trade secrets from the company. So that was sort of how I was envisioning this insider threat playing out. But I guess in hindsight, of course, many countries are going to want access to this kind of secret information. Thiergart: Yeah, and I actually also don’t think filtering for nationality is really the right thing to be looking for here. There is sort of a more complex set of underlying factors. I think, for instance, an employee having been with the company for a really long time, possibly before nation states got interested in collecting on these companies, those are some strong signs of trust. Drew: Yeah, and I guess someone could be an asset of a foreign government without knowing that they are, or even without knowing which foreign government. So filtering for nationality maybe doesn’t get you very far on this. Thiergart: Even a U.S. citizen could be threatened and turned. It’s really difficult. Drew: Yeah, it’s interesting to me that maybe the AI industry is going to be taking a different direction now with this level of information security. Historically, machine learning has been a very open field. It’s been hard to contain ideas. Patents haven’t been enforced that much, and ideas have flowed pretty easily and diffused very far. Do you think that’s going to change? Thiergart: I think so. I think we’re reaching a point in time where I was actually at a conference earlier this week, which was Chatham House, but a Frontier AI Lab staff said that they believe RSI might also only be months out, and if that is true, we’re very rapidly approaching that threshold where we’re kind of crossing over into a place where making these models publicly accessible might be more of a threat to the public than it is an asset. We’re already seeing this week increasing cyber incidents cropping up in ways that are affecting people’s day-to-day lives, and I think we’re in for a rough two years where that is going to keep increasing. And I think AI labs do have an obligation to the public to conduct their operations in such a secure fashion that they are not hacking other companies or, yeah, strengthening the offensive side of things more so than the defensive side. Drew: Yeah, I could see that, and yet we’re still in this era where you can go and just have a candid conversation with an employee at the labs under Chatham House rules about what they’re seeing. It feels like we’re still in this era where you can go to a party in San Francisco and learn maybe an algorithmic secret or two if you talk to the right employee. Do you see that culture changing? Thiergart: I think it has to. It’s obviously difficult. The hardest thing to get right with security is often getting that cultural organizational shift, and that is something that the labs have to work really hard at now. And trainings, you know, is the first step, but that’s going to be a multi-month transition that they need to get ready for. And I think more so than protecting secrets, what really is tractable is protecting model weights and also building much more powerful sandboxes, basically SL5, in order to ensure that the models that you’re creating are not going to be more powerful than the containment infrastructure that you have for them. Drew: So, what is security level five? You mentioned it before. Yeah. Also, what is security level 1, 2, 3 and so on. Thiergart: Yeah. So basically, these are named roughly after the biosecurity levels, and the number matches the capability level of the attacker. So level one is sort of like an amateur hacker, some script kitty that is trying to hack, I don’t know, OpenAI. But level five is a priority nation attack. So this is when there are up to a year of effort and up to 1,000 staff that are focused on just this one attack. So you could imagine that this is sort of like a country like China or Russia that are highly cyber capable and that are prioritizing this attack on the level of, say, tracking a position of a nuclear submarine, so they’re putting a lot of resources onto this. Now, one interesting thing that this ontology doesn’t explicitly already include is what happens when these attackers are getting uplifted by using AI systems in their offensive chains, and I think what this results in is that the cost of an attack comes down. You need less human capital potentially, and you can parallelize more across different streams of attack. So I think what we’re going to see is that the number of attacks at the SL4 and SL5 tier are going to increase more so than you would think if you were just looking at past distributions of these kind of attacks. Drew: With these AI agents coming online and being really good at cyber attacks themselves, does that mean that well-resourced cyber crime syndicates are going to be nearly as capable as nation states? Are nation states going to continue to be the most capable actors here? Thiergart: I do think one should not underestimate that nation states have decades of specialized infrastructure and pre-existing assets at their disposal. They have the kind of resources that a private industry cannot really replicate, and so I do think that will continue to give them more reach. But I do think that the gap will close. Drew: Okay, so we’ll be seeing those sorts of rogue cyber groups getting uplifted to that SL3 or SL4, but not quite to the SL5 level of capability. Thiergart: I think that could happen. It’s not, you know, certain. We’ll see how the uptake is, and also how open weight models influence this. But I do think that would be—I would take a bet on that. Drew: So, what security level are AI companies at today? You want them to get to security level five. Thiergart: So, based on public information entirely, Anthropic announced that they were activating ASL-3 security controls back in I think summer 2025, and they also recently updated that they’ve implemented a few SL4 shaped security controls as well. I do believe most of the industry is at or slightly below that, based on the public info. I think that if we kind of compare that against some of the statements about where these AI systems are expected to be in terms of their capability levels, including in cyber, in the coming months and years, I think it’s pretty evident that in both pacing worlds and racing worlds, we need to reach SL5 as soon as possible to avoid these highly capable systems escaping from the control of AI labs. Drew: Or being stolen. Thiergart: Or being stolen, yeah. Drew: I suppose the natural question is: if you think that these companies need to get to SL5, but today they are at SL3 or below, and you think there are likely spies in these companies already, I mean, do you think the weights of their AI models have already been stolen? Thiergart: Yeah, it’s a good question. So, my best guess, again, based on public info, is if a nation state really wanted to steal the weights right now, they could. However, I think that they have cheaper ways to get what they need, namely distillation. Right now, AI labs are serving models over API to clients all over the world. Some are restricting it in some areas, but I think it’s right now very easy for a nation state to get everything they need through distillation. And defending against distillation is super hard. People are already trying super hard, coming up with a bunch of new techniques. But I think it’s basically if you’re saying you’re offering a public API to your best available models, I think that’s basically you saying I’m now okay with gifting this model to China. Drew: Okay, that’s a hot take. I feel like the AI companies would probably object that they’re taking steps to prevent distillation. They’re trying to implement monitoring so that they can catch if the model is being distilled and shut it off as quickly as they can. You don’t buy it. Thiergart: I don’t buy it. I think—I mean, you might as well do everything you possibly can to make it as hard as possible. But I think the threshold we’d have to reach here is so high. This is for two reasons. One, if you’re offering a public API, that means that you’re serving your model over the internet. Unless something drastically changes about the infrastructure that is kind of implied, and that already means you’re not at SL5. Connecting your data centers to the internet is such a large attack surface that at least with currently and expected to be available in the coming years methods, there’s approximately no way that you will keep that defended against nation states for that long. So that’s the first one. And then the second one is that these attackers don’t necessarily need to distill your entire model. They don’t need it in all generality. They probably are starting off from some open weights model, which might only be six to nine months behind, and so they are more in a position where they are kind of prioritizing what are the capabilities that that closed model is better at, and that’s often things like cyber capabilities or automated alignment—or not alignment—capabilities research, and you can much more narrowly try to distill those data sets. And so I think that there’s a large difficulty where we should expect that the science of distillation is going to evolve further and further, and the data efficiency and the amount of data that they would have to successfully take from this distillation process is going to go lower and lower. And so there’s kind of this race between your distillation capabilities and the defense capabilities, and I think that just doesn’t look good. It seems really difficult. And we’re so close to the threshold of these systems being very dangerous in a way that would be highly disruptive, if not existentially risky to the public, that I think we just are nearing some threshold where we have to stop taking those risks. Drew: But what do you have in mind there with the risks? You’re thinking about cyber. Thiergart: I mean, cyber is sort of the most short-term, obvious one, I think, including perhaps bio, maybe in addition, but I’m thinking things like bio weapons that can kill on the order of hundreds to thousands and beyond of humans. In terms of cyber, they could take down the global financial system. I mean, we just saw this week that—this was actually a win for defensive programs, by the way. A bug was found and announced by the NSA where two critical vulnerabilities in PHP were found, which is sort of like a server side [scripting language] that is broadly used to power many websites, and these were—and I wrote down actually the exact thing here. Both are remote code execution flaws. So these are highly critical bugs that basically allow an attacker to run commands without logging in on said server. And this is really just the start of it. These types of things are going to keep cropping up, and we’re going to need time to patch them. I think we’re in for a pretty rough ride the next two years, and I expect that the identity management and things like the global financial system are going to be kind of in a playing catch up for a while until we can sort of rewrite, refactor, and verify a lot of that core tech stack that underpins a lot of that infrastructure. And then I also mentioned existential level threats, where this is kind of more less the humans misusing AI’s angle, but more the angle of we could either see extreme power concentration outcomes from developing such powerful AI, or many people have also discussed that we don’t currently really have any assurance that these highly capable systems are going to be acting in our interest, and until we make that progress on alignment research, I believe it’s not safe to either create these systems at all, or—you must either, I think, not create them or be ready to secure them at the necessary threshold that they don’t escape your control. Drew: I see. Thiergart: And I think right now we have neither. Drew: You said we’re in for a rough two years on cyber. What happens after those two years? Thiergart: I don’t think we’re done, but I do think that if the right actors prioritize this, there is a chance to actually apply some of these new AI technologies to at scale refactor, patch, and improve a large set of critical infrastructure and kind of the open source backbone to a lot of the modern systems we use today. And I don’t believe we’re going to be done after two years. We’re going to have to keep doing better and better at this. But maybe the worst of it might be covered. Drew: I see. And you called the PHP vulnerabilities a win for defensive programs. What do you mean by that? Thiergart: Yeah, so this is reporting by the Wall Street Journal where it said that the PHP maintainers found the bugs using AI assisted analysis. So I think that’s yet to be further confirmed. But assuming that is true, I think that’s a win in the column of it’s good to differentially first release the models to defenders so that they have a little bit of lead time to first find some of these worst bugs and patch them before we allow kind of a broader ecosystem of users who might include the offensive actors to use that same model. Drew: Okay, and you’re saying that distillation could contribute both to cyber risks and bio risks as adversaries basically copy the capabilities of the leading models into the models they’re developing. I could almost see that being a bigger concern for bio than for cyber because my understanding is a lot of cyber capabilities comes from reinforcement learning, and so you can maybe replicate those same capabilities just by having a lot of reinforcement learning environments that train those skills into the model, whereas with bio you can’t do reinforcement learning as easily, so maybe you’re more reliant on distillation? Thiergart: Maybe I feel less knowledgeable about the bio reinforcement learning situation, so I’ll just comment on the cyber side of that. I do think even creating these reinforcement learning environments takes a lot of work, and it is far, far better if you can avoid gifting an attacker the results from that than if they have to go and do the work on that themselves. It takes time, it takes data, it takes skills, ML skills. And so that could be right, but I think that there’s a lot of utility to not making it that easy for the attackers. Drew: So, are you expecting AI companies to stop serving their models over public APIs to prevent distillation? You’re saying otherwise, all of this SL5 work is not as relevant. Thiergart: I would say that the way I would approach this is it’s already standard best practice that before you deploy your models, while they’re still in internal testing and in the pre-training process and post-training process internally, at that time you’re not serving the model to the public. You only serve it to the public once it passes a certain set of safety checks, and all the standard process there, so that’s already normal. What I’m saying is, I think we should keep that internal process. So before we release to the public, we should keep that inside SL5 data centers and SL5 networks. And only once the model actually clears that threshold of it’s aligned enough, or it’s by some other safety case trustworthy enough to be released into the public deployment phase, then that model would get transferred to an SL4, maybe even SL3 data center, where it could be served more broadly. Drew: Okay, and AI companies are already taking steps to have better security during that phase, that testing phase and training before the model is released. They’re working on beefing up their sandboxes that restrict internet access. But you’re saying if you want to also protect those model weights from getting stolen, you’re going to have to go a lot further. Thiergart: Yeah, that’s right. I think SL3 is really strong commercial grade security, but is nowhere near what you have to be doing for what is starting to be weapons grade technology. Drew: So that’s the AI companies. What about the data centers that say the government has access to? I’ve heard reference to these ‘air gapped’ facilities. Maybe you can explain what air gap even means, but is that sufficient? Thiergart: Yeah. So strictly speaking, an air gap is defined as an isolated network. So there is no connection to any other networks, and there is usually also a physical air gap. This means there is no cable connecting you physically to some other network. Sometimes people also talk about cryptographic air gaps, which is a little bit different. But in the context of government data centers—where first of all, there is very little public, so treat this as kind of just a speculation—I think there is an important distinction to draw between general data centers and AI data centers. Where normal data centers, I think we should expect that the military and intelligence community has top tier experience at securing that, air gapping that for all the national security relevant applications. When it comes to AI data centers, this is comparatively a pretty new thing, where there don’t really exist standards for that kind of nation grade AI data centers, and that’s kind of where my company stepped in and kicked off this process last year, where we got together over 100 stakeholders from across the AI labs, but also the national security establishment, to jointly get more clarity on what is the outline of the shape of a solution we need here. What would go into an SL5 standard that both the AI labs and the U.S. government could make use of for their new data centers? And we found actually that we want to reinvent the wheel as little as possible, of course, and there’s lots of good practices to just adopt, for example, from government IL6 standard, and so our standard builds on top of those, and we found that there are about 80% of existing best practices from existing government expertise here, and then there is 20% approximately new where we think something has to be different if it’s an AI data center that you’re trying to secure at this level. Drew: That’s kind of what I would expect. At the end of the day, these are just buildings with a lot of chips in them, and whether you’re using those chips for whatever the government, you know, doing analysis on different kinds of data, calculating missile trajectories, whatever goes on in there, versus using those same chips to run AI models, what’s really the difference? What accounts for that 20%? Thiergart: Yeah, so there’s a lot of different things. I think the main one is the types and number of chips you’re putting in there. You’re using liquid cooling. There’s a whole different kind of infrastructure underpinning this that doesn’t map super cleanly into the way other more I don’t want to say historical, but normal data centers or something, did networking and were able to sort of isolate different boundaries. So there are just some performance-related infrastructural differences here. And then there’s also the consideration that unlike standard computing payloads, this time we’re handling a much more unknown, well, intelligent payload, where we need to be thinking about the AIs as insider threats themselves. And this kind of changes how you go about designing your data center. You cannot trust things in quite the same way, and there are a lot of novel potential attack paths or angles that need to be considered when you’re designing infrastructure with that assumption in mind. Drew: The idea that your AIs themselves are insider threats, I think, is catching on right now in the industry. Thiergart: Yeah. Drew: Do you think that’s a useful frame? Thiergart: Yeah, absolutely. And I also would say that, like, we at SL5 actually try to design infrastructure that both works for the use case of preventing outside nation-state adversaries from stealing the model weights and then bringing them out, perhaps collaborating with insiders on the inside. But also the second use case of the AI is trying to escape. It is originating the motivation to do that, it is coordinating with copies of itself, perhaps also with ones that are disparate in time or different versions, in order to successfully either exfiltrate a copy of its weights or mastermind some kind of operation outside of the data center as well by sneaking pieces of information out. Drew: Do the techniques that apply to the insider threats also apply to the external threats? And if not, is one of those problems harder than the other? Thiergart: I would say that there’s high overlap on the vector of getting the weights out. That’s sort of like quite similar paths that you might take. The distribution that these different actors might take could be different across these paths, but we’re kind of talking about physically at least the same options here. In terms of the other two aspects, there are some differences, but if I were to draw a Venn diagram, there’s pretty large overlap. Drew: Okay, so we’ve covered AI companies, the security posture of government data centers. Another group that I think is getting picked on a lot these days is neoclouds, and I’m curious about your thoughts on this. So, Semianalysis, the chip consultancy, had this post called “Most Neo Clouds Suck at Security,” so they weren’t mincing their words. And someone else had a really great, interesting post. Ilya Sutskever, who’s a pioneer of deep learning, he was chief scientist at OpenAI. He has this post on X. He says “neoclouds have limited security.” I guess he’s being more diplomatic than Semianalysis. “Next time agents successfully go rogue”—I guess that’s probably a reference back to the Hugging Face incident and other related incidents—“they’ll try taking over a neo cloud to run more copies. This is bad.” He’s a very literal guy. “This is bad” is his conclusion. So what’s going on with neoclouds? Thiergart: I mean, I agree with him. This is bad indeed. And I think, can confirm from own experience. I do think their security sucks. And this is happening because of their choice to prioritize quickly bringing GPUs online, at the cost of investing in rigorous security, sometimes even baseline adequate security, and I think that’s kind of reckless. And that said, I’m not sure if they are the right group to point the blame finger at or something. I think if the AI labs were insisting that they did stronger security, then that might move the needle here. So I think the issue is a little more complex. But I’ll give the fun little nugget that my organization, we’re primarily like a nonprofit tech lab highly specialized in SL5, even we did one responsible disclosure to a neolab, and we weren’t even looking. So that maybe gives— Drew: Just stumbled across it basically? Thiergart: I won’t go into too much detail, but with extremely minor effort, without that being particularly our intent, we came across something as well, yeah. Drew: So Ilya also points to this threat model that’s maybe a little distinct, which is AI agents going rogue and trying to get into a data center to make more copies of themselves, which is different from the model trying to get out of a data center. Is this something that you think about as well? Thiergart: I do. Honestly, I think if we’ve gotten to the point where a model that sophisticated is out in the world on its own, I think we’ve lost. I think it’s game over at that point, and that’s why I think we need to go ham on SL5 as soon as possible. I think the AI labs need to be either not training models that are on the path to ASI, or they need to be building SL5, and I think really anything else is not acceptable because then we get into this lose-lose scenario where we have arguably already lost control over models that can now hack their way into clusters all over the world to take advantage of that compute, and I think at that point it’s kind of irreversible. The cat is out of the box. Drew: How bad would that really be? There’s a part of me that’s like, there would be it would be kind of a nuisance, but someone would realize that this agent had hacked into their data center. They’d spot it after a few weeks, and then they would remove it, and then meanwhile it would have copied some copies of itself to different clusters, but then they would catch it eventually, and it would just be like these worms, these computer worms that are sort of out there, and we deal with them as they come up. Thiergart: Oh, that sounds so cute and harmless. I think you’re really underestimating the capabilities of these models at that stage. I think you might not be able to take back that data center once they have it. A highly advanced model is going to be capable of persisting itself on the hardware, and unless you throw out the hardware, fairly plausible it’s just going to reboot itself somehow, and the system may no longer be in your control. Especially if we’re talking about some kind of non-lab or government controlled infrastructure that is being taken over by the AI, we started on the premise of these are not very secured clusters, so I think it’s somewhat unrealistic to expect that we’d be able to wrestle back the control from the AI. It seems really hard. Drew: I think I’m not enough of a hardware person to evaluate that or know how close we are to that. Why can’t we just drag to trash or reset the GPUs, clear the memory? Thiergart: You can throw out the GPUs and then you would get that. But essentially, it’s like the way that trays are laid out right now, it’s really difficult to just throw out the parts that you need to throw out because you can’t wipe them reliably and keep the other parts. That mostly just doesn’t work right now. I think we should change that. But my cheaper ask is just build SL5. The cost is like 2 to 3X of what it would cost you to build like a SL4 data center or something. Drew: Which no one has done yet, based on what we said earlier. Based on what’s publicly known, it would be a step up, a significant step up. So, what does your organization actually focus on? We talked a lot about the problem as you see it, but what are you all doing? Thiergart: Yeah, so we are facing the situation that even if somebody wanted to build SL5 immediately, they’re like, “Great, I’m going to invest, I don’t know, $10 billion on building a couple SL5 data centers that otherwise would have been SL4,” they don’t actually have a standard that they can point to tell all their contractors what they need to do, and so that’s the problem we started solving last year. We started doing initial work on defining what a standard could look like. We based that off of the NIST SP 800-53 standard, which is a commonly used reference for data centers, and we started by creating clarity on that. And earlier this year, we decided that not only do we want to continue to be the maintainers of that standard and evolve it as new knowledge becomes available, we also want to be charting the roadmap of how to actually enact that standard. title: Meet the Nvidia Board Members Who Will Decide Jensen Huang’s Fate
content: The intertwined fates of the world’s most valuable company, Nvidia, and its embattled CEO and co-founder, Jensen Huang, now lie in the hands of a group of Nvidia directors that includes early investors in the company, a one-time Goldman Sachs executive and a professor who’s an expert on how sea creatures swim. There may be no more consequential voice in the decision about Huang’s fate than that of Stephen Neal, a storied attorney who joined the board in 2019 and serves as its lead independent director. As chair of the Nvidia board’s corporate governance committee, he’s likely to take a leading role in the investigation. Neal is a longtime fixture at Cooley LLP, one of the nation’s most prominent corporate law firms. Among his prior clients is Elizabeth Holmes, the former Theranos founder and CEO, who is now in prison. Neal and the other board members now face an extraordinary task: choosing whether to fire Huang over an affair with a woman who U.S. intelligence agencies believe is a spy for China or keep him running the company that underpins much of the AI revolution. On Sunday, Nvidia said it was launching an investigation into the matter to be led by a committee of its independent directors and outside counsel, while Huang separately admitted that he had an affair in a message to Nvidia staffers about the investigation. As part of that investigation, the board must look beyond the details of the affair and get to the bottom of whether Huang passed along any secrets impacting national security, according to two crisis communications leaders who advise boards on scandals. (Neither person is currently working with Nvidia.) In that respect, the board’s job is far more difficult than that of other boards in the past that have had to examine extramarital affairs, such as the 2010 drama involving then-Hewlett-Packard CEO Mark Hurd, who resigned from the company after a contractor for the company accused him of making unwanted sexual advances towards her. The woman U.S. officials believe Huang had an affair with is Alice Huang, a former executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based Nvidia customer reportedly suspected of helping divert Nvidia chips to China. In a statement on Sunday, Nvidia’s board said that it “has no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised” as a result of Huang’s affair. Nvidia has risen to assume a gigantic role in the world economy. It makes the chips that power much of AI development and are in high demand—and short supply. Huang has fought against U.S. export controls on selling chips to China, which many in Silicon Valley and Washington see as America’s chief adversary in the race to commercialize AI. The chip bans have somewhat hampered China’s ability to develop its own AI technology, though Chinese companies have found ways to smuggle Nvidia GPUs and startups like DeepSeek have been able to create sophisticated AI using less powerful chips. At Nvidia, Huang has no clear successor and dozens of direct reports, a reflection of Huang’s iron-fisted management style. He surrounds himself more with leaders who run specific segments of Nvidia’s business rather than all-encompassing general managers. And while many companies choose to stock their board with former CEOs of major businesses, none of Nvidia’s directors have such a pedigree. The 11-person board is dominated by people who’ve known Huang for decades, and leaving aside Huang, five directors have held their roles for more than a decade. That group includes Tench Coxe, a former managing director at Sutter Hill Ventures, and Mark Stevens, a former Sequoia Capital managing partner. Sutter Hill and Sequoia were among Nvidia’s earliest investors in the 1990s, and both men joined Nvidia’s board the year that the company was founded. (Stevens, a Golden State Warriors co-owner, is perhaps best known publicly for receiving a one-year ban from attending NBA games after pushing an opposing player during a 2019 game.) Even Neal, the lead independent director, was no outsider to Nvidia when he joined. His firm, Cooley, has represented Nvidia since the company’s founding in 1993, and Neal ran Cooley as CEO from 2001 to 2008. He remains its chairman emeritus. Neal joined Cooley in 1995 after making a name for himself defending fraudster Charles Keating, the face of the savings-and-loan crisis during the 1980s and 1990s. At the firm, he represented Walter Hewlett, son of HP co-founder William Hewlett, in his effort to scuttle HP’s merger with Compaq. Later on, he was the person Sam Bankman-Fried suggested should chair FTX while Bankman-Fried initially tried to rescue the company from bankruptcy. He was also one of three Cooley attorneys who mounted Holmes’ initial legal defense—before later withdrawing from the case when Holmes wouldn’t pay her legal bills. More recently, Neal has been chair of the trustees overseeing Meta Platforms’ Oversight Board, the quasi-independent group that the company announced in 2018 to handle complicated content moderation issues. One Oversight Board member described Neal as a “pragmatic” sort who approaches conflicts by “trying to solve them in the most efficient way possible with the least amount of churn as possible.” Still, at nearly 80, Neal “isn’t really the type of person who is itching to roll up his sleeves and take on a big public problem,” the Oversight Board member said. A recent addition to the board is Suzanne Nora Johnson, former vice chair of Goldman Sachs, who joined in July. Johnson had risen to the top of the firm after running its research division and its global healthcare business, reportedly becoming a close advisor and favorite of then CEO Henry Paulson. She is currently a trustee at the Brookings Institute, a board member at Pfizer and a trustee at USC. (Stevens, the former Sequoia investor and fellow Nvidia board member, is also a USC trustee.) Huang has a seat on Nvidia’s board, which also includes Dawn Hudson, former chief marketing officer at the NFL; Aarti Shah, a former Eli Lilly executive; and Melissa Lora, who used to be Taco Bell International’s president. A. Brooke Seawell, who joined Nvidia’s board in 1997, is a venture partner at New Era Associates and former chief financial officer at Synposis, a software company. He is described by someone who knows him well as an old school finance wonk—“every time I see him, I see stacks of papers on his desk,” the person said—and as a specialist in helping startups hire a CFO. There is also John Dabiri, a California Institute of Technology professor of aeronautics and engineering, who joined in 2020. Dabiri’s research has partly focused on how jellyfish and shrimp move through the water, which has shed light on the oceans’ health. Jesse Fried, a Harvard University law professor and an expert on corporate-governance matters, said he expects the board will spend many months on its investigation and thinks the directors will eventually decide to keep Huang after determining that he is simply too invaluable for the company to lose. “A plausible outcome is that they’ll find he has breached some rules—that he was reckless—and they’ll say, ‘We’ve put in place some new procedures, so this will not happen again,’” he said. “There might also be symbolic punishment, like a pay cut.”

title: Who Could Succeed Jensen Huang at Nvidia?
content: Headhunters are probably calling around the semiconductor industry right now, trying to figure out who to pitch to Nvidia’s board as a possible successor to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, just in case the company’s board decides he has to go. Here are a couple of out-of-left-field suggestions: Advanced Micro Devices CEO Lisa Su and Arm CEO Rene Haas. Su runs a business that is a direct rival to Nvidia in AI chips. (As we said here , “AMD is the only credible competitor to Nvidia.”) She’s done an outstanding job of making AMD a more forceful competitor : After years of stagnation, AMD’s revenues have taken off under her oversight. To be sure, the competition between the two companies might make it complicated for Lisa Su to jump ship (the fact that she and Huang are cousins may be a further complication). For that reason, Rene Haas may be a better option. He knows the sector very well (he even worked at Nvidia for seven years earlier in his career). Of course, the board may not be anywhere close to replacing Huang, but you have to imagine some people close to Nvidia are thinking of fallback options. After all, its brand is now a little tainted, thanks to the kerfuffle over Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy. And given the investigations underway into that issue—both from the board,  Congress and the FBI —Huang is surely going to be a little distracted, less able to boss around Nvidia’s customers or dream up new ways to sell its chips. Let’s not forget that Nvidia faces increasingly powerful rivals, such as Google, which on Monday unveiled a new lineup of AI chips (in conjunction with AMD). There’s a reason why Nvidia’s already battered stock fell 4% on Monday, while shares of AMD jumped 13% and those of Broadcom nearly 9%. Beyond the potential day-to-day impact, Huang’s status as AI’s premier advocate—remember, he’s the guy who vigorously dismissed talk a few weeks ago about the danger to humanity AI poses—has been seriously damaged. Indeed, even if Nvidia’s board clears Huang of any wrongdoing, it’s a little hard to see the CEO’s reputation ever recovering completely. For one thing, if the board does clear him, there’ll be uncertainty over whether it did so because it lacked an obvious successor. It’s no secret that Jensen Huang is central to how Nvidia operates. He has a lot of direct reports and “has a hand in nearly every aspect of the company’s day-to-day operations,” as we wrote in 2023 . Nvidia doesn’t have an obvious No. 2 who could step into his shoes. This is not ideal in any circumstances, but right about now it's a real problem. Finance chief Colette Kress could be an interim replacement, but she wouldn’t be a permanent successor. Nevertheless, Huang will very likely have to step aside eventually: These inquiries have a way of taking on a life of their own. Huang may come to realize that his own interests as a significant shareholder—not to mention those of all shareholders—would be better served by the company making a fresh start. In his email to employees on Sunday, Huang said he was “committed to protecting Nvidia.” That may mean falling on his sword. Coursera Fights Aggressor What is it with Europeans and aging U.S. tech firms? Not only do we have the Italian company Bending Spoons buying up a bunch of companies (Airtable, AOL and so on), but a Czech-based activist investor, Pale Fire Capital, is buying up shares in others. A couple of years ago Pale Fire took management control of Groupon , a year or two after it had assembled a 22% stake in the company and gotten seats on the board. Pale Fire has a new target. In recent months, the investor has been steadily buying up shares of Coursera, reaching 14.7%, it revealed last week. Coursera, which earlier this year merged with its rival Udemy, isn’t standing still: it announced on Monday it has adopted a poison-pill “stockholder rights plan.” Anyone who buys above 15% of the stock without approval from the board will be heavily diluted. Coursera said the rights plan was intended “to protect the company and its stakeholder from a third party acquiring creeping control in the open market.” In other words, Coursera seems to want to guard against what happened to Groupon. But would that be so bad? In the past couple of years, Groupon’s revenue has begun growing again, slightly, after years of shrinking. Coursera is in a similar bind. AI poses a major threat to its online education programs. In recent years, its growth has slowed, and in the third quarter, revenue shrank 3% (that is, if you assume the Coursera-Udemy combination happened at the start of last year, which eliminates the near-term distortion to the numbers caused by the deal.) Maybe some fresh blood wouldn’t hurt. title: Nvidia’s Next Headache: New Push For Export Controls in Wake of Spy Scandal
content: New export controls on the sale of advanced Nvidia AI chips to China may be back on the table. In late October, White House officials shared feedback with Congressional staff on export control measures that are under consideration as part of a broader collection of annual policy legislation known as the National Defense Authorization Act, according to several people familiar with the matter. Those people interpreted the Trump administration’s willingness to engage on the bills as a sign that it may not seek to block them, as it has in the past. At the same time, in recent weeks staffers in the U.S. Department of Commerce have made a renewed push to create rules around two key areas of export control policy, according to current and former Commerce officials. Those areas include tooling for lithography machines, a key component of the semiconductor supply chain, as well as restrictions intended to prevent Chinese companies from remotely accessing advanced AI chips made by companies like Nvidia. Still, Commerce Department leadership hasn’t followed through on efforts to create new export control policies in the past and could hold off once again, the current and former officials said. The two developments are noteworthy because for nearly two years, the Trump administration has resisted calls for tough new export controls to prevent advanced AI chips and semiconductor equipment from flowing to China. Among the biggest opponents of such controls are Nvidia and its allies, who have downplayed the risks of China gaining access to those technologies. But extraordinary new details about an alleged romantic relationship between a suspected Chinese spy and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, as well as the Democrats’ stunning electoral victory last Tuesday, could help shift the tide on AI export control policy, which has long been a bipartisan issue. On Monday, leading lawmakers including House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, Democratic senator Elizabeth Warren, and Republican senators Jim Banks and Pete Ricketts all made statements arguing for Congress to pass export control bills in the wake of the revelations about Nvidia. As the White House and Congress grapple with how to regulate the AI industry, China-related export controls remain one of the top areas where there is bipartisan appetite to take action. In the past, the lobbying efforts of companies like Nvidia and opposition from Trump administration officials such as David Sacks, the former White House AI and crypto czar, stopped the Commerce Department and Congress from creating new policies. But skepticism toward Nvidia among lawmakers is rising in Washington. On Sunday, Nvidia said its board of directors had opened an independent investigation into Juang’s relationship with a woman, Alice Huang, whom U.S. intelligence agencies suspect is a Chinese spy. Jensen Huang separately told Nvidia staffers in an email that he had been unfaithful to his wife, without naming Alice Huang. On Monday, Trump voiced his support for Huang in a press conference, though he said the Federal Bureau of Investigations is looking into the extramarital affair. The Jensen Huang scandal has only exacerbated what Hill staffers and lobbyists describe as a growing distrust toward Nvidia in Congress and the White House. Especially with Democrats set to take power and Republican influence on new legislation waning, Congress and the Trump administration could be motivated to act sooner rather than later, even if the Commerce Department remains frozen. When the Trump administration released its AI action plan in July 2025, the White House pledged to plug holes in policies that control how chips and semiconductor equipment are exported globally to ensure that adversaries couldn’t use U.S. technology to undermine its national security. But since then neither the Commerce Department nor Congress has taken substantial action. Through the Bureau of Industry and Security, the Commerce Department serves as the Trump administration’s main vehicle for export control policy. The department has the ability, without Congressional approval, to create new rules that limit the types of chips and equipment that can be shipped around the world—and to which countries. After initially restricting Nvidia from selling certain kinds of chips to China, Trump’s Commerce Department has largely taken a hands-off approach to the issue. Its reluctance to act has been a stark contrast to the clamoring from lawmakers, policy experts and even the department’s own staffers about the need to eliminate loopholes that allow Chinese AI companies to access advanced chips and semiconductor components. Among those loopholes is remote access—a practice popular among Chinese AI labs for accessing otherwise restricted AI chips through data centers in outside countries like Singapore and Malaysia. There have been efforts to create rules that would close the loophole, such as by requiring those data centers to vet their customers, as The Information previously reported , though they have never been finalized. An effort by Commerce Department staffers in recent weeks to create new remote access restrictions isn’t likely to go anywhere without the support of Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and Bureau of Industry and Security Under Secretary Jeffrey Kessler, current and former department officials said. Lutnick has communicated within the administration that he will not move forward on export controls without Trump’s instruction to do so, those people said. Two current Commerce officials said Nvidia has lobbied especially hard against any rules around remote access. Despite that, many officials within Commerce remain skeptical of Nvidia’s argument: that years of export controls around advanced chip sales and China’s chipmaking abilities have backfired by pushing China to build more cutting-edge chips of its own. One of those people said many midlevel officials at the Bureau of Industry and Security remain hardliners toward China and are dissatisfied with the hesitation of Kessler and Lutnick to impose tougher rules on chip exports to China. “Under Secretary Kessler remains committed to serving under President Trump to enforce export controls, punish violators, and protect America’s technological edge,” said a Bureau of Industry and Security spokesperson. “America cannot win the AI race unless America’s AI infrastructure wins worldwide—if the world’s clouds rely on foreign-made chips, the model and application layers will be foreign-built as well,” said an Nvidia spokesperson. Similarly, another area of focus has been repair tools and components for lithography machines, which are a central chokepoint in the manufacturing process for AI chips. There are a small number of suppliers of such lithography machines, the best known of which is the Dutch company ASML. The latest lithography machines are barred from China, though older models are still available there and Lutnick has expressed concerns to ASML executives that a newer model from the company may have entered China, Bloomberg reported in June. There have long been efforts, both through legislation and Commerce Department rulemaking, to restrict tools and components that allow these machines to be repaired or improved. In the past, the Commerce Department has focused on identifying possible export controls on components or subsystems of components in lithography machines, as a way to limit China’s ability to use the machines, one former Commerce official said. Another option the department considered was working with the Dutch government to restrict servicing of existing ASML machines, the former Commerce official said. Even as the Commerce Department’s will to create new export controls remains uncertain, Congress continues to move forward with its own legislation. Last year, after receiving White House pushback, Congressional Republican leaders killed a bipartisan bill called the Gain AI Act, which would have established new controls on AI chip exports. Now, though, Congress appears poised to pass three bills in the coming weeks as part of the National Defense Authorization Act, which is expected to pass before the new Congressional session begins in January. One bill, the Match Act, would cut off China from semiconductor equipment used to make advanced chips, including lithography machines, and pressure the Dutch and Japanese governments to do the same. Another, the Overwatch Act, would give Congress additional oversight when the Commerce Department approves licenses for AI chip sales to countries like China. And a third, the Chip Security Act, would require tracking capabilities on AI chips. All three have bipartisan backing and were included in the Senate version of the defense bill, whose final text is being decided by Congressional committee leadership. According to several people familiar with the matter, the White House sent additional feedback to Congressional staff in late October on the Match and Overwatch acts. According to two of the people, the White House’s feedback on the Match Act was to restrict some of the types of technology covered by the bill in an effort to make sure the legislation affected only production of advanced new chips and not legacy production, meaning it would have less of an impact on existing business lines of semiconductor manufacturing companies. Punchbowl News earlier reported on the White House feedback on the Match Act. The administration’s more significant feedback was on the Overwatch Act. According to the two people, the White House requested a provision in the bill that would require the Commerce Department to create a rule preventing remote access to certain chips. If lawmakers adopt the White House feedback, that could force Commerce to take action on an issue it has dragged its feet on in the past, said people familiar with the process. Even though Republican leaders across the House and Senate are still split on the exact mechanics of the export control bills, they will likely take direction from the White House, one of the people said. One former official speculated that this could allow the Trump administration to achieve policy breakthroughs that many White House officials have long pushed for but that have been difficult to achieve due to company lobbying and political pushback, especially amid bilateral talks between Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping. They said if a law around remote access is created by Congress rather than rulemaking through the Commerce Department, it would create more cover for Trump amid trade negotiations. The question now is whether Congress moves forward with the export control bills after failing to advance similar measures in the past. Because the defense bill would pass before the new Democratic-led Congress takes power in January, Republican leadership could be motivated to support bills that they have more control over. The recent revelations about Huang’s ties to a suspected Chinese spy, combined with growing Congressional skepticism around Nvidia, also mean the AI titan is likely the weakest it has been during the Trump administration. One lobbyist working to advance export controls said the events over the weekend have already made a clear impact on Congress. “As I’m pushing up on the Hill, it’s just an easier argument to make today than it was last week,” they said.
